children.title: Independent-Set View
children.top_down_role: Independence-system presentation of finite matroids.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((E,\mathcal I)\) is a matroid precisely when \(\mathcal I\) satisfies the three independence axioms.

notation.meaning: family of independent subsets of the ground set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-matroid independence-axiom view.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 5. Elements of matroid theory p. 172

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A family \(\mathcal I\subseteq 2^E\) is the independent-set family of a matroid on \(E\) if: \(\varnothing\in\mathcal I\); whenever \(I\in\mathcal I\) and \(J\subseteq I\), one has \(J\in\mathcal I\); and whenever \(I,J\in\mathcal I\) with \(|I|<|J|\), there exists \(e\in J\setminus I\) such that \(I\cup\{e\}\in\mathcal I\). Members of \(\mathcal I\) are called independent sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite matroid is specified by a nonempty hereditary family satisfying augmentation: a smaller independent set can acquire an element from any larger independent set.
knowledge_statements.title: Independent-Set View

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 5. Elements of matroid theory p. 172

children.title: Dependent-Set View
children.top_down_role: Dependence-system presentation complementary to the independent-set perspective.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal D=2^E\setminus\mathcal I\), and \(X\in\mathcal D\) exactly when \(X\) is not independent.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dependence as the complement of independence in \(2^E\).

source_refs.locator: Chapter 5. Elements of matroid theory p. 172

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The dependent-set family is \(\mathcal D:=2^E\setminus\mathcal I\). Thus \(D\subseteq E\) is dependent exactly when \(D\notin\mathcal I\). Equivalently, \(\mathcal D\) is upward closed: if \(D\in\mathcal D\) and \(D\subseteq X\subseteq E\), then \(X\in\mathcal D\). Moreover, every \(D\in\mathcal D\) contains an inclusion-minimal member of \(\mathcal D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dependent sets are exactly the nonindependent subsets. They are closed under taking supersets, and every dependent set contains an inclusion-minimal dependent set.
knowledge_statements.title: Dependent-Set View

children.title: Set-View Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Structural translation between independent-set data and dependent-set data.

knowledge_statements.title: Set-View Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complement correspondence between independent and dependent subsets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(\mathcal D:=2^E\setminus\mathcal I\). Then, for every \(X\subseteq E\), \[X\in\mathcal I\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad X\notin\mathcal D.\] Conversely, starting from this dependent-set family and defining \(\mathcal I':=2^E\setminus\mathcal D\) recovers \(\mathcal I'=\mathcal I\). Hence the independent-set and dependent-set views contain exactly the same set-system data.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independent and dependent subsets partition the power set, so taking complements converts either representation into the other without losing information.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal I\subseteq 2^E\) satisfies the matroid independence axioms.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal D=2^E\setminus\mathcal I\) and \(\mathcal I=2^E\setminus\mathcal D\), so either family uniquely determines the other.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 5. Elements of matroid theory p. 172

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A nonempty family \(\mathcal B\subseteq 2^E\) is a matroid basis family if, for all \(B_1,B_2\in\mathcal B\) and every \(x\in B_1\setminus B_2\), there exists \(y\in B_2\setminus B_1\) such that \((B_1\setminus\{x\})\cup\{y\}\in\mathcal B\). The members of \(\mathcal B\) are called bases; the exchange axiom implies that all of them have the same cardinality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty collection is a matroid basis family when any element exclusive to one basis can be exchanged for a suitable element exclusive to another basis.
knowledge_statements.title: Basis Families

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Direct-sum representation of bases compatible with a nested chain
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes bases of T_ell that induce bases on every set in a nested chain as bases of T_ell in a direct sum of contraction–deletion minors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let M be a matroid on S and let \varnothing=T_0\subseteq T_1\subseteq\cdots\subseteq T_{\ell+1}=S. For 0\leq i\leq\ell, define N_i=(M/T_i)\setminus\overline{T}_{i+1}, where \overline{T}_{i+1}=S\setminus T_{i+1}, and let N=N_0\oplus\cdots\oplus N_\ell. Then the bases K of T_\ell in M satisfying that K\cap T_i is a basis of T_i in M for every 1\leq i\leq\ell are exactly the bases of T_\ell in N.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given a nested chain from the empty set to the ground set, the bases of T_ell that restrict to a basis on every earlier member of the chain are exactly the bases of T_ell in the direct sum of the corresponding contraction–deletion minors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{K:K\text{ is a basis of }T_\ell\text{ in }M,\ K\cap T_i\text{ is a basis of }T_i\text{ in }M\ \forall i=1,\ldots,\ell\}=\{K:K\text{ is a basis of }T_\ell\text{ in }N\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Basis-axiom characterization of matroids
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence between the basis-family and independence-family presentations of a matroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The family \mathcal B(M) of bases of every matroid M satisfies (B1) and (B2). Conversely, if \mathcal B\subseteq 2^S satisfies (B1) and (B2), then \mathcal F:=\{F\subseteq S:\exists B\in\mathcal B,\ F\subseteq B\} satisfies the matroid independence axioms.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The bases of every matroid satisfy the basis axioms. Conversely, any set family satisfying those axioms generates a matroid whose independent sets are precisely the subsets of members of that family.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal B(M)\text{ satisfies (B1),(B2)},\qquad \mathcal F=\{F:\exists B\in\mathcal B,\ F\subseteq B\}\text{ satisfies the independence axioms}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Basis and Rank of a Subset in a Matroid
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines bases and rank for every subset of the ground set, including the usual abbreviation for bases of the whole matroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M=(S,\mathcal I)\) be a matroid and \(A\subseteq S\). A basis of \(A\) is a maximal independent subset of \(A\). All bases of \(A\) have the same cardinality, and this cardinality is the rank \(r(A)\). Bases of \(S\) are called bases of \(M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A basis of a subset is a maximal independent subset; its common cardinality is the subset's rank. Bases of the ground set are the bases of the matroid.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: r(A)=|B|\text{ for every basis }B\text{ of }A,\quad\text{and bases of }M\text{ are the bases of }S.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bases and rank of a matroid
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Foundational basis and rank definitions for a matroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let M=(S,\mathcal F) be a matroid. A set B\in\mathcal F is a basis if it is maximal under inclusion in \mathcal F. All bases have the same cardinality, called the rank r(M) of M. Moreover, the family of bases uniquely determines M.

children.title: Maximal Independent Sets
children.top_down_role: Maximal members of the independent-set system.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B\) is maximal independent exactly when \(B\in\mathcal I\) and \(B\cup\{e\}\notin\mathcal I\) for every \(e\in E\setminus B\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A set \(B\subseteq E\) is a maximal independent set if \(B\in\mathcal I\) and no strict superset of \(B\) belongs to \(\mathcal I\). By heredity, this is equivalent to the one-element condition \[B\in\mathcal I\quad\text{and}\quad B\cup\{e\}\notin\mathcal I\ \text{ for every }e\in E\setminus B.\] Maximality here is by inclusion, not merely maximal cardinality among a separately specified subfamily.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A maximal independent set is independent but ceases to be independent after adding any ground-set element outside it.
knowledge_statements.title: Maximal Independent Sets

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Independence Systems, Circuits, and Bases
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines an independence system and its basic inclusion-minimal and inclusion-maximal set classes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A set system $(E,\mathcal F)$ is an independence system if $\varnothing\in\mathcal F$ and, for all $X\subseteq Y\in\mathcal F$, one has $X\in\mathcal F$. Members of $\mathcal F$ are independent and members of $2^E\setminus\mathcal F$ are dependent. Inclusion-minimal dependent sets are circuits, inclusion-maximal independent sets are bases, and for $X\subseteq E$, a basis of $X$ is an inclusion-maximal member of $\{Y\in\mathcal F:Y\subseteq X\}$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An independence system is a hereditary family of subsets containing the empty set. Its members are independent; the other subsets are dependent. Circuits are minimal dependent sets, bases are maximal independent sets, and bases of a subset X are its maximal independent subsets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \varnothing\in\mathcal F\quad\text{and}\quad (X\subseteq Y\in\mathcal F\Rightarrow X\in\mathcal F),\quad\text{with circuits and bases defined by inclusion minimality and maximality.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Matroids, representations, and basic independence terminology
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Foundational independence-axiom definition and the associated linear, graphic, rank, circuit, and closure notions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A matroid is a pair $M=(E,\mathcal I)$, where $E$ is finite and $\mathcal I\subseteq 2^E$ satisfies $\varnothing\in\mathcal I$, heredity ($J\subseteq I\in\mathcal I\Rightarrow J\in\mathcal I$), and augmentation: if $I_p,I_{p+1}\in\mathcal I$ with $|I_p|=p$ and $|I_{p+1}|=p+1$, then some $e\in I_{p+1}\setminus I_p$ satisfies $I_p\cup\{e\}\in\mathcal I$. Members of $\mathcal I$ are independent; maximal independent sets are bases; $r(A)$ is the common cardinality of the maximal independent subsets of $A\subseteq E$; minimal dependent sets are circuits; $\operatorname{sp}(A)$ is the maximal superset of $A$ having rank $r(A)$; and $A$ is closed when $A=\operatorname{sp}(A)$. A matrix represents the matroid whose independent sets are its linearly independent column subsets. For a graph $G$, the binary node-arc incidence representation yields the graphic matroid, whose independent sets are exactly the cycle-free edge sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matroid is a finite ground set with a hereditary family of independent sets satisfying the augmentation axiom. Its maximal independent sets are bases, rank is the common size of maximal independent subsets, circuits are minimal dependent sets, span is the maximal rank-preserving superset, and closed sets equal their span. Matrices define representable matroids through column independence; a graph's binary incidence representation gives the graphic matroid, whose independent sets are forests.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (E,\mathcal I)\text{ is a matroid precisely under the stated independence axioms, with the stated induced notions and representations.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Independent Sets in a Matroid Contraction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes contraction independence using either every or some maximal independent subset of the contracted set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $M$ be a matroid on $S$, let $Z\subseteq S$, set $S':=S\setminus Z$, and let $M'=M/Z$. For every $F\subseteq S'$, the following are equivalent: (i) $F$ is independent in $M'$; (ii) for every inclusion-maximal independent subset $I\subseteq Z$ of $M$, $I\cup F$ is independent in $M$; (iii) there exists an inclusion-maximal independent subset $I\subseteq Z$ of $M$ such that $I\cup F$ is independent in $M$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A subset F of the retained ground set is independent after contracting Z exactly when adjoining F to every maximal independent subset of Z remains independent in M; equivalently, it is enough that this holds for one such maximal independent subset.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\in\mathcal I(M')\iff \bigl(\forall I\subseteq Z\text{ maximal independent in }M,\ I\cup F\in\mathcal I(M)\bigr)\iff \bigl(\exists I\subseteq Z\text{ maximal independent in }M,\ I\cup F\in\mathcal I(M)\bigr)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Matroid rank, bases, and recovery from bases
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines rank and bases and records the basis representation of the independence family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $M=(E,\mathcal I)$ be a matroid and $A\subseteq E$. The rank $r(A)$ is the common cardinality of the inclusion-maximal independent subsets of $A$. knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: r(A)=|I|\ \text{for every maximal independent }I\subseteq A,\qquad \mathcal I=\{I:\exists B\in\mathcal B,\ I\subseteq B\}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Matroid Bases as Maximal Independent Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines bases through inclusion-maximal independence, states their equicardinality, and formulates the minimum-weight basis problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $(E,\mathcal I)$ be a matroid. An independent set $I\in\mathcal I$ is maximal if $I\cup\{e\}\notin\mathcal I$ for every $e\in E\setminus I$. Every maximal independent set has the same cardinality, and the maximal independent sets are called bases. Given element weights $w:E\to\mathbb R$, the matroid optimization problem is $\min\{\sum_{e\in B}w(e):B\text{ is a basis}\}$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A maximal independent set cannot be enlarged by another ground-set element while preserving independence. In a matroid, all maximal independent sets have equal size and are called bases; minimum-weight matroid optimization seeks a basis of least total weight.
assumptions_latex: w:E\to\mathbb R\text{ for the optimization formulation}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: I\text{ is a basis}\iff I\in\mathcal I\ \land\ \forall e\in E\setminus I,\ I\cup\{e\}\notin\mathcal I;\qquad \min_{B\text{ basis}}\sum_{e\in B}w(e)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bijective basis exchange theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An elementwise exchange bijection between two matroid bases.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For any bases $B_1$ and $B_2$ of a matroid, there exists a bijection $f:B_1\setminus B_2\to B_2\setminus B_1$ such that $B_1-x+f(x)$ is a basis for every $x\in B_1\setminus B_2$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For any two matroid bases B1 and B2, there is a bijection from B1 minus B2 to B2 minus B1 such that replacing each x in B1 minus B2 by its image produces a basis.
assumptions_latex: $B_1$ and $B_2$ are bases of a matroid.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: $\exists$ a bijection $f:B_1\setminus B_2\to B_2\setminus B_1$ such that $B_1-x+f(x)$ is a basis for every $x\in B_1\setminus B_2$.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Relabeled basis representation for a Δ_X-exchange
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes bases after identifying the transformed matroid's ground set with E(M).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \Delta_X(M) be obtained from M by a \Delta_X-exchange and relabeled to have ground set E(M), where X=\{x_1,\ldots,x_n\}. Its bases are exactly the sets of one of the following forms: (i) X\cup Y', where Y' is a basis of M/X; (ii) (X-\{x_i\})\cup Y'' for some 1\le i\le n, where Y'' is a basis of M/x_i\setminus(X-\{x_i\}); or (iii) (X-\{x_i,x_j\})\cup Y''' for some 1\le i<j\le n, where Y''' is a basis of M\setminus X.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After the Δ_X-exchanged matroid is relabeled onto the original ground set, every basis consists of all of X plus a basis of M/X, all but one element of X plus a basis of the corresponding contraction-deletion minor, or all but two elements of X plus a basis of M with X deleted; every set of these forms is a basis.
assumptions_latex: \Delta_X(M)\text{ is obtained from }M\text{ by a defined }\Delta_X\text{-exchange}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lower and upper partition quotas for matroid bases
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basis-feasibility criteria under blockwise quotas; \(\widetilde f\), \(\widetilde g\), and \(\mathcal T^*\) retain their surrounding definitions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal T\) partition \(S\), let \(f,g:\mathcal T\to\mathbb Z_+\) satisfy \(f(X)\le g(X)\le |X|\) for every \(X\in\mathcal T\), and let \(M\) be a matroid on \(S\) with rank \(r\) and corank \(t\). Then:
\[
\exists B\text{ basis}:|B\cap X|\le g(X)\ \forall X\in\mathcal T
\iff \widetilde g(Z)\ge t(Z)\ \forall Z\in\mathcal T^*,
\]
equivalently \(\widetilde g(Z)+r(S-Z)\ge r(S)\) for every \(Z\in\mathcal T^*\);
\[
\exists B\text{ basis}:|B\cap X|\ge f(X)\ \forall X\in\mathcal T
\iff \widetilde f(Z)\le r(Z)\ \forall Z\in\mathcal T^*.
\]
Moreover, a basis satisfying \(f(X)\le |B\cap X|\le g(X)\) for every block exists if and only if some basis satisfies all upper bounds and some basis satisfies all lower bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For blockwise upper quotas, a feasible matroid basis exists exactly when every relevant union of blocks has enough total upper capacity to cover its corank. For blockwise lower quotas, feasibility is equivalent to every such union having rank at least its total lower requirement. Simultaneous lower and upper quotas are feasible exactly when the upper-bound system and lower-bound system are each feasible, possibly via different witness bases.
assumptions_latex: M\text{ is a matroid on }S\text{ with rank }r\text{ and corank }t
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \begin{aligned}&\exists B\text{ basis}\;\forall X\in\mathcal T:\ |B\cap X|\le g(X)\iff\forall Z\in\mathcal T^*:\widetilde g(Z)\ge t(Z)\iff\forall Z\in\mathcal T^*:\widetilde g(Z)+r(S-Z)\ge r(S),\\&\exists B\text{ basis}\;\forall X\in\mathcal T:\ |B\cap X|\ge f(X)\iff\forall Z\in\mathcal T^*:\widetilde f(Z)\le r(Z),\\&\exists B\text{ basis}\;\forall X\in\mathcal T:\ f(X)\le|B\cap X|\le g(X)\iff(\exists B_g\text{ satisfying all upper bounds})\land(\exists B_f\text{ satisfying all lower bounds}).\end{aligned}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bases of a segment–cosegment exchange
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes the bases before relabeling the complementary set Y as X.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \Delta_X(M)=P_X(\Theta_n,M)\setminus X is defined, with X=\{x_1,\ldots,x_n\} and corresponding Y=\{y_1,\ldots,y_n\}. A set D\subseteq E(\Delta_X(M)) is a basis of \Delta_X(M) iff exactly one of the following forms applies: (i) Y\subseteq D and D-Y is a basis of M/X; (ii) D\cap Y=Y-\{y_i\} for some i, and D-(Y-\{y_i\}) is a basis of M/x_i\setminus(X-\{x_i\}); or (iii) D\cap Y=Y-\{y_i,y_j\} for distinct i,j, and D-(Y-\{y_i,y_j\}) is a basis of M\setminus X.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The bases of the segment–cosegment exchange are precisely those containing all of Y and extending a basis of M/X, those omitting one corresponding element of Y and extending a basis of the indicated contraction-deletion minor, or those omitting two elements of Y and extending a basis of M with X deleted.
assumptions_latex: Y=\{y_1,\ldots,y_n\}\text{ is the corresponding set in }\Theta_n
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: D\in\mathcal B(\Delta_X(M))\iff\begin{cases}Y\subseteq D,\ D-Y\in\mathcal B(M/X),\quad\text{or}\\D\cap Y=Y-\{y_i\},\ D-(Y-\{y_i\})\in\mathcal B(M/x_i\setminus(X-\{x_i\})),\quad\text{or}\\D\cap Y=Y-\{y_i,y_j\},\ D-(Y-\{y_i,y_j\})\in\mathcal B(M\setminus X)\text{ for }i\ne j.\end{cases}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalent circuit characterizations of binary matroids
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The empty symmetric difference is permitted and is the disjoint union of the empty collection of circuits.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a matroid $M$, the following are equivalent: (i) $M$ is binary; (ii) $|C\cap C^*|$ is even for every circuit $C$ and cocircuit $C^*$; (iii) $C_1\triangle C_2$ contains a circuit whenever $C_1,C_2$ are distinct circuits; (iv) $C_1\triangle C_2$ is a disjoint union of circuits for all circuits $C_1,C_2$; (v) the symmetric difference of any set of circuits is empty or contains a circuit; (vi) the symmetric difference of any set of circuits is a disjoint union of circuits, allowing the empty union; (vii) for every basis $B$ and circuit $C$, $C=\bigtriangleup_{e\in C-B}C(e,B)$; (viii) there exists a basis $B$ for which the identity in (vii) holds for every circuit $C$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matroid is binary exactly when it satisfies any of several equivalent properties: even circuit-cocircuit intersections, closure of circuits under symmetric difference into circuits, or representation of each circuit as the symmetric difference of its basis-relative fundamental circuits. Empty symmetric differences are allowed.
assumptions_latex: $C(e,B)$ denotes the fundamental circuit of $e$ with respect to a basis $B$.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Conditions (i)--(viii) are equivalent.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Circuit decomposition under contraction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Describes every circuit contained in an original circuit after contraction, including an excluded-minor bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $C$ be a circuit of a matroid $M$ and let $e\in E(M)\setminus C$. Either $C$ is a circuit of $M/e$, or, for some integer $n>1$, there is a partition $C=X_1\mathbin{\dot\cup}\cdots\mathbin{\dot\cup}X_n$ into nonempty subsets such that $C\setminus X_1,\ldots,C\setminus X_n$ are exactly the circuits of $M/e$ contained in $C$. Moreover, if $M$ has no minor isomorphic to $U_{k,k+2}$, then $n\le k$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After an element outside a circuit is contracted, either the circuit remains a circuit, or it has a nontrivial partition whose part-complements are exactly all circuits of the contraction contained in the original circuit. If M has no U(k,k+2) minor, the number of parts is at most k.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: C\in\mathcal C(M/e)\ \lor\ \exists n>1,\ C=\mathbin{\dot\bigcup}_{i=1}^nX_i,\ X_i\ne\varnothing,\ \{D\in\mathcal C(M/e):D\subseteq C\}=\{C\setminus X_i:1\le i\le n\};\quad M\text{ has no }U_{k,k+2}\text{-minor}\Rightarrow n\le k

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Circuits, Loops, Parallel Elements, and Simple Matroids
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Foundational minimal-dependence definitions and associated local element types.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M=(S,\mathcal I)\) be a matroid. A set \(X\subseteq S\) is a circuit if \(X\notin\mathcal I\) and every proper subset of \(X\) belongs to \(\mathcal I\). A one-element circuit is a loop. The two elements of a two-element circuit are parallel. The matroid is simple if it has neither loops nor parallel elements; a simple matroid is also called a combinatorial geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A circuit is a minimally dependent set. A one-element circuit is a loop, and the elements of a two-element circuit are parallel. A matroid without loops or parallel elements is simple, also called a combinatorial geometry.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: X\text{ is a circuit}\iff X\notin\mathcal I\ \text{and}\ \forall Y\subsetneq X,\ Y\in\mathcal I;\quad M\text{ is simple}\iff M\text{ has no loops or parallel elements}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Circuit Characterizations of a Modular Flat
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Three equivalent conditions for a nonempty subset of a simple matroid to be a modular flat.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\varnothing\ne X\subseteq E(M)\), where \(M\) is simple. The following are equivalent: (i) \(X\) is a modular flat of \(M\); (ii) for every circuit \(C\) with \(C-X\ne\varnothing\), there exists \(x\in X\) such that \((C-X)\cup\{x\}\) is dependent; (iii) for every circuit \(C\) and every \(e\in C-X\), there exist \(f\in X\) and a circuit \(C'\) such that \(e\in C'\subseteq \{f\}\cup(C-X)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonempty subset X of a simple matroid, being a modular flat is equivalent to both the stated dependence condition for every circuit extending outside X and the stated local circuit-witness condition for each circuit element outside X.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Conditions (i), (ii), and (iii) are equivalent}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Construction of a matroid from circuit axioms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Circuit-family cryptomorphism for matroids.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal C\subseteq 2^S\) satisfy the three circuit axioms: \(\varnothing\notin\mathcal C\), no distinct members of \(\mathcal C\) contain one another, and weak circuit elimination. Define \(\mathcal F=\{F\subseteq S: \nexists C\in\mathcal C\text{ with }C\subseteq F\}\). Then \(\mathcal F\) satisfies the matroid independence axioms, and the circuits of \(M=(S,\mathcal F)\) are exactly the members of \(\mathcal C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any set family satisfying the circuit axioms determines a matroid whose independent sets are the subsets containing no circuit from that family, and whose circuits are exactly the given sets.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal C\subseteq 2^S\) satisfies (C1), (C2), and weak circuit elimination (C3).
\(\mathcal F=\{F\subseteq S: \nexists C\in\mathcal C\text{ such that }C\subseteq F\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal F\text{ satisfies the independence axioms and }\operatorname{Circuits}(S,\mathcal F)=\mathcal C.\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Circuit partition induced by a closure element
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Describes all circuits through an external nonloop within a circuit enlarged by that element, including an excluded-minor bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $C$ be a circuit of a matroid $M$ with $|C|\ge 2$, and let $e$ be a nonloop element of $\operatorname{cl}_M(C)\setminus C$. Then, for some integer $n>1$, there is a partition $C=X_1\mathbin{\dot\cup}\cdots\mathbin{\dot\cup}X_n$ into nonempty subsets such that the sets $(C\setminus X_i)\cup\{e\}$ are exactly the circuits of $M$ that contain $e$ and are contained in $C\cup\{e\}$. Moreover, if $M$ has no minor isomorphic to $U_{k,k+2}$, then $n\le k$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If an external nonloop lies in the closure of a circuit, the circuit has a nontrivial partition whose complementary parts, together with that element, are exactly the circuits through the element inside the enlarged circuit. If M has no U(k,k+2) minor, the number of parts is at most k.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists n>1,\ C=\mathbin{\dot\bigcup}_{i=1}^nX_i,\ X_i\ne\varnothing,\ \{D\in\mathcal C(M):e\in D\subseteq C\cup\{e\}\}=\{(C\setminus X_i)\cup\{e\}:1\le i\le n\},\quad M\text{ has no }U_{k,k+2}\text{-minor}\Rightarrow n\le k

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Recovery of Independence from Circuits
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normalizes the corrupted displayed formula and states the result under the finite-ground-set convention needed for uniqueness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $E$ be finite and let $\mathcal C\subseteq 2^E$ satisfy $\varnothing\notin\mathcal C$ and
\[
X,Y\in\mathcal C,\ X\subseteq Y\Longrightarrow X=Y.
\]
Then there is a unique hereditary independence system on $E$ whose circuit family is $\mathcal C$, namely
\[
\mathcal I:=\{X\subseteq E:\nexists C\in\mathcal C\text{ with }C\subseteq X\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a finite ground set, a nonempty-set antichain of proposed circuits uniquely determines an independence system: a set is independent exactly when it contains no circuit.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists!\,\mathcal I\subseteq 2^E\text{ hereditary with circuit family }\mathcal C,\qquad \mathcal I=\{X\subseteq E:\nexists C\in\mathcal C,\ C\subseteq X\}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Circuit characterization and circuit representation of closure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes circuits through elementwise closure dependence and represents closure membership by circuit witnesses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let M be a matroid and X\subseteq E(M). Then X is a circuit if and only if X is an inclusion-minimal nonempty set such that x\in\operatorname{cl}(X\setminus\{x\}) for every x\in X. Moreover, \operatorname{cl}(X)=X\cup\{x\in E(M):\exists C\in\mathcal C(M)\text{ with }x\in C\subseteq X\cup\{x\}\}.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Circuits are exactly the minimal nonempty sets in which every element is spanned by the others; closure consists of the original set together with elements having a circuit witness inside that set plus the element.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: X\in\mathcal C(M)\iff\bigl[X\ne\varnothing,\ X\text{ is inclusion-minimal, and }(\forall x\in X)\ x\in\operatorname{cl}(X\setminus\{x\})\bigr];\quad \operatorname{cl}(X)=X\cup\{x\in E(M):\exists C\in\mathcal C(M),\ x\in C\subseteq X\cup\{x\}\}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dependent sets, circuits, and spans in a matroid
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines three related matroid structures without asserting uniqueness of a span.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $M=(E,\mathcal I)$ be a matroid with rank function $r$. A set $D\subseteq E$ is dependent if $D\notin\mathcal I$. A circuit is an inclusion-minimal dependent subset of $E$. For $A\subseteq E$, a span of $A$ is an inclusion-maximal set $S$ such that $A\subseteq S\subseteq E$ and $r(S)=r(A)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dependent set is a nonindependent subset of the ground set, and a circuit is a minimal dependent set. A span of a set is a maximal superset having the same rank.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Circuits as minimal dependent sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Includes recovery of independent sets from circuits and uniqueness of the circuit representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a matroid \(M\), a circuit is an inclusion-minimal dependent subset of \(E(M)\), and the circuit family is denoted \(\mathcal C(M)\). knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual structural notions for a matroid.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Circuits of an Independence System
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines circuits as inclusion-minimal dependent sets and records conditional loop and graphic-matroid specializations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For an independence system $M=(E(M),\mathcal I(M))$, the dependent sets are $2^{E(M)}\setminus\mathcal I(M)$, and the circuit family is
\[
\mathcal C(M):=\{X\subseteq E(M):X\notin\mathcal I(M)\text{ and }X\setminus\{e\}\in\mathcal I(M)\ \forall e\in X\}.
\]
Thus circuits are the inclusion-minimal dependent sets. A one-element circuit of a matroid is called a loop. If $M$ is the graphic matroid of a graph $G$, then its circuits are the cycles of $G$, and its loops are precisely the graph loops.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In an independence system, circuits are the inclusion-minimal dependent sets. A one-element matroid circuit is a loop. In a graphic matroid, circuits are graph cycles and matroid loops are graph loops.
assumptions_latex: M=(E(M),\mathcal I(M))\text{ is an independence system}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal C(M)=\{X\subseteq E(M):X\notin\mathcal I(M),\ X\setminus\{e\}\in\mathcal I(M)\ \forall e\in X\}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Recovery of circuits avoiding a fixed element
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reconstruction of all circuits avoiding an element from circuits containing that element.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(M\) be a connected matroid, let \(e\in E(M)\), and let \(\mathcal C_e=\{C\in\mathcal C(M):e\in C\}\). Then the circuits of \(M\) not containing \(e\) are precisely the inclusion-minimal sets of the form
\[
(C_1\cup C_2)\setminus\bigcap\{C\in\mathcal C_e:C\subseteq C_1\cup C_2\},
\]
where \(C_1\) and \(C_2\) are distinct members of \(\mathcal C_e\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a connected matroid, the circuits avoiding a fixed element are exactly the inclusion-minimal sets obtained from two distinct circuits containing that element by removing the intersection of all such circuits contained in their union.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal C(M)\setminus\mathcal C_e=\min_{\subseteq}\left\{(C_1\cup C_2)\setminus\bigcap\{C\in\mathcal C_e:C\subseteq C_1\cup C_2\}:C_1,C_2\in\mathcal C_e,\ C_1\ne C_2\right\}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Affine Dependence and Homogenization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines affine dependence for finite multisets over a field, including the equivalent homogenized formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A multiset \(\{v_1,\ldots,v_k\}\subseteq \mathbb F^m\), with \(k\ge 1\), is affinely dependent if there exist \(a_1,\ldots,a_k\in\mathbb F\), not all zero, such that \(\sum_{i=1}^k a_i v_i=0\) and \(\sum_{i=1}^k a_i=0\). Equivalently, \(\{(1,v_1),\ldots,(1,v_k)\}\subseteq\mathbb F^{m+1}\) is linearly dependent. The multiset is affinely independent otherwise; every affinely independent multiset has no repeated member and hence is a set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty multiset of vectors is affinely dependent when a nontrivial linear combination has both zero vector sum and zero coefficient sum. This is equivalent to linear dependence after adjoining a leading coordinate equal to one. Affine independence is the negation, and an affinely independent multiset cannot contain repetitions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{v_i\}_{i=1}^k\text{ is affinely dependent}\iff \{(1,v_i)\}_{i=1}^k\text{ is linearly dependent};\quad \text{affine independence implies all }v_i\text{ are distinct}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalence of weak and strong circuit axiom systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Circuit axioms and equivalence of the weak and strong elimination formulations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a set system \(\mathcal C\subseteq 2^S\), let (C1) require \(\varnothing\notin\mathcal C\), let (C2) require that no distinct members of \(\mathcal C\) contain one another, and let (C3) be weak circuit elimination. Under (C1) and (C2), (C3) implies strong circuit elimination (C3'): for distinct \(C_1,C_2\in\mathcal C\), \(e\in C_1\cap C_2\), and \(e_1\in C_1\setminus C_2\), there is \(C\in\mathcal C\) with \(e_1\in C\subseteq (C_1\cup C_2)\setminus\{e\}\). Consequently, \(\{\mathrm{C1},\mathrm{C2},\mathrm{C3}\}\) and \(\{\mathrm{C1},\mathrm{C2},\mathrm{C3'}\}\) are equivalent axiom systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For nonempty, inclusion-minimal circuit families, weak circuit elimination implies strong circuit elimination; hence the weak and strong circuit axiom systems are equivalent.
assumptions_latex: For distinct \(C_1,C_2\in\mathcal C\), neither is contained in the other.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathrm{(C3')}\text{ holds, and }\{\mathrm{C1},\mathrm{C2},\mathrm{C3}\}\Longleftrightarrow\{\mathrm{C1},\mathrm{C2},\mathrm{C3'}\}.\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Circuit-family characterization of matroids
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes matroid circuit systems by ordinary and strong circuit elimination.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be a set and let \(\mathcal C\) be a collection of nonempty subsets of \(S\), no two of which contain one another. The following are equivalent: (i) \(\mathcal C\) is the circuit family of a matroid; (ii) for distinct \(C,C'\in\mathcal C\) and \(x\in C\cap C'\), the set \((C\cup C')\setminus\{x\}\) contains a member of \(\mathcal C\); (iii) for \(C,C'\in\mathcal C\), \(x\in C\cap C'\), and \(y\in C\setminus C'\), the set \((C\cup C')\setminus\{x\}\) contains a member of \(\mathcal C\) that contains \(y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An antichain of nonempty subsets is the circuit family of a matroid exactly when it satisfies circuit elimination, equivalently the stated strong elimination property preserving any chosen element outside the second circuit.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{(i)}\iff\text{(ii)}\iff\text{(iii)}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Matroid Circuit Properties
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the nonemptiness, minimality, and elimination axioms satisfied by a matroid's circuit family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If $M$ is a matroid, then its circuit family $\mathcal C(M)$ satisfies: (C1) $\varnothing\notin\mathcal C(M)$; (C2) for $X,Y\in\mathcal C(M)$, $X\subseteq Y$ implies $X=Y$; and (C3) for distinct $X,Y\in\mathcal C(M)$ and every $e\in X\cap Y$, there exists $Z\in\mathcal C(M)$ such that $Z\subseteq (X\cup Y)\setminus\{e\}$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The circuits of a matroid form a nonempty-set antichain and satisfy circuit elimination: if two distinct circuits share an element, deleting that element from their union leaves a set containing a circuit.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \varnothing\notin\mathcal C(M),\quad [X,Y\in\mathcal C(M),\ X\subseteq Y\Rightarrow X=Y],\quad [X\ne Y,\ e\in X\cap Y\Rightarrow \exists Z\in\mathcal C(M):Z\subseteq(X\cup Y)\setminus\{e\}]

knowledge_statements.title: Dependence-to-Circuit Recovery
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-matroid recovery of a circuit from any dependent set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\) be a finite matroid. If \(X\subseteq E\) is dependent, then \(X\) contains an inclusion-minimal dependent subset \(C\). knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite set is dependent exactly when it contains a circuit; a circuit is recovered by taking an inclusion-minimal dependent subset.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists C\subseteq X\) such that \(C\) is a circuit of \(M\).

knowledge_statements.title: Fundamental Circuits
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fundamental circuit relative to a basis in a finite matroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\) be a finite matroid, let \(B\) be a basis, and let \(e\in E\setminus B\). The set \(B\cup\{e\}\) contains a unique circuit, denoted \(C_M(e,B)\), called the fundamental circuit of \(e\) with respect to \(B\). Moreover, \(e\in C_M(e,B)\subseteq B\cup\{e\}\), and for every \(b\in B\), \(b\in C_M(e,B)\) if and only if \((B\setminus\{b\})\cup\{e\}\) is a basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding a nonbasis element to a basis creates one unique circuit; its basis elements are exactly those exchangeable with the added element.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_M(e,B)\) is the unique circuit in \(B\cup\{e\}\), with \(b\in C_M(e,B)\iff B-b+e\) a basis.

notation.meaning: fundamental circuit of e relative to B

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fundamental Cycles Relative to a Spanning Tree
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unique cycles and spanning-tree exchanges induced by nontree edges.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $G=(V,E)$ be a connected graph with $|V|=n$ and $|E|=m$, and let $T$ be a spanning tree of $G$. For each nontree edge $e\in E\setminus E(T)$, the graph $T+e$ contains exactly one cycle, called the fundamental cycle of $e$ with respect to $T$. There are $m-n+1$ fundamental cycles relative to $T$. If $f$ is any edge of that cycle, then $(T+e)-f$ is a spanning tree of $G$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding a nontree edge to a spanning tree creates exactly one fundamental cycle. There is one for each of the m minus n plus one nontree edges, and deleting any edge of the created cycle yields a spanning tree.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T+e\text{ contains a unique cycle }C_T(e);\qquad |E\setminus E(T)|=m-n+1;\qquad \forall f\in C_T(e),\ (T+e)-f\text{ is a spanning tree of }G.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Matroid-matching circuits and fundamental-circuit exchange
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Circuit notions are for subsets of the pair collection, rather than circuits of the underlying matroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a collection of pairs \(E\), call \(C\subseteq E\) a circuit if it is inclusionwise minimal subject to \(r(C)=2|C|-1\). Every \(F\subseteq E\) satisfying \(r(F)=2|F|-1\) contains a unique such circuit. If \(M\) is a matching and \(e\in E\) satisfies \(r(M\cup\{e\})=r(M)+1\), the unique circuit in \(M\cup\{e\}\) is denoted \(C(M,e)\). For every \(f\in C(M,e)\), \((M\cup\{e\})\setminus\{f\}\) is again a matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A circuit of a collection of matroid pairs is a minimal rank-deficient-by-one subcollection. Every deficiency-one collection contains a unique circuit. Adding an element to a matching with rank increase one creates a unique fundamental circuit, and deleting any member of that circuit restores a matching.
assumptions_latex: M\subseteq E\text{ is a matroid matching}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall f\in C(M,e),\quad (M\cup\{e\})\setminus\{f\}\text{ is a matroid matching}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fundamental circuits and realization of arbitrary circuits
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition of a basis-relative fundamental circuit, together with the stated realization property for all matroid circuits.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $B$ be a basis of a matroid $M$ and let $e\in E(M)\setminus B$. The unique circuit $C(e,B)\subseteq B\cup\{e\}$ is called the fundamental circuit of $e$ with respect to $B$. Moreover, every circuit $C$ of $M$ equals $C(e,B)$ for some basis $B$ of $M$ and some $e\in E(M)\setminus B$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The unique circuit formed by adding an external element e to a basis B is called the fundamental circuit of e with respect to B. Every circuit of a matroid is fundamental with respect to some basis.
assumptions_latex: For the definition, $B$ is a basis of $M$ and $e\in E(M)\setminus B$.
For the realization property, $C$ is a circuit of $M$.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: $C(e,B)$ is the fundamental circuit of $e$ with respect to $B$, and $(\forall C\in\mathcal C(M))(\exists B\text{ a basis of }M)(\exists e\in E(M)\setminus B)\;C=C(e,B)$.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basis-relative bipartite representation derived from fundamental circuits.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) be a matroid with basis \(B\). knowledge_statements.statement_title: Tree Potentials, Fundamental Circuits, and Their Reduced Costs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions and cost identity for a rooted tree basis in a bidirected network.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $T$ be rooted at $r$ in the bidirected graph $\overleftrightarrow G$. The potential $\pi(v)$ is the length of the $r$-$v$ path using edges of $T$ or their reversals. For $e=(v,w)\in E(\overleftrightarrow G)$, its fundamental circuit consists of $e$ together with the $w$-$v$ tree path; the vertex of this circuit closest to $r$ in $T$ is its peak. If $e\notin T$, then $c_\pi(e)=c(e)+\pi(v)-\pi(w)$ is the cost of sending one unit of flow around this fundamental circuit.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a rooted directed tree basis, a vertex potential is its rooted tree-path length. Adding an edge creates a fundamental circuit whose closest vertex to the root is its peak; for a non-tree edge, its reduced cost equals the cost of one unit of circulation around that circuit.
assumptions_latex: T\text{ is a tree rooted at }r\text{ in }\overleftrightarrow G
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: c_\pi(e)=c(e)+\pi(v)-\pi(w)=\text{the cost of one unit of flow along the fundamental circuit of }e

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Legs of a Tipless Spike and Their Uniqueness Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines tipless-spike legs intrinsically in rank at least five and records the ambiguity possible in lower ranks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) be a tipless rank-\(r\) spike and let \(N\) be a rank-\(r\) spike with tip \(t\), legs \(L_1,\ldots,L_r\), and \(N\setminus t=M\). If \(r\ge 5\), whenever two distinct 4-circuits of \(M\) intersect, their intersection equals \(L_i\setminus\{t\}\) for some \(i\); consequently, the sets \(L_1\setminus\{t\},\ldots,L_r\setminus\{t\}\) are uniquely determined by the 4-circuits of \(M\) and are called the legs of \(M\). If \(r\le 4\), distinct tipped-spike extensions of \(M\) may induce different legs, so the legs need not be intrinsically determined; in that case, one specifies \(r\) pairwise disjoint 2-element subsets of \(E(M)\) to serve as the legs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a tipless rank-r spike obtained by deleting the tip from a rank-r spike, if r is at least 5, the intersection of any two intersecting distinct 4-circuits is one of the tip-deleted legs. Thus the legs are uniquely recoverable from the 4-circuits. For r at most 4, different tipped-spike extensions may give different legs, so the legs can be ambiguous; one must then specify r disjoint two-element subsets as the chosen legs.
assumptions_latex: N\text{ is a rank-}r\text{ spike with tip }t\text{ and legs }L_1,\ldots,L_r
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: r\ge5\Rightarrow\bigl(C_1,C_2\in\mathcal C(M),\ |C_1|=|C_2|=4,\ C_1\ne C_2,\ C_1\cap C_2\ne\varnothing\Rightarrow\exists i,\ C_1\cap C_2=L_i\setminus\{t\}\bigr),\text{ and the legs are unique};\quad r\le4\Rightarrow\text{the induced legs may be nonunique}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fundamental circuit relative to an independent set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition and associated single-element exchange property.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) be independent, let \(e\in S\setminus F\), and suppose \(F\cup\{e\}\) is dependent. Its unique circuit is the fundamental circuit of \(e\) belonging to \(F\), denoted \(C(F,e)\). For every \(f\in C(F,e)\), the set \((F\cup\{e\})\setminus\{f\}\) is independent; if \(F\) is a basis, this set is also a basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If adding e to an independent set F creates dependence, the resulting unique circuit is C(F,e). Removing any element of that circuit restores independence, and restores a basis when F was a basis.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C(F,e)\text{ is the unique circuit in }F\cup\{e\},\quad \forall f\in C(F,e),\ (F\cup\{e\})\setminus\{f\}\text{ is independent, and is a basis if }F\text{ is a basis}.\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Ordered Fundamental-Circuit Multiple Exchange Lemma
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A sufficient condition for simultaneously replacing several elements of an independent set while preserving independence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let I be independent in a matroid M on S. Let x_1,\ldots,x_\ell\in I and y_1,\ldots,y_\ell\in S\setminus I, with I\cup\{y_i\} dependent for every i. If x_i\in C(I,y_i) for every i and x_h\notin C(I,y_j) whenever h>j, then \left(I\setminus\{x_1,\ldots,x_\ell\}\right)\cup\{y_1,\ldots,y_\ell\} is independent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Suppose each outside element y_i creates a fundamental circuit containing x_i, while no later x_h belongs to an earlier circuit. Replacing all the x_i by all the y_i then preserves independence.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \left(I\setminus\{x_1,\ldots,x_\ell\}\right)\cup\{y_1,\ldots,y_\ell\}\text{ is independent}.

knowledge_statements.title: Fundamental Cocircuits
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fundamental cocircuit relative to a basis in a finite matroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\) be a finite matroid, let \(B\) be a basis, and let \(b\in B\). The set \((E\setminus B)\cup\{b\}\) contains a unique cocircuit, denoted \(D_M(b,B)\), called the fundamental cocircuit of \(b\) with respect to \(B\). Moreover, \(b\in D_M(b,B)\), and for every \(e\in E\setminus B\), \(e\in D_M(b,B)\) if and only if \((B\setminus\{b\})\cup\{e\}\) is a basis.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_M(b,B)\) is the unique cocircuit in \((E\setminus B)\cup\{b\}\), with \(e\in D_M(b,B)\iff B-b+e\) a basis.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) be a finite matroid on \(E\) with basis \(B\). For every \(e\in E\setminus B\) and \(b\in B\), \[b\in C_M(e,B)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad e\in D_M(b,B)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad (B\setminus\{b\})\cup\{e\}\text{ is a basis of }M.\] Define \(A\in\{0,1\}^{(E\setminus B)\times B}\) by \(A_{e,b}=1\) exactly when \(b\in C_M(e,B)\), and define \(Q\in\{0,1\}^{B\times(E\setminus B)}\) by \(Q_{b,e}=1\) exactly when \(e\in D_M(b,B)\). Then \(A=Q^{\mathsf T}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A basis element belongs to a nonbasis element's fundamental circuit exactly when the nonbasis element belongs to that basis element's fundamental cocircuit, equivalently when exchanging the two elements produces a basis. Consequently, the explicitly indexed circuit- and cocircuit-incidence matrices are transposes.

knowledge_statements.title: Circuit–Cocircuit Orthogonality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-theoretic orthogonality in an arbitrary finite matroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) be a finite matroid on \(E\). For every circuit \(C\) of \(M\) and every cocircuit \(D\) of \(M\), their intersection cannot have cardinality one: \[|C\cap D|\ne 1.\] Equivalently, if \(e\in C\cap D\), then there exists \(f\in (C\cap D)\setminus\{e\}\). This is set-theoretic matroid orthogonality and does not assert that \(|C\cap D|\) is always even.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A circuit and a cocircuit never meet in exactly one element; their intersection may otherwise be empty or have at least two elements.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a circuit and \(D\) is a cocircuit of \(M\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|C\cap D|\ne 1.\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Signability and Orientability via Signed Circuit–Cocircuit Incidence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Signed overlap conditions for signability and orientability, together with their class relations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For signed circuit and cocircuit incidence vectors, define \(S_+(C,C^*)=\{e\in E(M):v'_C(e)=v'_{C^*}(e)
e0\}\) and \(S_-(C,C^*)=\{e\in E(M):v'_C(e)=-v'_{C^*}(e)
e0\}\). A matroid \(M\) is signable if signings can be chosen such that \(|S_+(C,C^*)|=|S_-(C,C^*)|\) for every circuit \(C\) and cocircuit \(C^*\). It is orientable if signings can be chosen such that \(C\cap C^*
e\varnothing\) implies both \(S_+(C,C^*)\) and \(S_-(C,C^*)\) are nonempty. Every signable matroid is orientable, and the class of signable matroids equals the class of binary orientable matroids.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Signability requires every signed circuit–cocircuit overlap to contain equally many agreeing and opposing signs. Orientability only requires both kinds to occur whenever the overlap is nonempty. Every signable matroid is orientable, and a matroid is signable exactly when it is both binary and orientable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M\text{ signable}\Rightarrow M\text{ orientable},\qquad M\text{ signable}\iff\bigl(M\text{ is binary and orientable}\bigr)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cocircuits characterized by circuit orthogonality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes cocircuits as the inclusion-minimal nonempty sets having no singleton intersection with any circuit.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) be a matroid on \(S\). The cocircuits of \(M\) are exactly the inclusion-minimal nonempty subsets \(D\subseteq S\) such that \(|D\cap C|\ne 1\) for every circuit \(C\) of \(M\). Equivalently, every circuit and cocircuit have intersection size different from one, and every nonempty \(D\subseteq S\) satisfying \(|D\cap C|\ne1\) for every circuit \(C\) contains a cocircuit and hence is dependent in \(M^*\).

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: D\text{ is a cocircuit}\iff D\text{ is inclusion-minimal among nonempty sets satisfying }\forall C\in\mathcal C(M),\ |D\cap C|\ne1

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Matroid circuit cone and sums-of-circuits property
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the circuit cone, states its universally valid cocircuit inequalities, and defines when those inequalities give an exact description.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a matroid M=(E,\mathcal I), its circuit cone is \operatorname{cone}\{\chi^C:C\text{ is a circuit of }M\}. Every x in this cone satisfies x_f\le x(D\setminus\{f\}) for every cocircuit D and every f\in D. The matroid has the sums-of-circuits property when the circuit cone is determined by this family of inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The circuit cone is generated by the incidence vectors of a matroid's circuits. Every vector in it satisfies the cocircuit inequality that the coordinate at any cocircuit element is at most the sum of the other cocircuit coordinates. The sums-of-circuits property means that these inequalities describe the cone completely.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x_f\le x(D\setminus\{f\});\qquad M\text{ has the sums-of-circuits property when these inequalities determine its circuit cone.}

knowledge_statements.title: Rank View
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite matroids represented by integer-valued rank functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A function \(r:2^E\to\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\) is the rank function of a matroid on finite \(E\) exactly when, for all \(X,Y\subseteq E\), \(0\le r(X)\le |X|\), \(X\subseteq Y\) implies \(r(X)\le r(Y)\), and \[r(X)+r(Y)\ge r(X\cup Y)+r(X\cap Y).\] The represented independent sets are precisely \(\mathcal I_r=\{I\subseteq E:r(I)=|I|\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Normalized, cardinality-bounded, monotone, submodular integer functions are exactly finite-matroid rank functions; equality with cardinality identifies independent sets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r\) is a matroid rank function if and only if it satisfies the displayed rank axioms.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalent local axioms for matroid rank
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines submodularity and gives local one-element and two-element conditions equivalent to the standard matroid-rank axioms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A set function \(r:\mathcal P(S)\to\mathbb Z_+\) is submodular when \(r(T\cap U)+r(T\cup U)\le r(T)+r(U)\) for all \(T,U\subseteq S\). The standard matroid-rank axioms are equivalent to the following local conditions: (i) \(r(\varnothing)=0\); (ii) for every \(U\subseteq S\) and \(s\in S\setminus U\), \(r(U)\le r(U\cup\{s\})\le r(U)+1\); (iii) for every \(U\subseteq S\) and \(s,t\in S\setminus U\), if \(r(U\cup\{s\})=r(U\cup\{t\})=r(U)\), then \(r(U\cup\{s,t\})=r(U)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Submodularity is the diminishing-returns inequality for unions and intersections. For nonnegative integer-valued set functions, the usual matroid-rank axioms are equivalently expressed by normalization, rank increments of zero or one, and a local closure condition for pairs of elements.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{standard matroid-rank axioms}\iff\begin{cases}r(\varnothing)=0,\\r(U)\le r(U\cup\{s\})\le r(U)+1,\\r(U\cup\{s\})=r(U\cup\{t\})=r(U)\Rightarrow r(U\cup\{s,t\})=r(U).\end{cases}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) be a matroid with rank function \(r\), and let \(X\subseteq E(M)\). Then: (i) \(X\) is independent if and only if \(|X|=r(X)\); (ii) \(X\) is a basis if and only if \(|X|=r(X)=r(M)\); and (iii) \(X\) is a circuit if and only if \(X\ne\varnothing\) and, for every \(x\in X\), \(r(X\setminus\{x\})=|X|-1=r(X)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set is independent exactly when its rank equals its size. It is a basis exactly when this value also equals the matroid rank. It is a circuit exactly when it is nonempty and its rank, as well as the rank of every one-element deletion, equals one less than its size.
assumptions_latex: M\text{ is a matroid with rank function }r
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: X\in\mathcal I(M)\iff |X|=r(X);\quad X\in\mathcal B(M)\iff |X|=r(X)=r(M);\quad X\in\mathcal C(M)\iff X\ne\varnothing\ \land\ \forall x\in X,\ r(X\setminus\{x\})=|X|-1=r(X).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Tipless spikes and uniqueness of the tipped extension
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines tipless spikes and records the rank-four ambiguity and rank-at-least-five uniqueness boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If N is a rank-r tipped spike with tip t, then M=N\setminus t is called a tipless spike; it has |E(M)|=2r and r(M)=r. It is a tipless free spike when N may be chosen free. Rank four can admit more than one way to adjoin a tip, because the \mathcal C_2- and \mathcal C_3-circuits then have the same cardinality. If M is a tipless spike of rank r\ge5, however, there is a unique tipped spike N with tip t such that N\setminus t=M.

A rank-four tipless spike may have several possible tipped extensions, but every tipless spike of rank at least five has a unique tipped spike extension.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: |E(M)|=2r,\quad r(M)=r;\qquad r\ge5\Rightarrow\exists!\,N\text{ with tip }t\text{ such that }N\setminus t=M.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Matroid Independence Polytope and Rank Inequalities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polyhedral representation of all independent sets of a finite matroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a matroid \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\), its independence polytope is \(\operatorname{IND}(M)=\operatorname{conv}\{\chi^I\in\mathbb R^E:I\in\mathcal I\}\). Maximum-weight independent-set optimization is equivalently \(\max\{c^Tx:x\in\operatorname{IND}(M)\}\). Every incidence vector of an independent set, and hence every point of \(\operatorname{IND}(M)\), satisfies \(x_e\ge0\) for all \(e\in E\) and \(x(F)\le r(F)\) for every \(F\subseteq E\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The matroid independence polytope is the convex hull of independent-set incidence vectors. Linear optimization over it is the maximum-weight independent-set problem, and all its points satisfy nonnegativity and every rank inequality.
assumptions_latex: r\text{ is the rank function of }M
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{IND}(M)=\operatorname{conv}\{\chi^I:I\in\mathcal I\},\quad x\in\operatorname{IND}(M)\Rightarrow x\ge0\text{ and }x(F)\le r(F)\ \forall F\subseteq E.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Matroid restriction and subset rank
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines subset rank through restriction and records the restriction's circuits, elementary rank bounds, and monotonicity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\) be a matroid and \(X\subseteq E\). Define \(\mathcal I|X=\{I\subseteq X:I\in\mathcal I\}\). The restriction is \(M|X=(X,\mathcal I|X)=M\setminus(E-X)\), with \(\mathcal C(M|X)=\{C\in\mathcal C(M):C\subseteq X\}\). The rank \(r_M(X)\) is the cardinality of any basis of \(M|X\), and \(r(M)=r_M(E)\). Moreover, \(0\le r_M(X)\le |X|\), and for all \(X\subseteq Y\subseteq E\), \(r_M(X)\le r_M(Y)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Restricting a matroid to X retains its independent sets contained in X and exactly its circuits contained in X. The rank of X is the common size of the bases of this restriction. Rank is bounded by set size and is monotone under inclusion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M|X=(X,\mathcal I|X),\quad \mathcal C(M|X)=\{C\in\mathcal C(M):C\subseteq X\},\quad r_M(X)=|B|\text{ for every basis }B\text{ of }M|X,\quad 0\le r_M(X)\le |X|,\quad X\subseteq Y\subseteq E\Rightarrow r_M(X)\le r_M(Y).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Rank-function axioms for finite matroids
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent global and local characterizations of matroid rank functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) be finite and \(r:2^E\to\mathbb Z_+\). The following are equivalent: (i) \(r\) is the rank function of a matroid on \(E\), whose independent sets are \(\mathcal F=\{F\subseteq E:r(F)=|F|\}\); (ii) for all \(X,Y\subseteq E\), \(r(X)\le |X|\), \(X\subseteq Y\Rightarrow r(X)\le r(Y)\), and \(r(X\cup Y)+r(X\cap Y)\le r(X)+r(Y)\); (iii) \(r(\varnothing)=0\), for all \(X\subseteq E\) and \(y\in E\), \(r(X)\le r(X\cup\{y\})\le r(X)+1\), and for all \(x,y\in E\), if \(r(X\cup\{x\})=r(X\cup\{y\})=r(X)\), then \(r(X\cup\{x,y\})=r(X)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonnegative integer-valued set function on a finite ground set is a matroid rank function exactly when it satisfies either the global boundedness, monotonicity, and submodularity axioms or the stated equivalent local axioms.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: r\text{ is a matroid rank function}\iff\text{the global rank axioms hold}\iff\text{the stated local rank axioms hold}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Matroid Rank Characterization and Rank under Deletion and Contraction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rank-function cryptomorphism for finite matroids together with the definitions and rank effects of single-element deletion and contraction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a matroid \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\) and \(F\subseteq E\), all maximal independent subsets of \(F\) have the same cardinality, called \(r(F)\). The rank function satisfies \(r(\varnothing)=0\), monotonicity, \(r(S)\leq |S|\), and submodularity. Moreover, \(S\in\mathcal I\iff r(S)=|S|\), so \(r\) uniquely determines \(M\); conversely, every integer-valued \(r:2^E\to\mathbb Z\) satisfying these four properties is the rank function of a unique matroid. Deletion of \(e\) restricts \(\mathcal I\) to \(E\setminus\{e\}\). If \(\{e\}\in\mathcal I\), contraction has independent sets \(\{S\setminus\{e\}:e\in S\in\mathcal I\}\); if \(\{e\}\notin\mathcal I\), it equals deletion. For \(F\subseteq E\setminus\{e\}\), \(r_{M\setminus e}(F)=r_M(F)\) and \(r_{M/e}(F)=r_M(F\cup\{e\})-r_M(\{e\})\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Matroid rank is the common size of maximal independent subsets of a set. Normalization, monotonicity, subcardinality, submodularity, and integer values characterize matroid rank functions. Deletion preserves rank on remaining subsets, while contraction obeys the stated rank formula, including the loop case.
assumptions_latex: M=(E,\mathcal I)\text{ is a finite matroid}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S\in\mathcal I\iff r(S)=|S|,\qquad r_{M\setminus e}(F)=r_M(F),\qquad r_{M/e}(F)=r_M(F\cup\{e\})-r_M(\{e\}).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Co-rank, Flats, Hyperplanes, and Matroid Closure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions and elementary representations of co-rank and rank-closure structures for a matroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) be a matroid on \(S\) with rank function \(r\), and define \(t(X):=\min\{|X\cap B|:B\text{ is a basis of }M\}\). Then \(r(X)=\max\{|X\cap B|:B\text{ is a basis of }M\}\), \(t(S)=r(S)\), and \(t(X)=r(S)-r(S\setminus X)\). Consequently, \(t(X)+t(Y)\le t(X\cap Y)+t(X\cup Y)\) for all \(X,Y\subseteq S\). A set \(F\subseteq S\) is a flat precisely when \(r(F\cup\{x\})>r(F)\) for every \(x\in S\setminus F\); its complement is open, \(S\) is a flat, and a flat of rank \(r(S)-1\) is a hyperplane. Moreover, \(\operatorname{cl}(X):=\{e\in S:r(X\cup\{e\})=r(X)\}\) is the unique largest superset of \(X\) having rank \(r(X)\), and equals the intersection of all flats containing \(X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rank is the maximum intersection size with a basis, while co-rank is the minimum and equals total rank minus the rank of the complement; co-rank is supermodular. Flats are sets whose rank increases upon adding any outside element, hyperplanes are flats of codimension one, and the closure of a set is both its largest same-rank superset and the intersection of all flats containing it.
assumptions_latex: M\text{ is a matroid on the finite ground set }S
r\text{ is the rank function of }M
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: t(X)=r(S)-r(S\setminus X),\quad t(X)+t(Y)\le t(X\cap Y)+t(X\cup Y),\quad \operatorname{cl}(X)=\max_{\subseteq}\{Z\supseteq X:r(Z)=r(X)\}=\bigcap\{F\supseteq X:F\text{ is a flat}\}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Rank-function characterization of finite matroids
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Whitney's local rank-increment characterization and the induced independent-set representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(r\) is the rank function of a matroid on \(E\), then \(r(\varnothing)=0\); for every \(A\subseteq E\) and \(e\notin A\), \(r(A\cup\{e\})\in\{r(A),r(A)+1\}\); and for \(e_1,e_2\notin A\), if \(r(A\cup\{e_1\})=r(A\cup\{e_2\})=r(A)\), then \(r(A\cup\{e_1,e_2\})=r(A)\). Conversely, if a function \(r\) on the subsets of a finite set \(E\) satisfies these conditions, then \(\mathcal I=\{I\subseteq E:r(I)=|I|\}\) is the independent-set family of a matroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matroid rank is zero on the empty set, increases by zero or one when a single new element is added, and remains unchanged when two elements are added together if each separately leaves it unchanged. Conversely, on a finite ground set these conditions define a matroid through the subsets whose rank equals their cardinality.
assumptions_latex: For the forward implication, \(r\) is the rank function of a matroid on \(E\).
For the converse, \(E\) is finite and \(r\) is a function on \(2^E\) satisfying the three stated conditions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal I=\{I\subseteq E:r(I)=|I|\}\text{ is the independent-set family of a matroid, and every matroid rank function satisfies the stated conditions.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Paving matroids and m-partitions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines paving matroids and the distinct notion of an m-partition; an m-partition must not be conflated with a partition matroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A matroid \(M\) is paving if it has no circuit of cardinality less than \(r(M)\); consequently every matroid of rank less than two is paving. For integers \(k>1\) and \(m>0\), a family \(\mathcal T=\{T_1,\ldots,T_k\}\) of subsets of \(E\) is an \(m\)-partition of \(E\) if \(|T_i|\ge m\) for every \(i\), and every \(m\)-element subset of \(E\) is contained in exactly one member of \(\mathcal T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A paving matroid has no circuit smaller than its rank, so every matroid of rank below two is paving. An m-partition is a family of more than one subsets, each of size at least m, such that every m-element subset of the ground set lies in exactly one family member.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M\text{ is paving}\iff(\forall C\in\mathcal C(M))\ |C|\ge r(M);\qquad \mathcal T\text{ is an }m\text{-partition}\iff[(\forall i)\ |T_i|\ge m\ \land\ (\forall X\subseteq E,|X|=m)\ (\exists!i)\ X\subseteq T_i].

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Matroid Rank-Function Axioms

children.top_down_role: Numerical presentation emphasizing excess size over rank.

assumptions_latex: \(M\) is a matroid on a finite ground set \(E\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite matroid \(M\) on \(E\) with rank function \(r_M\), define its nullity function by \[n_M(X)=|X|-r_M(X)\qquad(X\subseteq E).\] For every \(X\subseteq E\), \(n_M(X)\) equals the number of elements of \(X\) outside any inclusion-maximal independent subset of \(X\). For every \(I\subseteq E\), \(I\) is independent exactly when \(n_M(I)=0\), and \(I\) is dependent exactly when \(n_M(I)>0\). Hence \(n_M\) determines \(M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The nullity of a subset is its cardinality minus its rank, equivalently the number of its elements outside any inclusion-maximal independent subset. Zero-nullity sets are exactly the independent sets, so the nullity function determines the finite matroid.

knowledge_statements.title: Rank–Nullity Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mutually inverse conversion between rank and nullity on a finite ground set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) be finite. Rank and nullity functions of a matroid on \(E\) determine one another pointwise by \[n(X)=|X|-r(X),\qquad r(X)=|X|-n(X)\qquad(X\subseteq E).\] Under this correspondence, rank monotonicity becomes \(n(Y)-n(X)\le |Y\setminus X|\) for \(X\subseteq Y\), rank submodularity becomes nullity supermodularity, and the independent subsets are exactly the zero sets of \(n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rank and nullity are complementary to subset cardinality and therefore encode the same finite matroid, with submodularity converted to supermodularity.
assumptions_latex: \(r\) and \(n\) are respectively the rank and nullity functions of one matroid on \(E\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(n(X)=|X|-r(X)\) and \(r(X)=|X|-n(X)\) for every \(X\subseteq E\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Matroid cryptomorphic structures and duality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Composite foundational definition covering the structures explicitly assembled in the extract.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let E be finite. A matroid is a pair (E,\mathcal I) such that \varnothing\in\mathcal I, I_1\subseteq I_2\in\mathcal I\Rightarrow I_1\in\mathcal I, and I_1,I_2\in\mathcal I,\ |I_1|<|I_2|\Rightarrow\exists e\in I_2\setminus I_1:\ I_1\cup\{e\}\in\mathcal I. Its bases are inclusion-maximal independent sets and satisfy basis exchange; its circuits are inclusion-minimal dependent sets and satisfy circuit elimination. Its rank and closure are \rho(X)=\max\{|I|:I\subseteq X, I\in\mathcal I\} and \operatorname{cl}(X)=\{e\in E:\rho(X\cup\{e\})=\rho(X)\}. The rank is integer-valued, 0\leq\rho(X)\leq|X|, monotone, submodular, and has unit increments. For I\in\mathcal I and e\in\operatorname{cl}(I)\setminus I, I\cup\{e\} contains a unique fundamental circuit C(I\mid e), and (I\cup\{e\})\setminus\{e'\}\in\mathcal I for every e'\in C(I\mid e). Each of the independent-set, basis, circuit, rank, and closure axiom systems uniquely determines the matroid; in particular, an integer-valued \rho satisfying the rank axioms gives \mathcal I=\{I\subseteq E:\rho(I)=|I|\}. If \mathcal B^*=\{E\setminus B:B\in\mathcal B\}, then (E,\mathcal B^*) is the dual matroid M^*, with (M^*)^*=M.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matroid can be specified equivalently by its independent sets, bases, circuits, rank function, or closure operator. These structures satisfy their respective exchange, elimination, rank-submodularity, and closure axioms; fundamental circuits govern single-element exchanges. Complements of bases form the dual matroid, and dualizing twice returns the original matroid.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal I,\mathcal B,\mathcal C,\rho,\operatorname{cl}\text{ are cryptomorphic matroid descriptions, and }(M^*)^*=M.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closed sets, matroid closure, and redundant nonclosed rank inequalities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines closedness for an independence system, states existence and uniqueness of matroid closure, and records the associated rank-inequality redundancy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an independence system $M$, a set $T\subseteq E(M)$ is closed if $r_M(T\cup\{e\})>r_M(T)$ for every $e\in E(M)\setminus T$. If $M$ is a matroid, every $T$ has a unique maximal superset $\operatorname{cl}_M(T)$ satisfying $r_M(\operatorname{cl}_M(T))=r_M(T)$. Consequently, if $T$ is not closed, then under nonnegativity the inequality $x(T)\le r_M(T)$ follows from $x(\operatorname{cl}_M(T))\le r_M(T)$ and $-x_j\le0$ for $j\in\operatorname{cl}_M(T)\setminus T$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set is closed when every outside element increases its rank. In a matroid, every set has a unique maximal same-rank superset, called its closure or span. The rank inequality of a nonclosed set is therefore implied by the closure inequality and nonnegativity.
assumptions_latex: M\text{ is an independence system for the definition of closedness}
M\text{ is a matroid for existence and uniqueness of }\operatorname{cl}_M(T)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: r_M(\operatorname{cl}_M(T))=r_M(T),\qquad x(\operatorname{cl}_M(T))\le r_M(T),\ x\ge0\Longrightarrow x(T)\le r_M(T)

children.title: Closure Operators
children.top_down_role: Matroid structure expressed through closure behavior.

assumptions_latex: \(M\) is a matroid on \(E\) with rank function \(r_M\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The operator \(\operatorname{cl}_M\) satisfies extensivity, monotonicity, idempotence, and Mac Lane–Steinitz exchange; conversely, these axioms characterize closure operators of unique matroids on \(E\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite matroids represented by closure operators satisfying exchange.

source_refs.locator: Section 5.1, Independence and rank, p. 173

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) be a matroid on a finite set \(E\), with rank function \(r_M\), and define \[\operatorname{cl}_M(X)=\{e\in E:r_M(X\cup\{e\})=r_M(X)\}\qquad(X\subseteq E).\] For all \(X,Y\subseteq E\), this operator is extensive, monotone, and idempotent: \(X\subseteq\operatorname{cl}_M(X)\), \(X\subseteq Y\Rightarrow\operatorname{cl}_M(X)\subseteq\operatorname{cl}_M(Y)\), and \(\operatorname{cl}_M(\operatorname{cl}_M(X))=\operatorname{cl}_M(X)\). For all \(X\subseteq E\) and \(x,y\in E\), it also satisfies Mac Lane–Steinitz exchange: \[y\in\operatorname{cl}_M(X\cup\{x\})\setminus\operatorname{cl}_M(X)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x\in\operatorname{cl}_M(X\cup\{y\}).\] Conversely, every map \(\operatorname{cl}:2^E\to2^E\) satisfying these four properties is the closure operator of a unique matroid on \(E\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Matroid closure consists of the elements whose addition does not increase rank. It is extensive, monotone, idempotent, and satisfies exchange; conversely, an operator on a finite ground set with these properties determines a unique matroid.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closure-operator axioms for finite matroids
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cryptomorphic characterization of finite matroids through closure operators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) be finite and \(\sigma:2^E\to2^E\). Then \(\sigma\) is the closure operator of a matroid on \(E\) if and only if, for all \(X,Y\subseteq E\) and \(x,y\in E\): \(X\subseteq\sigma(X)\); \(X\subseteq Y\Rightarrow\sigma(X)\subseteq\sigma(Y)\); \(\sigma(\sigma(X))=\sigma(X)\); and if \(y\notin\sigma(X)\) and \(y\in\sigma(X\cup\{x\})\), then \(x\in\sigma(X\cup\{y\})\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set operator on a finite ground set is a matroid closure operator exactly when it is extensive, monotone, idempotent, and satisfies the matroid closure-exchange axiom.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sigma\text{ is a matroid closure operator}\iff\sigma\text{ satisfies extensivity, monotonicity, idempotence, and closure exchange}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closure-Axiom Cryptomorphism for Matroids
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constructs a matroid from a set map satisfying the four matroid closure axioms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) be a set and let \(\operatorname{cl}:2^E\to2^E\) satisfy \((\mathrm{CL1})\)–\((\mathrm{CL4})\). knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The closure operator of a matroid on \(E\) satisfies \[(\mathrm{CL1})\quad X\subseteq\operatorname{cl}(X)\qquad(X\subseteq E),\] \[(\mathrm{CL2})\quad X\subseteq Y\subseteq E\Longrightarrow\operatorname{cl}(X)\subseteq\operatorname{cl}(Y),\] \[(\mathrm{CL3})\quad \operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{cl}(X))=\operatorname{cl}(X)\qquad(X\subseteq E),\] and \[(\mathrm{CL4})\quad y\in\operatorname{cl}(X\cup\{x\})\setminus\operatorname{cl}(X)\Longrightarrow x\in\operatorname{cl}(X\cup\{y\})\] for \(X\subseteq E\) and \(x,y\in E\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Matroid closure is extensive, monotone, and idempotent. It also satisfies exchange: if y becomes newly spanned after adding x, then x is spanned after adding y.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{cl}_M\text{ satisfies }(\mathrm{CL1})\text{--}(\mathrm{CL4})

children.title: Matroid Span
children.top_down_role: Spanning relationships induced by closure.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(X\subseteq E\) and \(e\in E\), \(X\text{ spans }e\iff e\in\operatorname{cl}_M(X)\iff r_M(X\cup\{e\})=r_M(X)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rank and circuit characterizations of spanning elements and sets.

source_refs.locator: Sections 5.1–5.2, Independence and rank; Circuits and connectivity, pp. 173–176

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) be a finite matroid on \(E\). For every \(X\subseteq E\) and \(e\in E\), the set \(X\) spans \(e\) when \(e\in\operatorname{cl}_M(X)\), equivalently when \(r_M(X\cup\{e\})=r_M(X)\). If \(e\notin X\), these conditions are equivalent to the existence of a circuit \(C\) of \(M\) such that \(e\in C\subseteq X\cup\{e\}\). For \(Y\subseteq E\), the set \(X\) spans \(Y\) when \(Y\subseteq\operatorname{cl}_M(X)\), and \(X\) spans \(M\) when \(\operatorname{cl}_M(X)=E\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set spans an element exactly when adding that element does not increase rank; for an element outside the set, this is also equivalent to completing a circuit supported by the set. A set spans another set when it spans every one of its elements, and it spans the matroid when its closure is the whole ground set.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Matroid Bases, Span, and Generators
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rank-based definitions of spanning and generating sets, including their connection to bases.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M=(S,\mathcal I)\) be a matroid with rank function \(r\). A basis is a maximal independent subset of \(S\). For \(X,Y\subseteq S\), \(X\) spans (or generates) \(Y\) if \(r(X\cup Y)=r(X)\). A set \(X\subseteq S\) is a generator of \(M\) if it spans \(S\), equivalently, if it contains a basis of \(M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a matroid, a basis is a maximal independent subset of the ground set. A set X spans Y when adjoining Y does not increase the rank of X. A generator spans the whole ground set, equivalently it contains a basis.
assumptions_latex: M=(S,\mathcal I)\text{ is a matroid with rank function }r
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: X\text{ spans }Y\iff r(X\cup Y)=r(X),\qquad X\text{ generates }M\iff r(X)=r(S)\iff X\text{ contains a basis of }M.
