knowledge_statements.statement_title: One-element test for a matroid splitter
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient splitter criterion for a 3-connected matroid in a minor-closed class, including wheel–whirl maximality conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \mathcal N be a class of matroids closed under minors and isomorphism. Let N\in\mathcal N be 3-connected with |E(N)|\ge 4. Suppose that, if N is a wheel, it is the largest wheel in \mathcal N, and, if N is a whirl, it is the largest whirl in \mathcal N. If no 3-connected member of \mathcal N has N as a minor and exactly one more element than N, then N is a splitter for \mathcal N; that is, no 3-connected member of \mathcal N has N as a proper minor.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a minor- and isomorphism-closed matroid class, let N be 3-connected with at least four elements and maximal among the class's wheels or whirls when applicable. If no 3-connected class member with exactly one more element has N as a minor, then N is a splitter, so no 3-connected class member has N as a proper minor.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal N\text{ is closed under minors and isomorphism}
N\text{ is a wheel}\Rightarrow N\text{ is the largest wheel in }\mathcal N
N\text{ is a whirl}\Rightarrow N\text{ is the largest whirl in }\mathcal N
\nexists M\in\mathcal N:\ M\text{ is 3-connected},\ |E(M)|=|E(N)|+1,\ N\preccurlyeq M
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: N\text{ is a splitter for }\mathcal N

children.top_down_role: Extension or coextension sequences used to navigate between connected minors.

knowledge_statements.title: Constructive Splitter Sequences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Iterated sequence form of the classical splitter conclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the classical Splitter Theorem hypotheses, there is a sequence \(N=M_0,M_1,\ldots,M_k=M\) of 3-connected matroids such that each \(M_i\) is a minor of \(M\) and \(|E(M_i)|=|E(N)|+i\). For every \(i<k\), the matroid \(M_{i+1}\) is a single-element extension or single-element coextension of \(M_i\). Equivalently, deleting or contracting the newly added element of \(M_{i+1}\) recovers \(M_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The splitter theorem can be iterated into a chain from N to M whose 3-connected members differ by one extension or coextension.
assumptions_latex: The hypotheses of the classical Splitter Theorem hold for \(M\) and \(N\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N=M_0\prec M_1\prec\cdots\prec M_k=M\), with every \(M_i\) 3-connected and \(|E(M_{i+1})\setminus E(M_i)|=1\).

notation.meaning: the ground-set size difference between M and N

review_flags: The sequence formulation requires an exact splitter-theorem source locator.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A sequence representation fits the leaf, but an exact source is needed to justify iteration of the splitter conclusion through every intermediate matroid. The conclusion also uses the undefined relation symbol \(\prec\) and literal ground-set differences despite the statement formulating the objects only as minors up to isomorphism.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Connected Two-Element Splitter Alternative with Exchange Corrections
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A two-element splitter theorem requiring connectivity of the double reduction and allowing bounded exchange corrections.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(N\) be a 3-connected minor of a 3-connected matroid \(M\), with \(|E(N)|\ge4\), and suppose \(r(M)-r(N)\ge2\) or \(r(M^*)-r(N^*)\ge2\). Then at least one holds: (i) there are distinct \(x,y\in E(M)\) such that \(M/x,y\) is connected and each of \(\operatorname{si}(M/x)\), \(\operatorname{si}(M/y)\), and \(\operatorname{si}(M/x,y)\) is 3-connected and has an \(N\)-minor; (ii) there are distinct \(x,y\in E(M)\) such that \(M\setminus x,y\) is connected and each of \(\operatorname{co}(M\setminus x)\), \(\operatorname{co}(M\setminus y)\), and \(\operatorname{co}(M\setminus x,y)\) is 3-connected and has an \(N\)-minor; (iii) \(|E(M)-E(N)|\in\{3,4\}\), and a single \(\Delta-Y\) exchange followed by at most one series contraction produces a 3-connected matroid for which (i) holds; or (iv) \(|E(M)-E(N)|\in\{3,4\}\), and a single \(Y-\Delta\) exchange followed by at most one parallel deletion produces a 3-connected matroid for which (ii) holds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under a rank or corank gap of at least two, either a connected two-element contraction or deletion reduction preserves the minor and 3-connectivity after simplification or cosimplification, or—when three or four elements separate the matroids—one exchange and at most one specified corrective operation produces such a reduction.
assumptions_latex: N\text{ is a 3-connected minor of the 3-connected matroid }M
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{At least one of alternatives (i)--(iv) stated above holds}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Constructive splitter sequence between 3-connected minors
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A splitter-theorem corollary giving a chain of 3-connected single-element reductions from a matroid to a specified minor.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) and \(N\) be 3-connected matroids such that \(N\) is a minor of \(M\) and \(|E(N)|\ge 4\). Assume that if \(N\) is a wheel, then \(M\) has no larger wheel as a minor, and if \(N\) is a whirl, then \(M\) has no larger whirl as a minor. Then there are 3-connected matroids \(M_0,M_1,\ldots,M_n\) with \(M_0\cong N\) and \(M_n=M\) such that, for every \(i\in\{0,\ldots,n-1\}\), \(M_i\) is a single-element deletion or a single-element contraction of \(M_{i+1}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If N is a 3-connected minor of a 3-connected matroid M, has at least four elements, and satisfies the stated wheel or whirl maximality condition, then N and M are joined by a sequence of 3-connected matroids whose successive backward steps are single-element deletions or contractions.
assumptions_latex: N\text{ is a wheel}\implies M\text{ has no larger wheel as a minor}
N\text{ is a whirl}\implies M\text{ has no larger whirl as a minor}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists M_0,\ldots,M_n:\ M_0\cong N,\ M_n=M,\ \text{each }M_i\text{ is 3-connected, and each }M_i\text{ is a single-element deletion or contraction of }M_{i+1}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: One-step splitter minor theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence of a connected, simple, cosimple intermediate minor differing from N by one deletion or contraction, subject to wheel–whirl boundary hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let N be a nonempty, connected, simple, cosimple minor of a 3-connected matroid M. Suppose that, if N is a wheel, M has no larger wheel as a minor, and, if N is a whirl, M has no larger whirl as a minor. Then either M=N, or M has a connected, simple, cosimple minor M_1 such that M_1\setminus e\cong N or M_1/e\cong N for some e\in E(M_1). Moreover, if N is 3-connected, then M_1 is 3-connected.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Let N be a nonempty connected, simple, and cosimple minor of a 3-connected matroid M, with no larger wheel or whirl minor when N is respectively a wheel or whirl. Either M equals N, or M has a connected, simple, and cosimple minor M1 from which one deletion or contraction produces N. If N is 3-connected, M1 is also 3-connected.
assumptions_latex: N\text{ is a nonempty, connected, simple, cosimple minor of }M
N\text{ is a wheel}\Rightarrow M\text{ has no larger wheel minor}
N\text{ is a whirl}\Rightarrow M\text{ has no larger whirl minor}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M=N\ \lor\ \exists M_1\preccurlyeq M\ \exists e\in E(M_1):\ M_1\text{ is connected, simple, and cosimple},\ (M_1\setminus e\cong N\ \lor\ M_1/e\cong N),\text{ and }(N\text{ 3-connected}\Rightarrow M_1\text{ 3-connected})

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Constructive 3-Connected Splitter Sequence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A stepwise splitter sequence under circuit and cocircuit size restrictions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(N\) be a 3-connected minor of a 3-connected matroid \(M\), and suppose that \(N\) has no circuits or cocircuits with fewer than four elements. Then there is a sequence \(M_0,M_1,\ldots,M_n\) of 3-connected matroids with \(M_0=N\) and \(M_n=M\) such that, for every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\), there is an element \(e_i\in E(M_i)\) for which \(M_{i-1}\) is a cosimple matroid associated with \(M_i\setminus e_i\), or a simple matroid associated with \(M_i/e_i\), and \(|E(M_i)-E(M_{i-1})|\le 2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If N is a 3-connected minor of M and has no circuit or cocircuit of size below four, N can be linked to M by 3-connected matroids whose successive steps use deletion or contraction with the corresponding cosimple or simple association, adding at most two ground-set elements per step.

N\text{ has no circuit or cocircuit with fewer than four elements}

knowledge_statements.title: Strengthened Splitter Variants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong sequence form controlling consecutive extensions and coextensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the classical splitter hypotheses, the 3-connected sequence from \(N\) to \(M\) can, after dualizing if necessary, be chosen in blocks containing at most two consecutive single-element extensions followed by at most one single-element coextension. Whenever a block adds two extension elements and then one coextension element, its three new elements form a triad in the matroid at the end of that block. Thus both intermediate size and the local configuration of added elements are controlled.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strong splitter sequence can bound consecutive extensions and coextensions; a maximal three-element block creates a triad.
assumptions_latex: The classical splitter hypotheses hold for \(M\) and \(N\)
Dualization of the sequence is allowed
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The sequence may be ordered into extension–coextension blocks of size at most \(3\), with every size-\(3\) block's new elements forming a triad.

knowledge_statements.title: Splitter Exceptions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nested wheels and whirls refute the splitter conclusion without its exceptional proviso.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \(r\ge 3\), the rank-\(r\) wheel \(M(W_r)\) is a proper minor of \(M(W_{r+1})\), and the rank-\(r\) whirl \(\mathcal W^r\) is a proper minor of \(\mathcal W^{r+1}\). Nevertheless, for every element \(e\) of the larger matroid, both its deletion and contraction fail to be 3-connected. Hence omitting the wheel–whirl maximality proviso makes the literal single-element conclusion of the classical Splitter Theorem false.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Consecutive wheels or whirls form nested 3-connected minors, yet no deletion or contraction of the larger member remains 3-connected.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The pairs \((M(W_{r+1}),M(W_r))\) and \((\mathcal W^{r+1},\mathcal W^r)\) violate the unqualified splitter conclusion.
review_flags: The nested-minor construction and exception require an exact source locator.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Minor-Closed Classes and Excluded Minors
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines minor-closed matroid classes and their minor-minimal obstructions and states the resulting obstruction characterization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A class \(\mathcal C\) of matroids is minor-closed if every minor of every \(M\in\mathcal C\) also belongs to \(\mathcal C\). A matroid \(N\) is an excluded minor for \(\mathcal C\) if \(N\notin\mathcal C\) but every proper minor of \(N\) lies in \(\mathcal C\). Every minor-closed class of finite matroids is characterized by its excluded minors: \(M\in\mathcal C\) if and only if no excluded minor for \(\mathcal C\) is a minor of \(M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matroid class is minor-closed when it contains every minor of each member. An excluded minor is a matroid outside the class whose every proper minor belongs to the class. For finite matroids, a minor-closed class consists exactly of the matroids having none of its excluded minors as a minor.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal C\) is a minor-closed class of finite matroids.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\in\mathcal C\iff\text{ no excluded minor for }\mathcal C\text{ is a minor of }M\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Deletion, contraction, and minors of grafts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines single-edge and setwise minor operations for a graph with a distinguished set of colored vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a graft \((G,\gamma)\) and \(x\in E(G)\), deletion deletes \(x\) from \(G\) while leaving the colored vertices unchanged. Contraction also leaves the coloring unchanged except when \(x\) has distinct ends \(u,v\); then \((G,\gamma)/x=(G/x,\gamma')\), where the identified vertex \(w\) is colored if and only if exactly one of \(u,v\) is colored. Equivalently, \(A_{(G/x,\gamma')}\) is obtained from \(A_{(G,\gamma)}\) by deleting column \(x\) and replacing rows \(u,v\) by their sum modulo \(2\). A graft minor is obtained by a sequence of single-edge deletions and contractions, and \((G,\gamma)\setminus X/Y\) is well-defined for disjoint \(X,Y\subseteq E(G)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Graft deletion removes an edge without changing the colored vertices. When an edge with distinct ends is contracted, the identified vertex is colored exactly when one of its two original ends was colored. Graft minors are produced by sequences of deletions and contractions, and deleting X and contracting disjoint Y is well-defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (G,\gamma)\setminus x,\ (G,\gamma)/x,\text{ and }(G,\gamma)\setminus X/Y\text{ are defined by the stated graph and parity-coloring operations}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Grafts and graft matroids
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines grafts using the convention that the distinguished vertex set need not have even cardinality and records the odd-cardinality boundary case.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A graft is a pair $(G,\gamma)$, where $G$ is a graph and $\gamma\subseteq V(G)$. Over $\mathrm{GF}(2)$, the graft incidence matrix $A_{(G,\gamma)}$ is obtained from the vertex-edge incidence matrix of $G$ by adjoining the incidence-vector column $e_\gamma$. The associated graft matroid is $M(G,\gamma)=M[A_{(G,\gamma)}]$ with ground set $E(G)\cup\{e_\gamma\}$. This convention does not require $|\gamma|$ to be even. If $|\gamma|$ is odd, then no circuit contains $e_\gamma$, so $e_\gamma$ is a coloop and $M(G,\gamma)$ is graphic.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A graft is a graph G together with a vertex subset gamma. Its binary incidence matrix is the mod-2 vertex-edge incidence matrix of G with an additional column equal to the incidence vector of gamma, and its graft matroid is the represented matroid on E(G) plus that new element. Gamma is not required to have even size. If gamma has odd size, the new element is a coloop and the graft matroid is graphic.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M(G,\gamma)=M[A_{(G,\gamma)}],\quad E(M(G,\gamma))=E(G)\cup\{e_\gamma\};\qquad |\gamma|\text{ odd}\Rightarrow e_\gamma\text{ is a coloop and }M(G,\gamma)\text{ is graphic}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Excluded minors for graphic-or-cographic matroids
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complete obstruction list, including direct-sum and basepoint-restricted 2-sum families.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The excluded minors for the class of matroids that are graphic or cographic are: (i) U_{2,4}, F_7, F_7^*, R_{10}, and R_{12}; (ii) the four direct sums G\oplus H^*, where G\in\{M(K_5),M(K_{3,3})\} and H^*\in\{M^*(K_5),M^*(K_{3,3})\}; and (iii) the nine 2-sums G\oplus_2 H^*, where G\in\{M(K_5),M(K_{3,3}),M(K'_{3,3})\} and H^*\in\{M^*(K_5),M^*(K_{3,3}),M^*(K'_{3,3})\}. The 2-sum basepoints are arbitrary in M(K_5), M(K_{3,3}), M^*(K_5), and M^*(K_{3,3}), but must be z in M(K'_{3,3}) and M^*(K'_{3,3}).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The excluded minors for matroids that are either graphic or cographic comprise five named matroids, four direct sums pairing a graphic obstruction with a cographic obstruction, and nine corresponding 2-sums. For the primed K3,3 matroids the 2-sum basepoint must be z; in the other listed factors it is arbitrary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{Ex}(\mathcal C)\text{ is exactly the families (i)--(iii), with the stated 2-sum basepoint restrictions.}

knowledge_statements.title: Cographic Excluded Minors
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual form of the finite graphic excluded-minor characterization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite matroid \(M\) is cographic if and only if it has no minor isomorphic to any member of \[\{U_{2,4},F_7,F_7^*,M(K_5),M(K_{3,3})\}.\] This follows under matroid duality because deletion and contraction are interchanged, \(U_{2,4}\) is self-dual, \(F_7\) and \(F_7^*\) are dual, and \(M^*(G)^*=M(G)\).

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\text{ is cographic}\iff M\text{ has no minor in }\{U_{2,4},F_7,F_7^*,M(K_5),M(K_{3,3})\}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Duality across Obstruction Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Describes how excluded-minor families transform under matroid duality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal C\) be a minor-closed class of finite matroids, and define \(\mathcal C^*=\{M^*:M\in\mathcal C\}\). If \(\operatorname{Ex}(\mathcal C)\) denotes the excluded minors for \(\mathcal C\), then \[\operatorname{Ex}(\mathcal C^*)=\{X^*:X\in\operatorname{Ex}(\mathcal C)\}.\] Hence graphic and cographic obstruction families are dual, while the regular obstruction family is closed under duality because \(U_{2,4}\) is self-dual and \(F_7^*=F_7^*\) pairs with \(F_7\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dualizing a minor-closed class dualizes every excluded minor; graphic and cographic obstructions correspond, while regular obstructions are duality-invariant.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal C\) is a minor-closed class of finite matroids
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Ex}(\mathcal C^*)=\operatorname{Ex}(\mathcal C)^*\).

The family may be chosen as the excluded minors: every \(N\in\mathcal{X}_q\) is not representable over \(\operatorname{GF}(q)\), while every proper minor of \(N\) is representable over \(\operatorname{GF}(q)\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interface sizes and deletion convention for binary 1-, 2-, and 3-sums.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In the binary-sum representation of a decomposition edge, a \(1\)-sum has \(T=\varnothing\), a \(2\)-sum uses an identified one-element set \(T\), and a \(3\)-sum uses an identified three-element set \(T\). For a proper \(2\)-sum the interface element is neither a loop nor a coloop in either piece. For a proper binary \(3\)-sum, \(T\) is a circuit in each piece and contains no cocircuit of either piece. The interface elements are auxiliary and are deleted from the recomposed matroid.

assumptions_latex: \(M_1\) and \(M_2\) are binary matroids with \(E(M_1)\cap E(M_2)=T\).
\(T\) has three elements, is a circuit of each matroid, and contains no cocircuit of either.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The specified cycle family determines the binary three-sum \(M_1\oplus_3 M_2\) on \((E(M_1)\cup E(M_2))\setminus T\).

notation.meaning: the family of cycles of M

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cycle-space definition of a proper binary three-sum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The binary three-sum \(M=M_1\oplus_3 M_2\) has ground set \((E(M_1)\cup E(M_2))\setminus T\). Its cycles are the sets
\[
\mathcal{Z}(M)=\{Z_1\triangle Z_2: Z_i\in\mathcal{Z}(M_i),\ Z_1\cap T=Z_2\cap T\}.
\]
Because the traces on \(T\) agree, every displayed symmetric difference avoids \(T\). The resulting family is a binary cycle space and therefore determines a binary matroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A binary three-sum matches the two cycle spaces along a common triangle and then removes that triangle.
knowledge_statements.title: Binary Three-Sums

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cycle-space formula is plausible and well formed, but its hypotheses and exact binary three-sum convention are unsupported by a citation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bottom-up recomposition of a binary decomposition tree.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize each leaf \(v\) with its supplied matroid \(M_v\). Process internal nodes in postorder. If \(v\) has children \(a,b\), validate their identified interface and set \(M_v=M_a\oplus_{k_v}M_b\), deleting the interface elements according to the chosen sum convention. Stop after processing the root \(r\), and output \(M_r\). If any interface fails its size, circuit, cocircuit, or element-identification conditions, output an invalid-decomposition report instead of a matroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recompose a decomposition tree bottom-up, validating each interface and applying its indicated one-, two-, or three-sum.
knowledge_statements.title: Three-Sum Recomposition

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits recomposition, but correctness depends on exact sum conventions and interface-validation rules for which no source is supplied.

children.title: Three-Sum Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Boundary data controlling which decomposition pieces can be recomposed.

assumptions_latex: \(M_1\) and \(M_2\) are binary matroids and \(T=E(M_1)\cap E(M_2)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Under these predicates, the cycle-space gluing along \(T\) defines a proper binary three-sum.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compatibility predicate for a proper binary three-sum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The pieces are three-sum compatible when \(|T|=3\); the restrictions of their labels to \(T\) identify the same three elements; \(T\) is a circuit of both \(M_1\) and \(M_2\); and no cocircuit of either matroid is contained in \(T\). Equivalently, \(T\) contains no circuit of \(M_1^*\) or \(M_2^*\). A proper-sum convention may additionally require each piece to retain sufficiently many elements outside \(T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Three-sum compatibility requires a consistently identified common triangle that contains no cocircuit of either piece.
knowledge_statements.title: Three-Sum Compatibility

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The compatibility conditions are convention-sensitive, and the phrase 'sufficiently many elements' leaves a possible properness hypothesis unspecified.

children.title: Recomposition Ambiguity
children.top_down_role: Noncanonical decomposition trees, equivalent recompositions, plus exceptional overlaps.

assumptions_latex: \(M_1\) and \(M_2\) have a compatible three-element interface \(T\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Interface maps differing by \(\phi|_T\) can encode isomorphic recomposed matroids, so decomposition data are not uniquely recoverable from the result.

notation.meaning: an automorphism of the second piece

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonuniqueness caused by interface symmetries and alternative separation choices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose an interface identification \(f:T\to T\) glues \(M_1\) to \(M_2\). Replacing it by \(\phi|_T\circ f\) changes the labeled gluing data whenever \(\phi|_T\) is nontrivial, but applying \(\phi\) on the second piece induces an isomorphism between the two recomposed matroids. Thus a recomposed matroid need not determine its interface identification. More generally, choosing different valid three-separations can yield nonisomorphic decomposition trees with isomorphic roots.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Interface symmetries or different three-separations can produce distinct decomposition descriptions of the same matroid.
knowledge_statements.title: Recomposition Ambiguity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The automorphism argument is plausible, but the labeled-versus-unlabeled convention and broader claim about nonunique decomposition trees need a source or explicit example.

assumptions_latex: A supplied tree has graphic, cographic, or \(R_{10}\) leaves and valid \(1\)-, \(2\)-, or \(3\)-sum nodes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The validated tree certifies that \(M\) is regular; conversely, every regular matroid admits such a tree.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural recognition certificate based on Seymour decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Verify each leaf as graphic, cographic, or isomorphic to \(R_{10}\). At every internal node, verify the stated interface conditions and that its stored matroid equals the indicated \(1\)-, \(2\)-, or \(3\)-sum of its children. Finally verify that the root is isomorphic to \(M\). Since the three leaf classes are regular and regularity is preserved by these sums, the tree certifies regularity. children.title: Optimization over Decomposition Trees
children.top_down_role: Optimization interfaces that combine solutions across a decomposition tree.

assumptions_latex: A rooted decomposition tree represents a binary matroid, and every parent-child interface has at most three elements.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The root table yields the maximum weight of an independent set and backtracking yields an optimizer.

notation.meaning: the rank-marginal signature of I on interface T
the best weight at node v with signature sigma

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-interface dynamic programming for maximum-weight independence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each node \(v\), each independent set \(I\) in its submatroid induces the interface signature \(\sigma_I(X)=r(I\cup X)-r(I)\) for every \(X\subseteq T_v\). At a leaf, compute \(F_v(\sigma)=\max\{w(I):I\text{ is independent and has signature }\sigma\}\). At an internal node, enumerate pairs of child signatures compatible with its sum, combine their values while subtracting any counted interface contribution, and retain the maximum for each parent signature. Output the unrestricted optimum at the root and recover a maximizing set by stored back-pointers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dynamic programming records each partial independent set's rank behavior on the small interface and combines compatible child states.
knowledge_statements.title: Optimization over Decomposition Trees

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source establishes that the proposed rank-marginal signature is sufficient to combine independent-set solutions across every permitted interface.

assumptions_latex: Every leaf supplies a locally checkable certificate and every internal sum supplies its interface map.
The certified property is preserved by each permitted sum when the interface predicates hold.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The collection of leaf certificates, interface checks, and bottom-up transfer records is a certificate for the root property.

notation.meaning: a certificate attached to tree node v
the matroid represented at tree node v

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compositional certificate schema for properties preserved by matroid sums.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Attach to each leaf \(v\) a certificate \(C_v\) verifiable directly for \(M_v\). For an internal node \(v\) with children \(a,b\), verify the interface \(T_v\), verify that \(M_v=M_a\oplus_{k_v}M_b\), and apply the property's stated transfer rule to \(C_a,C_b\) to construct \(C_v\). A verifier processes the tree in postorder and accepts only if every local certificate, interface predicate, and transfer step succeeds. The resulting root object \(C_r\) certifies the property for \(M_r\).

children.title: Decomposition Overheads
children.top_down_role: Costs caused by finding, representing, traversing, or recomposing decomposition pieces.

knowledge_statements.title: Decomposition Overheads
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ground-set duplication overhead in a bounded-adhesion regular-matroid decomposition tree.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) have \(n\) elements and be represented by a tree \(T\) of \(t\) pieces combined by 1-, 2-, or 3-sums. Suppose every tree edge has an adhesion set of size at most \(3\), stored in both incident pieces, and reconstruction deletes the copied adhesion elements. Then the aggregate number of stored ground-set incidences is at most \(n+6(t-1)\). Consequently, tree navigation and interface storage require \(O(t)\) additional space, while scanning all explicitly stored pieces requires \(O(n+t)\) time, excluding decomposition construction and piece-local optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded-adhesion decomposition duplicates only constantly many elements per tree edge, so explicit piece storage and traversal add linear overhead.
assumptions_latex: \(T\) is a finite tree of 1-, 2-, or 3-sum pieces.
Each adhesion set has cardinality at most \(3\).
Each adhesion element is stored at most once at each endpoint of its tree edge.

notation.meaning: stored ground set of the piece at node v

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The bound depends on the precise conventions for 1-, 2-, and 3-sum interfaces, copied adhesion elements, and deletion during reconstruction. No source is supplied, so the exact coefficient and accounting model cannot be validated reliably.

knowledge_statements.title: Independence Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boolean independence-query model for a finite matroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite matroid \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\), an independence oracle is a procedure \(\mathcal O_{\mathrm{ind}}\) that accepts any subset \(X\subseteq E\) and returns \(1\) exactly when \(X\in\mathcal I\), and returns \(0\) otherwise. Oracle complexity counts calls to \(\mathcal O_{\mathrm{ind}}\) separately from ordinary computation and from the cost of encoding or reading subsets of \(E\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An independence oracle answers whether a queried subset of the ground set is independent in the matroid.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal O_{\mathrm{ind}}(X)=1\iff X\in\mathcal I\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Matroid Independence Oracle and Probes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the unit-cost independence-query model and the hereditary deductions supplied by each answer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a matroid M=(E,\mathcal I), an independence oracle is a function \Omega:2^E\to\{\mathrm{YES},\mathrm{NO}\} such that \Omega(X)=\mathrm{YES} if X\in\mathcal I and \Omega(X)=\mathrm{NO} if X\notin\mathcal I. Each unit-time application of \Omega to a subset X\subseteq E is a probe. If \Omega(X)=\mathrm{YES}, then \Omega(Y)=\mathrm{YES} for every Y\subseteq X; if \Omega(X)=\mathrm{NO}, then \Omega(Z)=\mathrm{NO} for every Z\supseteq X.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An independence oracle reports in unit time whether a queried subset is independent, and each query is called a probe. A YES answer also certifies every subset as independent, while a NO answer certifies every superset as dependent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Omega(X)=\mathrm{YES}\iff X\in\mathcal I;\quad \Omega(X)=\mathrm{YES}\Rightarrow\forall Y\subseteq X,\ \Omega(Y)=\mathrm{YES};\quad \Omega(X)=\mathrm{NO}\Rightarrow\forall Z\supseteq X,\ \Omega(Z)=\mathrm{NO}.

knowledge_statements.title: Rank Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integer-valued rank-query model for a finite matroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite matroid \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\), a rank oracle is a procedure \(\mathcal O_r\) that accepts any subset \(X\subseteq E\) and returns its matroid rank \[\mathcal O_r(X)=r_M(X)=\max\{ |I|:I\subseteq X,\ I\in\mathcal I\}.\] Thus every response is an integer between \(0\) and \(|X|\), inclusive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rank oracle returns the maximum cardinality of an independent subset of the queried set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal O_r(X)=r_M(X)\in\{0,\ldots,|X|\}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Closure Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-valued closure-query model for a finite matroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite matroid \(M\) with rank function \(r_M\), a closure oracle is a procedure \(\mathcal O_{\mathrm{cl}}\) that accepts \(X\subseteq E\) and returns \[\mathcal O_{\mathrm{cl}}(X)=\operatorname{cl}_M(X)=\{e\in E:r_M(X\cup\{e\})=r_M(X)\}.\] The response is the entire closure subset, so one oracle call may have output length proportional to \(|E|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closure oracle returns all elements whose addition does not increase the queried set's rank.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(e\in\mathcal O_{\mathrm{cl}}(X)\iff r_M(X\cup\{e\})=r_M(X)\).

children.title: Oracle Simulation Relationships
children.top_down_role: Relative simulation power plus query overheads among the three interfaces.

knowledge_statements.title: Oracle Simulation Relationships
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial query equivalence of independence, rank, and full-set closure oracles.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) be a matroid on \(E\), with \(n=|E|\). A rank query decides independence by testing \(r_M(X)=|X|\). Scanning \(X\) and greedily retaining an element when independence is preserved computes \(r_M(X)\) with at most \(|X|\) independence queries. Rank computes \(\operatorname{cl}_M(X)\) with at most \(n+1\) rank queries. Conversely, scanning \(X\) and adding \(e\) precisely when \(e\notin\operatorname{cl}_M(I)\) computes rank with at most \(|X|\) closure queries. Hence the three models polynomially simulate one another.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independence, rank, and full-set closure oracles simulate one another using only linearly many queries per derived query.
assumptions_latex: A closure response explicitly returns all of \(\operatorname{cl}_M(X)\).
Complexity is measured by oracle-query count.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal O_{\mathrm{ind}}\equiv_{\mathrm{poly}}\mathcal O_r\equiv_{\mathrm{poly}}\mathcal O_{\mathrm{cl}}\), with \(O(n)\) queries per simulation.

knowledge_statements.title: Fundamental-Circuit Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-valued fundamental-circuit query model relative to a supplied basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) be a finite matroid, let \(B\) be a basis, and let \(e\in E\setminus B\). A fundamental-circuit oracle returns the unique circuit \(C_M(e,B)\) contained in \(B\cup\{e\}\). Its output satisfies \(e\in C_M(e,B)\) and, for every \(x\in B\), \[x\in C_M(e,B)\setminus\{e\}\iff (B\setminus\{x\})\cup\{e\}\text{ is a basis of }M.\] Queries whose supplied set is not a basis lie outside this oracle's promised input domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given a basis and an outside element, the oracle returns the unique circuit created by adjoining that element.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_M(e,B)\) is the unique circuit contained in \(B\cup\{e\}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Structural-Oracle Comparisons
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rank predicates characterizing bases, circuits, and fundamental-circuit membership.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite matroid \(M\) on \(E\), rank queries characterize the structural predicates by \[B\text{ is a basis}\iff r_M(B)=|B|=r_M(E),\] and, for nonempty \(C\), \[C\text{ is a circuit}\iff r_M(C)=|C|-1\text{ and }r_M(C\setminus\{e\})=|C|-1\text{ for every }e\in C.\] If \(B\) is a basis and \(f\notin B\), then \(e\in C_M(f,B)\setminus\{f\}\) exactly when \((B\setminus\{e\})\cup\{f\}\) is a basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rank determines basis and circuit membership, while basis-exchange tests determine every element of a fundamental circuit.
assumptions_latex: For the exchange formula, \(B\) is a basis and \(f\notin B\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Basis, circuit, and fundamental-circuit predicates admit the displayed rank and exchange characterizations.

children.title: Explicit Graphic Representations
children.top_down_role: Graph-based encodings of graphic matroids plus their direct computational access.

knowledge_statements.title: Explicit Graphic Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graph presentation of a finite graphic matroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite undirected multigraph \(G=(V,E)\), allowing loops and parallel edges, its cycle matroid \(M(G)\) has ground set \(E\) and independent sets \[\mathcal I(G)=\{F\subseteq E:(V,F)\text{ contains no graph cycle}\}.\] Thus bases restrict on each connected component to spanning trees, nonloop circuits are edge sets of simple cycles, loops form singleton circuits, and parallel nonloop edges form two-element circuits. The explicit input consists of the vertex and edge lists with each edge's endpoints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A graph explicitly represents its cycle matroid: independent edge sets are exactly forests.
assumptions_latex: Loops and parallel edges are permitted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\in\mathcal I(M(G))\iff (V,F)\text{ is a forest}\).

children.title: Explicit Linear Representations
children.top_down_role: Matrix-based encodings over specified fields plus their direct computational access.

knowledge_statements.title: Explicit Linear Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Matrix presentation of a finite field-representable matroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb F^{m\times n}\) be a matrix over a field \(\mathbb F\), with columns indexed by a finite set \(E\). The column matroid \(M[A]\) has ground set \(E\), and \(X\subseteq E\) is independent exactly when the columns \(A_X\) are linearly independent over \(\mathbb F\). Consequently, \[r_{M[A]}(X)=\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb F}(A_X).\] An explicit linear representation specifies \(\mathbb F\), the matrix entries, and the column-to-element indexing.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matrix represents a matroid whose independent sets are the linearly independent subsets of its indexed columns.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb F^{m\times n}\) has columns indexed by \(E\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(X\in\mathcal I(M[A])\iff \operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb F}(A_X)=|X|\).

notation.meaning: submatrix formed by columns indexed by X

children.title: Representation Conversion
children.top_down_role: Conversion or recovery between explicit encodings when structural conditions permit.

knowledge_statements.title: Representation Conversion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conversion of an explicit graph into a linear representation of its cycle matroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected multigraph, choose an orientation of every nonloop edge, and let \(D\) be its signed vertex-edge incidence matrix over a field \(\mathbb F\): a nonloop column has entries \(1\) and \(-1\) at its head and tail, and a loop column is zero. Then \[M[D]=M(G).\] Hence an explicit graphic representation converts to an explicit linear representation over every field in time \(O(|V|+|E|)\) when columns are stored sparsely.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The signed incidence matrix converts any explicit graph into a linear representation of the same cycle matroid over every field.
assumptions_latex: \(D\) is stored by its nonzero column entries.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M[D]=M(G)\), and sparse construction takes \(O(|V|+|E|)\) time.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal R\) be an explicit representation class for finite matroids, and let \(\operatorname{enc}_{\mathcal R}(M)\) be the binary encoding of \(M\) in \(\mathcal R\). An algorithm has representation-sensitive running time \(T_{\mathcal R}\) if, on every valid encoding \(x=\operatorname{enc}_{\mathcal R}(M)\), it terminates within \(T_{\mathcal R}(|x|)\) elementary bit operations. It is polynomial-time for \(\mathcal R\) when some constant \(c\) satisfies \(T_{\mathcal R}(L)=O(L^c)\). This classification is attached to the representation: changing \(\mathcal R\) can change the input length, available primitive operations, and resulting complexity bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Complexity is measured against the length and primitive operations of a chosen matroid encoding; changing the representation can change whether an algorithm is polynomial-time.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a class \(\mathfrak M\) of finite matroids and oracle interfaces \(O_1,O_2\). Define \(O_1\equiv_{\mathrm p}O_2\) exactly when both \(O_1\preceq_{\mathrm p}O_2\) and \(O_2\preceq_{\mathrm p}O_1\). The equivalence classes of \(\equiv_{\mathrm p}\) partition the oracle interfaces under consideration.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two matroid oracles are equivalent when each can answer the other's queries with polynomially many oracle calls and polynomial auxiliary work.

children.title: One-Way Oracle Simulations
children.top_down_role: Directional reductions where one interface can emulate another without a matching reverse reduction.

knowledge_statements.title: One-Way Oracle Simulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directed simulation between two matroid oracle interfaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For oracle interfaces \(O_A\) and \(O_B\) on the same class of finite matroids, a one-way simulation \(O_A\preceq O_B\) is an algorithm that receives a query \(q\) admissible for \(O_A\), accesses the unknown matroid only through adaptive queries to \(O_B\), and returns exactly \(O_A(M,q)\). If at most \(f(n,|q|)\) calls to \(O_B\) and \(g(n,|q|)\) auxiliary bit operations are used, then \((f,g)\) is the simulation cost. No reverse simulation is implied.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A one-way simulation answers every query of one interface by querying another interface, with separately stated oracle-call and auxiliary-work costs.
assumptions_latex: \(O_A\) and \(O_B\) refer to the same finite matroid \(M\).
Every simulated query \(q\) is valid for \(O_A\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The simulator returns \(O_A(M,q)\) using only access to \(O_B\).

children.title: Simulation Overheads
children.top_down_role: Query, arithmetic, encoding, plus adaptivity costs incurred by oracle simulation.

knowledge_statements.title: Simulation Overheads
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Composition law for directed oracle simulations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(O_A\) is simulated by \(O_B\) using at most \(f(n)\) calls per query, and \(O_B\) is simulated by \(O_C\) using at most \(h(n)\) calls per query. Replacing every \(O_B\)-call in the first simulator by the second simulator yields an \(O_C\)-simulation of \(O_A\) using at most \(f(n)h(n)\) oracle calls. If their auxiliary costs are \(g(n)\) and \(k(n)\) per simulated query, respectively, the composed auxiliary cost is at most \(g(n)+f(n)k(n)\), excluding query-copying costs already included in those bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Simulation overheads compose multiplicatively for oracle calls and by substitution for auxiliary work.
assumptions_latex: Both simulations apply to the same \(n\)-element input class.
The inner cost bounds hold uniformly for every adaptive query.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q_{A\leftarrow C}(n)\le f(n)h(n)\) and \(W_{A\leftarrow C}(n)\le g(n)+f(n)k(n)\).

notation.meaning: number of calls to the underlying oracle

children.title: Oracle Separation Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Information gaps preventing efficient simulation between oracle models.

knowledge_statements.title: Oracle Separation Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of unrestricted conversion from abstract oracle access to linear representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V_8\) denote the Vámos matroid and let \(V_8^{\oplus k}\) be the direct sum of \(k\) copies. An independence oracle is well defined for every \(V_8^{\oplus k}\), but no algorithm, regardless of its number of independence queries, can output a matrix over any field representing that matroid: \(V_8\) is not representable over any field, and a restriction of a representable matroid is representable. Thus independence-oracle access cannot simulate a total linear-representation interface on the class of all matroids; a representability promise is indispensable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independence access cannot produce linear representations for arbitrary matroids: direct sums of the Vámos matroid have valid oracles but no field representation.
assumptions_latex: The input class contains arbitrary finite matroids.
A successful representation query must output a matrix over some field representing the input matroid.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No total simulation from independence oracles to linear-representation output exists on this class.

children.title: Dual-Matroid Oracle Construction
children.top_down_role: Derived oracle access for a dual matroid from an oracle for the primal matroid.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual-Matroid Oracle Construction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constructing a dual independence oracle from a primal independence oracle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Input an independence oracle for \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\) and a query \(X\subseteq E\). Compute \(r_M(E)\) and \(r_M(E\setminus X)\) by scanning each relevant set in any order, retaining an element exactly when its addition preserves independence. Return YES precisely when
\[r_M(E\setminus X)=r_M(E)-|X|.\]
The equality is equivalent to \(r_{M^*}(X)=|X|\), so the answer is YES exactly when \(X\) is independent in the dual matroid \(M^*\). The value \(r_M(E)\) may be cached for later queries.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compute two primal ranks greedily; a set is dual-independent exactly when deleting it lowers the primal rank by its cardinality.
assumptions_latex: \(M\) is a finite matroid on known ground set \(E\).
The oracle decides primal independence for every subset of \(E\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(X\in\mathcal I(M^*)\iff r_M(E\setminus X)=r_M(E)-|X|\).

notation.meaning: rank function of the primal matroid

children.title: Minor Oracle Construction
children.top_down_role: Derived oracle access for deletion or contraction minors.

knowledge_statements.title: Minor Oracle Construction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Independence-oracle construction for a deletion-contraction minor.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C,D\subseteq E\) be disjoint and set \(N=M/C\setminus D\), whose ground set is \(E\setminus(C\cup D)\). Given a query \(X\) in this ground set, compute \(r_M(C)\) and \(r_M(C\cup X)\) using the independence oracle and greedy rank computation. Return YES precisely when
\[r_M(C\cup X)-r_M(C)=|X|.\]
Because \(r_{M/C}(X)=r_M(C\cup X)-r_M(C)\), this answers independence in \(N\); deletion requires no further oracle calls. Cache \(r_M(C)\) across queries.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set is independent in a deletion-contraction minor exactly when adjoining it to the contracted set increases primal rank by its size.
assumptions_latex: \(M\) is finite and supplied by an independence oracle.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(X\in\mathcal I(M/C\setminus D)\iff r_M(C\cup X)-r_M(C)=|X|\).

notation.meaning: contraction of C followed by deletion of D
rank function obtained from the primal independence oracle

children.title: Sum Oracle Construction
children.top_down_role: Derived oracle access for matroids assembled through direct sums or higher sums.

knowledge_statements.title: Sum Oracle Construction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Independence oracle for a direct sum of matroids on disjoint ground sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Input independence oracles for matroids \(M_i=(E_i,\mathcal I_i)\), where the sets \(E_1,\ldots,E_k\) are pairwise disjoint. For a query \(X\subseteq\bigcup_{i=1}^k E_i\), form \(X_i=X\cap E_i\) and submit \(X_i\) to the oracle for \(M_i\). Return YES if and only if every component oracle returns YES. The resulting interface is an independence oracle for the direct sum \(M=\bigoplus_{i=1}^k M_i\), since
\[X\in\mathcal I(M)\iff (\forall i)\;X_i\in\mathcal I_i.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: To test independence in a direct sum, intersect the query with each component ground set and accept exactly when every component accepts.
assumptions_latex: The component ground sets \(E_i\) are pairwise disjoint.
Each component independence oracle is correct.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(X\in\mathcal I(\bigoplus_i M_i)\iff (\forall i)\;X\cap E_i\in\mathcal I_i\).

notation.meaning: direct sum of the component matroids
component query X intersected with the i-th ground set

children.title: Derived-Oracle Overheads
children.top_down_role: Query plus representation costs introduced by the derived constructions.

knowledge_statements.title: Derived-Oracle Overheads
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Independence-query bounds for standard derived-matroid oracle constructions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an \(n\)-element matroid, greedy computation of \(r_M(S)\) uses at most \(|S|\) independence calls. Consequently, after caching \(r_M(E)\), a dual-independence query on \(X\) uses at most \(n-|X|\) calls. After caching \(r_M(C)\), an independence query to \(M/C\setminus D\) uses at most \(|C|+|X|\le n\) calls by computing \(r_M(C\cup X)\). For a direct sum of \(k\) oracle-presented components, one independence query uses exactly one component-oracle call per component, hence \(k\) calls, plus set-partitioning work.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cached rank values make dual and minor queries linear in ground-set size; a direct-sum query uses one call to each component oracle.
assumptions_latex: Rank is computed greedily from an independence oracle.
Cached preprocessing costs are excluded from each subsequent query.
Direct-sum components have disjoint ground sets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q_{M^*}(X)\le n-|X|\), \(Q_{M/C\setminus D}(X)\le |C|+|X|\), and \(Q_{\oplus_iM_i}=k\).

notation.meaning: underlying oracle calls needed for a query to derived matroid N
cardinality of the original ground set

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sharp Rank-Quotient Bound for Best-In Greedy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Here $q(E,\mathcal F)$ is the independence-system parameter appearing in the source; the multiplicative form remains meaningful when the optimum value is zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $(E,\mathcal F)$ be an independence system. For every $c:E\to\mathbb R_+$, if $G(E,\mathcal F,c)$ is the value returned by BEST-IN-GREEDY and $\operatorname{OPT}(E,\mathcal F,c)$ is the maximum feasible value, then $q(E,\mathcal F)\operatorname{OPT}(E,\mathcal F,c)\leq G(E,\mathcal F,c)\leq\operatorname{OPT}(E,\mathcal F,c)$. Consequently, when $\operatorname{OPT}>0$, $q(E,\mathcal F)\leq G/\operatorname{OPT}\leq1$. Some nonnegative cost function attains the lower bound.

children.title: Oracle-Call Complexity
children.top_down_role: Complexity measured by the number or structure of oracle queries.

knowledge_statements.title: Oracle-Call Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Query complexity for algorithms accessing a matroid through a fixed oracle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a matroid oracle interface \(O\). For an algorithm \(A\) and an \(n\)-element input matroid \(M\), the oracle-call complexity is the maximum number \(Q_A^O(n)\) of calls to \(O\) made before termination, maximized over all admissible \(M\), ordinary inputs of the prescribed size, and, for randomized algorithms, internal random outcomes unless an expected bound is explicitly declared. Computation between calls is not charged to \(Q_A^O\). A polynomial-query algorithm satisfies \(Q_A^O(n)\le p(n)\) for some polynomial \(p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Oracle-call complexity counts worst-case queries to the chosen matroid interface, separately from computation performed between queries.
assumptions_latex: The oracle interface \(O\) and admissible input class are fixed.
Each oracle invocation counts as one call regardless of its implementation cost.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q_A^O(n)\le p(n)\) characterizes polynomial oracle-call complexity.

notation.meaning: worst-case number of calls made by algorithm A to oracle O

children.title: Arithmetic Complexity
children.top_down_role: Field-operation or numerical-operation costs beyond oracle access.

knowledge_statements.title: Arithmetic Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operation-count complexity for explicitly represented numerical matroid data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a field \(\mathbb F\) and an arithmetic model in which addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by a nonzero element, and equality tests in \(\mathbb F\) have specified unit or separately stated costs. For an algorithm \(A\) operating on an explicit representation of size parameter \(N\), its arithmetic complexity \(C_A^{\mathrm{arith}}(N)\) is the maximum number of such field operations performed on any admissible input of size \(N\). This measure excludes coefficient bit lengths and bit-level operation costs unless they are incorporated explicitly; therefore an arithmetic polynomial bound alone need not imply polynomial bit complexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Arithmetic complexity counts field operations on an explicit representation and does not by itself control coefficient growth or bit complexity.
assumptions_latex: Inputs are explicitly represented over a specified field \(\mathbb F\).
The charged arithmetic operations are fixed in advance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_A^{\mathrm{arith}}(N)\) counts charged field operations, independently of uncharged operand bit lengths.

children.title: Encoding Complexity
children.top_down_role: Bit length, representation size, plus data-access costs.

knowledge_statements.title: Encoding Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bit-length accounting for explicit matroid inputs, queries, and numerical data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a fixed binary encoding map \(\operatorname{enc}\), the encoding complexity of an instance \(I\) is its bit length \(L(I)=|\operatorname{enc}(I)|\). For a matrix-represented matroid, the encoding must specify the dimensions, field or coefficient domain, entries, and any auxiliary weights; rational entries are encoded by signed binary numerators and positive binary denominators under a stated convention. An algorithm is polynomial in the encoding when its bit-operation count is bounded by a polynomial in \(L(I)\), including the cost of reading, writing, and manipulating all queries, answers, and intermediate numbers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Encoding complexity is total binary input length; polynomial bit complexity must also account for queries, answers, and growth of intermediate numbers.
assumptions_latex: A uniquely decodable binary encoding convention is fixed.
All explicit numerical and combinatorial input data are included.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Polynomial encoding complexity means a bit-operation bound \(O(L(I)^c)\) for some constant \(c\).

children.title: Cost-Measure Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Regimes where improvements under one cost measure increase another resource.

knowledge_statements.title: Cost-Measure Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates oracle calls, auxiliary computation, and representation-dependent oracle-evaluation cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an algorithm issuing queries \(q_1,\ldots,q_Q\), let \(A\) be its auxiliary bit-operation cost and let \(C_\rho(q_i)\) be the cost of answering \(q_i\) from representation \(\rho\). Its implemented running time satisfies \[T_\rho=A+\sum_{i=1}^{Q}C_\rho(q_i).\] Thus a bound on \(Q\) alone is a unit-cost oracle bound. It yields a polynomial bit-time bound only when \(A\), \(Q\), and every relevant \(C_\rho(q_i)\) are polynomially bounded in the encoded input length.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Oracle-call complexity becomes a bit-time guarantee only after accounting for auxiliary work and the representation-dependent cost of answering each query.
assumptions_latex: \(Q<\infty\) and each oracle response is computed from an encoding \(\rho\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_\rho=A+\sum_{i=1}^{Q}C_\rho(q_i)\), so query and bit complexities need not coincide.

notation.meaning: cost of answering query q under representation rho

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider instances with combinatorial dimension \(n\) and finitely encoded rational numerical data. Relative to a specified arithmetic and oracle model, an algorithm is strongly polynomial if the number \(N_{\mathrm{op}}\) of arithmetic operations, comparisons, and specified unit-cost oracle calls is bounded by a polynomial in \(n\), independently of the numerical values and their encoding lengths, and every intermediate rational number has encoding length polynomial in the input length. Thus the operation-count bound, though not necessarily the actual operation count, is unaffected when numerical magnitudes grow while \(n\) is fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong polynomiality requires a combinatorial operation bound independent of numerical magnitudes and polynomially bounded intermediate encodings; the bound need not make the actual operation count identical on all inputs of the same combinatorial size.

children.title: Weakly Polynomial Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Cases where encoding length or numerical magnitude prevents a strongly polynomial classification.

knowledge_statements.title: Weakly Polynomial Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes ordinary bit-polynomial algorithms from strongly polynomial and pseudopolynomial algorithms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n\) be combinatorial size, \(L\) the total binary encoding length, and \(U\) the largest encoded magnitude. A running-time bound polynomial in \(n\) and \(L\), but whose arithmetic or iteration count depends on \(L\), is polynomial-time yet not thereby strongly polynomial. A bound polynomial in \(n\) and \(U\) is only pseudopolynomial: because \(L\) may be \(\Theta(\log U)\), such a bound can be exponential in the binary input length.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dependence polynomial in encoding length may prevent strong polynomiality; dependence polynomial in numeric magnitude may even be exponential in binary input size.
assumptions_latex: \(U\ge 2\) is binary encoded, so its contribution to \(L\) is \(\Theta(\log U)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{poly}(n,L)\) need not be strongly polynomial, while \(\operatorname{poly}(n,U)\) need not be polynomial in \(L\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For finitely encoded rational instances, a strongly polynomial algorithm is polynomial-time in the bit model because its operation count is bounded polynomially in the combinatorial size and its intermediate encodings remain polynomially bounded. The reverse implication does not hold in general: a bit-polynomial algorithm may have an iteration count depending on the numerical encoding length. Separately, a pseudopolynomial bound that is polynomial in a numerical magnitude \(U\) need not be polynomial in the binary encoding length of \(U\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong polynomiality implies bit-polynomial time, but bit-polynomial time need not be strongly polynomial, and a pseudopolynomial magnitude bound need not be bit-polynomial.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition of a worst-case deterministic decision-tree lower bound for a fixed matroid oracle model and computational task.

source_refs.locator: The Running Time of Oracle Algorithms p. 26

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix an instance class \(\mathcal X\), a size function \(s:\mathcal X\to\mathbb N\), the subclass \(\mathcal X_n=\{x\in\mathcal X:s(x)=n\}\), an oracle \(O_x\) for each \(x\in\mathcal X\), and a valid-output relation \(R\). A deterministic oracle-query lower bound \(Q(n)\) means that every deterministic algorithm which, on every \(x\in\mathcal X_n\), produces some output \(y\) satisfying \((x,y)\in R\), has an instance \(x\in\mathcal X_n\) on which it submits at least \(Q(n)\) oracle queries. Computation between queries is unrestricted unless the model explicitly imposes another cost bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A deterministic query lower bound forces every algorithm correct on all size-n instances to make at least the stated number of oracle queries on some size-n instance, irrespective of unrestricted computation between queries.

children.title: Adaptivity Lower Bounds
children.top_down_role: Limits on the number of sequential query rounds required under parallel access.

knowledge_statements.title: Adaptivity Lower Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Round-adaptivity lower bounds in a batched matroid-oracle decision model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An \(r\)-round oracle algorithm partitions its queries into batches \(B_1,\ldots,B_r\), where \(B_i\) may depend on all answers to earlier batches but queries within \(B_i\) are fixed before any answer from that batch is received. An adaptivity lower bound \(r(n)\) for a task means that every algorithm correct on all size-\(n\) instances requires at least \(r(n)\) such rounds on some instance, subject to the stated query budget and success criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An adaptivity lower bound forces many sequential batches even though every query within a batch may be issued in parallel.
assumptions_latex: The oracle, correctness requirement, and any total-query budget are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\forall A\,\exists x\in\mathcal X_n:\ \operatorname{rounds}_A(x)\ge r(n)\).

children.title: Randomized Query Boundaries

knowledge_statements.title: Randomized Query Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounded-error randomized query complexity with explicit worst-case success and cost conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(0<\delta<1/2\). A randomized oracle algorithm has bounded-error query complexity at most \(Q(n)\) if, for every size-\(n\) instance \(x\), it returns a valid output with probability at least \(1-\delta\) and uses at most \(Q(n)\) queries under the declared worst-case or expected-query convention. A randomized lower bound must use the same convention and quantify over every randomized algorithm; an average-case distribution alone does not establish a worst-case bound without an applicable minimax argument.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Randomized query claims must specify error probability, worst-case success, and whether query cost is worst-case or expected.
assumptions_latex: \(0<\delta<1/2\), and probability is over the algorithm's internal randomness.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{x\in\mathcal X_n}\Pr[R(x,A(x))]\ge1-\delta\) together with the declared \(Q(n)\) query bound.

children.title: Query–Adaptivity Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Lower-bound regimes linking total query volume to the number of adaptive rounds.

knowledge_statements.title: Query–Adaptivity Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pareto representation of total-query cost versus sequential oracle rounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a fixed task and oracle model, define \(Q_r(n)\) as the minimum worst-case number of queries among algorithms using at most \(r\) adaptive rounds, with value \(+\infty\) if no such algorithm exists. Then \[Q_{r+1}(n)\le Q_r(n).\] Dually, if \(R_Q(n)\) is the minimum number of rounds among algorithms using at most \(Q\) queries, then \(R_{Q+1}(n)\le R_Q(n)\). The attainable pairs \((r,Q)\) form an upward-closed set whose minimal elements describe the query–adaptivity frontier.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Allowing more rounds cannot increase minimum query complexity, and allowing more queries cannot increase minimum round complexity.
assumptions_latex: The task, oracle, correctness criterion, and deterministic or randomized convention are fixed.

knowledge_statements.title: Representation-Sensitive Tractability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transfers oracle tractability to bit tractability only through an efficient representation-specific simulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\rho\) encode a matroid on a ground set of size \(n\). Suppose an oracle algorithm makes at most \(Q(n)\) queries, performs \(A(n,|\rho|)\) auxiliary bit operations, and every query can be answered from \(\rho\) in at most \(C(n,|\rho|)\) bit operations. Then its implementation runs in at most \[A(n,|\rho|)+Q(n)C(n,|\rho|)\] bit operations. Hence polynomial oracle complexity implies polynomial-time tractability for \(\rho\) only when the representation and required oracle simulation are polynomially manageable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polynomial-query matroid algorithm is polynomial in an explicit representation only when its required oracle can also be simulated polynomially.
assumptions_latex: \(\rho\) is a finite representation from which every required oracle answer is computable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_\rho\le A(n,|\rho|)+Q(n)C(n,|\rho|)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Rado–Edmonds lexicographic characterization of matroids
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes finite matroids through universal maximum-weight optimality of lexicographically maximum feasible sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $(E,\mathcal I)$ be a finite hereditary set system satisfying the source's axiom (3.1). Then $(E,\mathcal I)$ is a matroid if and only if, for every nonnegative weighting $w:E\to\mathbb R_{\ge 0}$, a lexicographically maximum member of $\mathcal I$ has maximum total weight over $\mathcal I$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite hereditary set system is a matroid exactly when, under every nonnegative element weighting, a lexicographically maximum feasible set also has maximum total weight.
assumptions_latex: (E,\mathcal I)\text{ satisfies the hereditary condition referenced as (3.1)}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (E,\mathcal I)\text{ is a matroid}\iff\forall w\ge 0,\ \text{a lexicographically maximum }I\in\mathcal I\text{ maximizes }\sum_{e\in I}w(e).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gale-optimal matroid base
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines elementwise weight dominance over every independent set of a weighted matroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $M=(E,\mathcal I)$ be a matroid with weights $w:E\to\mathbb R$. A set $B\in\mathcal I$ is Gale optimal in $\mathcal I$ if, for every $I\in\mathcal I$, there exists an injective map $h:I\to B$ such that $w(e)\le w(h(e))$ for every $e\in I$. Equivalently, after arranging weights in nonincreasing order, the $k$th-largest weight in $B$ is at least the $k$th-largest weight in every $I\in\mathcal I$ at each position present in $I$. A Gale-optimal independent set is necessarily a base.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matroid independent set is Gale optimal when every other independent set can be injected into it so that every element is matched to one of at least equal weight. Such a set must be a base.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: B\text{ is Gale optimal}\iff\forall I\in\mathcal I\ \exists\text{ injective }h:I\to B\ \forall e\in I,\ w(e)\le w(h(e));\qquad B\text{ Gale optimal}\Rightarrow B\text{ is a base}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bimatroids correspond to matroids with a distinguished base
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterization of a bimatroid through its associated family of subsets of the combined ground set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let U and W be the ground sets in a triple (U,W,\Lambda), and let \mathcal{B} be the associated set family that determines \Lambda. Then (U,W,\Lambda) is a bimatroid if and only if \mathcal{B} is the collection of bases of a matroid on U\cup W and U\in\mathcal{B}. Consequently, bimatroids are in one-to-one correspondence with pairs (M,B), where M is a matroid and B is a base of M.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A triple consisting of two ground sets and its associated relation is a bimatroid exactly when the associated set family is the full base family of a matroid on the union and contains the first ground set as a base. Thus bimatroids correspond bijectively to matroids equipped with a distinguished base.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal{B}\text{ is the set family associated with }(U,W,\Lambda)\text{ and determines }\Lambda
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (U,W,\Lambda)\text{ is a bimatroid}\iff \exists M\text{ on }U\cup W:\ \mathcal{B}=\mathcal{B}(M)\text{ and }U\in\mathcal{B}(M)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exchange Optimality Condition for a Maximum-Weight Basis
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes maximum-weight bases using all feasible single-element basis exchanges.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $M=(S,\mathcal I)$ be a matroid, let $c\in\mathbb R^S$, and let $J$ be a basis of $M$. Then $J$ is a maximum-weight basis if and only if, for every $e\notin J$ and $f\in J$ such that $(J\cup\{e\})\setminus\{f\}\in\mathcal I$, one has $c_e\leq c_f$.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: J\text{ is a maximum-weight basis}\iff\forall e\notin J\ \forall f\in J,\ ((J\cup\{e\})\setminus\{f\}\in\mathcal I\Rightarrow c_e\leq c_f)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Rank Function and Bases
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions for an independence system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an independence system \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\), define \(r_M(X):=\max\{|Y|:Y\subseteq X,\ Y\in\mathcal I\}\) for every \(X\subseteq E\). The rank of \(M\) is \(r_M(E)\). A set \(S\subseteq E\) is a base of \(M\) if \(S\in\mathcal I\) and \(|S|=r_M(E)\); write \(\mathcal B(M)\) for the family of all bases.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The rank of a subset is the largest cardinality of an independent subset it contains. The rank of the system is the rank of its ground set, and a base is an independent set attaining that rank.
assumptions_latex: M=(E,\mathcal I)\text{ is an independence system}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: r_M(X)=\max\{|Y|:Y\subseteq X,\ Y\in\mathcal I\},\qquad \mathcal B(M)=\{S\in\mathcal I:|S|=r_M(E)\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Rank characterization of finite matroids
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficiency of the rank axioms and recovery of the independent sets and rank function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $E$ be finite and let $r:2^E\to\mathbb R$ satisfy: (i) $r(X)$ is an integer and $0\le r(X)\le |X|$ for every $X\subseteq E$; (ii) $X\subseteq Y$ implies $r(X)\le r(Y)$; and (iii) $r(X\cup Y)+r(X\cap Y)\le r(X)+r(Y)$ for all $X,Y\subseteq E$. Then $$\mathcal I=\{Y\subseteq E:|Y|=r(Y)\}$$ is the independent-set family of a matroid $M$ on $E$, and $r_M=r$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every integer-valued set function on a finite ground set that is cardinality-bounded, monotone, and submodular is the rank function of the matroid whose independent sets are exactly the sets Y satisfying r(Y)=|Y|.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal I=\{Y\subseteq E:|Y|=r(Y)\}\text{ defines a matroid }M\text{ on }E\text{ with }r_M=r

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hereditary subset system and its weighted optimization problem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a finite independence system and the associated nonnegative-weight maximization problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A subset system is a pair $(E,\mathcal I)$ in which $E$ is finite and $\mathcal I\subseteq 2^E$ is hereditary: if $A\in\mathcal I$ and $A'\subseteq A$, then $A'\in\mathcal I$. knowledge_statements.statement_title: Optimality Conditions for a Maximum-Weight Independent Set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes global weighted optimality through element signs, feasible augmentation, and feasible one-element exchanges.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $M=(S,\mathcal I)$ be a matroid, $c\in\mathbb R^S$, and $J\in\mathcal I$. Then $J$ is a maximum-weight independent set if and only if all of the following hold: (a) $c_e\geq0$ for every $e\in J$; (b) if $e\notin J$ and $J\cup\{e\}\in\mathcal I$, then $c_e\leq0$; and (c) if $e\notin J$, $f\in J$, and $(J\cup\{e\})\setminus\{f\}\in\mathcal I$, then $c_e\leq c_f$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An independent set is maximum-weight exactly when its selected elements have nonnegative weights, every feasible addition has nonpositive weight, and no feasible one-element exchange replaces a selected element by a heavier unselected element.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: J\text{ is maximum-weight}\iff\begin{cases}\forall e\in J,\ c_e\geq0,\\ \forall e\notin J,\ J\cup\{e\}\in\mathcal I\Rightarrow c_e\leq0,\\ \forall e\notin J,\forall f\in J,\ (J\cup\{e\})\setminus\{f\}\in\mathcal I\Rightarrow c_e\leq c_f.\end{cases}

knowledge_statements.title: Exchange Sufficiency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficiency direction of the finite matroid greedy characterization for nonnegative weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) be finite and let \(\mathcal I\subseteq2^E\) be nonempty, hereditary, and satisfy augmentation: whenever \(I,J\in\mathcal I\) and \(|I|<|J|\), some \(e\in J\setminus I\) has \(I\cup\{e\}\in\mathcal I\). For any weight function \(w:E\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}\), inspect elements in nonincreasing weight order and add an inspected element exactly when independence is preserved. The resulting set \(G\) satisfies \[w(G)=\max\{w(I):I\in\mathcal I\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The hereditary and augmentation axioms ensure that descending-weight greedy returns a maximum-weight independent set for every nonnegative weighting.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) is finite and \((E,\mathcal I)\) satisfies heredity and augmentation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{I\in\mathcal I}\sum_{e\in I}w(e)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exchange characterization of maximum-weight independent sets of fixed size
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Here c(S) denotes the total weight of S, and C(X,y) is the circuit created by adjoining y to X when the resulting set is dependent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $(E,\mathcal F)$ be a matroid, $c:E\to\mathbb R$, $k\in\mathbb N$, and $X\in\mathcal F$ with $|X|=k$. Then
\[
c(X)=\max\{c(Y):Y\in\mathcal F,\ |Y|=k\}
\]
if and only if both conditions hold: (a) for every $y\in E\setminus X$ such that $X\cup\{y\}\notin\mathcal F$ and every $x\in C(X,y)$, $c(x)\ge c(y)$; and (b) for every $y\in E\setminus X$ such that $X\cup\{y\}\in\mathcal F$ and every $x\in X$, $c(x)\ge c(y)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An independent set X of cardinality k has maximum total weight among all independent k-element sets exactly when every element that could replace an element through a fundamental circuit has no greater weight than any eligible circuit element, and every element that can be added while preserving independence has no greater weight than every element of X.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: c(X)=\max\{c(Y):Y\in\mathcal F,\ |Y|=k\}\iff\bigl[(a)\land(b)\bigr]

knowledge_statements.title: Universal-Weight Converse
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Converse greedy characterization for finite hereditary independence systems and nonnegative weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) be finite and let \(\mathcal I\subseteq2^E\) be nonempty and hereditary. Suppose that, for every \(w:E\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}\) and every ordering nonincreasing in \(w\), the algorithm that accepts an element exactly when its addition preserves membership in \(\mathcal I\) returns a maximum-weight member of \(\mathcal I\). Then augmentation holds: for all \(I,J\in\mathcal I\) with \(|I|<|J|\), there exists \(e\in J\setminus I\) such that \(I\cup\{e\}\in\mathcal I\). Thus \((E,\mathcal I)\) is a matroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If descending-weight greedy is optimal for every nonnegative weighting, a finite hereditary system must satisfy augmentation and therefore be a matroid.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) is finite, and \(\mathcal I\) is nonempty and hereditary.
Greedy is optimal for every nonnegative weight function and every compatible tie ordering.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\forall I,J\in\mathcal I,\ |I|<|J|\Rightarrow\exists e\in J\setminus I:\ I\cup\{e\}\in\mathcal I\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Independence-Correlated, Spanning-Correlated, and Correlated Matroids
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the weighted correlation classes and records the stated dual equivalence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $M$ be a matroid on $E$ and $\mathbf z:E\to\mathbb R$. For disjoint $U,V\subseteq E$, let $i_U^V(M;\mathbf z)$ be the sum of $\mathbf z(A)=\prod_{a\in A}\mathbf z(a)$ over independent sets $A$ containing $U$ and avoiding $V$, and let $s_U^V(M;\mathbf z)$ be the analogous sum over spanning sets. The matroid $M$ is independence-correlated if, for every distinct $e,f\in E$ and every positive $\mathbf z$, \[i_e(M;\mathbf z)i_f(M;\mathbf z)-i_{ef}(M;\mathbf z)i(M;\mathbf z)\geq0.\] It is spanning-correlated when the analogous inequality holds with $i$ replaced by $s$, and it is correlated when both conditions hold. Moreover, \[M\text{ is independence-correlated}\iff M^*\text{ is spanning-correlated}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weighted sums are formed over independent sets or spanning sets subject to containment and avoidance conditions. Independence correlation and spanning correlation require the corresponding pairwise inequality for every distinct pair of elements and every positive weight function. A matroid is correlated when it has both properties, and independence correlation of a matroid is equivalent to spanning correlation of its dual.
assumptions_latex: $M$ is a matroid on ground set $E$.
$\mathbf z:E\to\mathbb R$ is positive for the correlation inequalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M\text{ is independence-correlated}\iff M^*\text{ is spanning-correlated},\qquad M\text{ is correlated}\iff(M\text{ has both properties}).
