knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cardinality Min–Max Theorem for Matroid Intersection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equates the maximum cardinality of a common independent set with a rank-function minimum over bipartitions of the ground set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let M_1=(E,\mathcal I_1) and M_2=(E,\mathcal I_2) be matroids with rank functions r_1 and r_2. Then
\[
\max\{|I|:I\in\mathcal I_1\cap\mathcal I_2\}=\min\{r_1(S)+r_2(E\setminus S):S\subseteq E\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The maximum size of a set independent in both matroids equals the minimum, over all subsets of the ground set, of the first matroid's rank on the subset plus the second matroid's rank on its complement.
assumptions_latex: M_1=(E,\mathcal I_1)\text{ and }M_2=(E,\mathcal I_2)\text{ are matroids}.
r_1\text{ and }r_2\text{ are their respective rank functions}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \max\{|I|:I\in\mathcal I_1\cap\mathcal I_2\}=\min_{S\subseteq E}\bigl(r_1(S)+r_2(E\setminus S)\bigr).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Matroid Intersection Augmenting-Path Algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unweighted intersection of two matroids using independence tests and the relevant fundamental circuits.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $M=(E,\mathcal I_M)$ and $N=(E,\mathcal I_N)$ be matroids, and maintain $I\in\mathcal I_M\cap\mathcal I_N$, initially $I=\varnothing$. For each $e\in E\setminus I$, make $e$ a source if $I+e\in\mathcal I_M$ and a sink if $I+e\in\mathcal I_N$. If $I+e$ is independent in both matroids, replace $I$ by $I+e$. Otherwise construct the directed exchange graph: when $I+e$ is dependent in $M$, add $(f,e)$ for every $f$ other than $e$ in its fundamental circuit; when $I+e$ is dependent in $N$, add $(e,f)$ for every $f$ other than $e$ in its fundamental circuit. Search from the sources. Upon reaching a sink along a directed path $P$, replace $I$ by $I\triangle V(P)$ and rebuild the graph. If no sink is reachable, return $I$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Begin with the empty common independent set. Build the directed exchange graph determined by the two matroids, search from elements addable in the first matroid to elements addable in the second, and toggle membership along each discovered augmenting path. Rebuild after every augmentation and return the set when no augmenting path exists.
assumptions_latex: M=(E,\mathcal I_M)\text{ and }N=(E,\mathcal I_N)\text{ are matroids on the same finite ground set }E.
\text{The supplied procedures determine the required independence conditions and fundamental circuits.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: I\in\mathcal I_M\cap\mathcal I_N\quad\text{and, at termination,}\quad |I|=\max\{|J|:J\in\mathcal I_M\cap\mathcal I_N\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Generalized-polymatroid intersection theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasibility characterization and integral-element guarantee for the intersection of two generalized polymatroids.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let (p_1,b_1) and (p_2,b_2) be paramodular pairs, and let Q_i=Q(p_i,b_i) for i=1,2. Then Q_1\cap Q_2\neq\varnothing if and only if p_1(X)\le b_2(X) and p_2(X)\le b_1(X) for every X\subseteq S. If p_1,b_1,p_2,b_2 are integer-valued and Q_1\cap Q_2\neq\varnothing, then Q_1\cap Q_2 contains an integral element.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two generalized polymatroids defined by paramodular pairs intersect exactly when each lower border is pointwise at most the other upper border. If all four border functions are integer-valued, every nonempty intersection contains an integral element.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
Q_1\cap Q_2
eq\varnothing\iff [p_1\le b_2\ 	ext{and}\ p_2\le b_1];\quad p_1,b_1,p_2,b_2	ext{ integral and }Q_1\cap Q_2
eq\varnothing\implies (Q_1\cap Q_2)\cap\mathbb{Z}^S
eq\varnothing.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Infinitesimal and minimal rigidity in the plane
knowledge_statements.scope_note: For a framework in the plane with underlying graph G and its associated infinitesimal-motion linear system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A planar framework is infinitesimally rigid if its only infinitesimal motions are rigid motions of the plane; equivalently, its associated linear system has rank \(2|V(G)|-3\). If \(|E(G)|<2|V(G)|-3\), the framework is not infinitesimally rigid. An infinitesimally rigid framework is said to have unnecessary lines if \(|E(G)|>2|V(G)|-3\). It is minimally infinitesimally rigid if it is infinitesimally rigid and deletion of any line destroys infinitesimal rigidity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A planar framework is infinitesimally rigid when its only infinitesimal motions are rigid motions of the plane, equivalently when the associated system has rank 2|V|-3. Fewer than 2|V|-3 lines preclude infinitesimal rigidity. A rigid framework with more lines is said to have unnecessary lines, while minimal rigidity means that deleting any line destroys rigidity.
assumptions_latex: G\text{ is the underlying graph of a framework in }\mathbb{R}^2
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{infinitesimal rigidity}\iff \operatorname{rank}(\text{associated linear system})=2|V(G)|-3;\quad |E(G)|<2|V(G)|-3\Rightarrow\text{not infinitesimally rigid}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Common-Basis Subset-Intersection Min-Max Formula
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A partition formula for the minimum intersection of a common basis with a prescribed subset.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M_1\) and \(M_2\) be rank-\(k\) matroids on a common ground set \(S\), and suppose that they have a common basis. For \(T\subseteq S\), let \(r_{12}(T)\) be the maximum cardinality of a common independent subset of \(T\). Then, for every \(R\subseteq S\), \[\min\{|R\cap B|:B\text{ is a common basis}\}=\max_{\{R_1,\ldots,R_t\}\text{ a partition of }R}\sum_{i=1}^t\bigl[k-r_{12}(S\setminus R_i)\bigr].\]

M_1\text{ and }M_2\text{ have a common basis}
r_{12}(T)=\max\{|I|:I\subseteq T\text{ is independent in both }M_1\text{ and }M_2\}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weight maximality and fixed-cardinality common-independence notation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted set families and common independent sets of two matroids.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $M_i=(S,\mathcal F_i)$ for $i=1,2$, let $c:S\to\mathbb R$, and let $\mathcal H\subseteq2^S$. A set $X\in\mathcal H$ is $c$-maximal in $\mathcal H$ if
\[
c(X)\ge c(Y)\quad\text{for every }Y\in\mathcal H.
\]
For $k\ge0$, define $\mathcal H^k:=\{X\in\mathcal H:|X|=k\}$ and
\[
\mathcal F_{12}^k:=\{X\in\mathcal F_1\cap\mathcal F_2:|X|=k\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A member of a weighted set family is c-maximal if its total weight is at least that of every other member. The superscript k denotes the k-element subfamily, and F_12^k denotes the k-element sets independent in both matroids.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: X\text{ is }c\text{-maximal in }\mathcal H\iff X\in\mathcal H\text{ and }c(X)\ge c(Y)\ \forall Y\in\mathcal H;\quad \mathcal H^k=\{X\in\mathcal H:|X|=k\},\quad \mathcal F_{12}^k=\{X\in\mathcal F_1\cap\mathcal F_2:|X|=k\}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Minimum cover by common partial transversals
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Min-max formula for covering a ground set by common partial systems of distinct representatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal A=(A_1,\ldots,A_n)\) and \(\mathcal B=(B_1,\ldots,B_n)\) be families of subsets of \(S\), each with union \(S\). The minimum number of common partial transversals of \(\mathcal A\) and \(\mathcal B\) needed to cover \(S\) equals
\[
\left\lceil\max_{\varnothing\ne X\subseteq S}\max\left\{\frac{|X|}{|\{i\mid A_i\cap X\ne\varnothing\}|},\frac{|X|}{|\{i\mid B_i\cap X\ne\varnothing\}|}\right\}\right\rceil.
\]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Augmenting-Path Algorithm for Cardinality Matroid Intersection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An augmentation step for a common independent set, or a certificate that its cardinality is maximum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given matroids \(M_1=(S,\mathcal I_1)\), \(M_2=(S,\mathcal I_2)\), and \(I\in\mathcal I_1\cap\mathcal I_2\), define
\[
X_j=\{x\in S\setminus I:I\cup\{x\}\in\mathcal I_j\},\qquad j=1,2.
\]
In the associated exchange digraph \(D_{M_1,M_2}(I)\), if an \(X_1\)-to-\(X_2\) path exists, choose one having the minimum number of arcs and output \(I'=I\triangle V(P)\); a length-zero path is allowed when \(X_1\cap X_2\ne\varnothing\). If no such path exists, conclude that \(I\) is a maximum-size common independent set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Search the matroid-intersection exchange digraph for a shortest path between the two sets of elements individually addable in the respective matroids. Symmetric difference with the path vertices supplies the proposed augmentation; if no such path exists, the current common independent set is maximum-size.
assumptions_latex: M_1=(S,\mathcal I_1)\text{ and }M_2=(S,\mathcal I_2)\text{ are matroids on the same ground set }S
D_{M_1,M_2}(I)\text{ is the associated directed exchange graph}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \begin{cases}I'=I\triangle V(P),&\text{if a minimum-arc }X_1\text{-to-}X_2\text{ path }P\text{ exists},\\ I\text{ is maximum-size in }\mathcal I_1\cap\mathcal I_2,&\text{if no such path exists.}\end{cases}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Criterion for disjoint common partial transversals of prescribed size
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact intersection-cardinality criterion for packing equal-size common partial transversals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal A=(A_1,\ldots,A_n)\) and \(\mathcal B=(B_1,\ldots,B_m)\) be families of sets, and let \(k,p\in\mathbb Z_+\). With \(A_I:=\bigcup_{i\in I}A_i\) and \(B_J:=\bigcup_{j\in J}B_j\), there exist \(k\) pairwise disjoint common partial transversals, each of size \(p\), if and only if
\[
|A_I\cap B_J|\ge k\bigl(|I|+|J|+p-n-m\bigr)
\]
for all \(I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and \(J\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: There are k disjoint common partial transversals of size p exactly when every pair of index subsets satisfies the stated lower bound on the intersection of the corresponding unions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\ k\text{ pairwise disjoint common partial transversals of size }p\iff \forall I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\},\ \forall J\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\},\ |A_I\cap B_J|\ge k(|I|+|J|+p-n-m)

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every common independent set \(I\in\mathcal I_1\cap\mathcal I_2\) and every \(U\subseteq E\), one has \(|I|\leq r_1(U)+r_2(E\setminus U)\). Moreover, equality is attained after maximizing over common independent sets and minimizing over subsets:
\[\max_{I\in\mathcal I_1\cap\mathcal I_2}|I|=\min_{U\subseteq E}\left(r_1(U)+r_2(E\setminus U)\right).\]
Thus a common independent set and a subset attaining equal values form primal and dual optimality certificates.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Chainwise Characterization of Maximum Common Subbases
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global-to-local decomposition along a maximal chain of the specified lattice.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal C:S^-=S_1\subset S_2\subset\cdots\subset S_k=S^+\) be any maximal chain of \(\mathcal L\), with \(S_0=\varnothing\) and \(S_{k+1}=E\). Then \(x\) is a maximum common subbase of \((\mathcal D_1,f_1)\) and \((\mathcal D_2,f_2)\) if and only if, for every \(i=1,\ldots,k+1\), the restriction \(x^{S_i-S_{i-1}}\) is a maximum common subbase of \((\mathcal D_1,f_1)\cdot S_i/S_{i-1}\) and \((\mathcal D_2,f_2)\cdot(E-S_{i-1})/(E-S_i)\). In addition, \(x^{S_i-S_{i-1}}\) is a base of the first minor for \(i=1,\ldots,k\) and a base of the second minor for \(i=2,\ldots,k+1\). The case \(i=1\) is omitted when \(S_1=\varnothing\), and the case \(i=k+1\) is omitted when \(S_k=E\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Along any maximal chain from S-minus to S-plus, a vector is a global maximum common subbase exactly when each layer restriction is a maximum common subbase of the corresponding minors, with the stated base conditions on the first and second systems and omission of empty boundary layers.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal C:S^-=S_1\subset\cdots\subset S_k=S^+\) is a maximal chain of \(\mathcal L\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\text{ is a maximum common subbase}\iff\forall i,\ x^{S_i-S_{i-1}}\text{ satisfies the stated maximum-common-subbase and base conditions for the corresponding minors, subject to the boundary omissions}.\)

There exists an oracle-polynomial weighted matroid-intersection algorithm that returns a set
\[I^*\in\arg\max\left\{w(I):I\in\mathcal I_1\cap\mathcal I_2\right\}.\]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Min–max formula for maximum-weight common partial transversals
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted common-partial-transversal min–max characterization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal A=(A_1,\ldots,A_k)\) and \(\mathcal B=(B_1,\ldots,B_l)\) be families of subsets of \(S\), and let \(w:S\to\mathbb Z_+\). Then
\[
\max\{w(T):T\text{ is a common partial transversal of }\mathcal A\text{ and }\mathcal B\}
=
\min_{\substack{w_1,w_2\in\mathbb Z_+^S\\w_1+w_2\leq w}}
\left(\sum_{i=1}^k\max_{s\in A_i}w_1(s)+\sum_{i=1}^l\max_{s\in B_i}w_2(s)+(w-w_1-w_2)(S)\right).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For two families of subsets of S and a nonnegative integer weight function, the maximum weight of a common partial transversal equals the stated minimum over nonnegative integer weight functions w1 and w2 satisfying w1+w2≤w.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \max\{w(T):T\text{ is a common partial transversal of }\mathcal A,\mathcal B\}=\min_{\substack{w_1,w_2\in\mathbb Z_+^S\\w_1+w_2\leq w}}\left(\sum_{i=1}^k\max_{s\in A_i}w_1(s)+\sum_{i=1}^l\max_{s\in B_i}w_2(s)+(w-w_1-w_2)(S)\right).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weighted Common-Independent-Set Augmentation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-step augmentation of an extreme common independent set using a minimum-length exchange-digraph path.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given matroids $M_1=(S,\mathcal I_1)$ and $M_2=(S,\mathcal I_2)$, a weight function $w:S\to\mathbb Q$, and an extreme common independent set $I$, assign $l(x)=w(x)$ for $x\in I$ and $l(x)=-w(x)$ for $x\notin I$. If $D_{M_1,M_2}(I)$ has an $X_1$-$X_2$ path, choose a minimum-length such path $P$, breaking ties by the minimum number of arcs, and set $I'=I\triangle VP$. The specified output is an extreme common independent set satisfying $|I'|=|I|+1$. If no $X_1$-$X_2$ path exists, no common independent set is larger than $I$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Use vertex lengths equal to weights on the current set and negated weights outside it. Augment along a minimum-length exchange path, breaking ties by the fewest arcs; the algorithm specifies an extreme common independent set one element larger. If no augmenting path exists, no larger common independent set exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \begin{cases}I'=I\triangle VP\text{ is an extreme common independent set and }|I'|=|I|+1,&\text{if the selected path exists},\\\nexists J\in\mathcal I_1\cap\mathcal I_2\text{ with }|J|>|I|,&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the common independent-set family \(\mathcal F=\mathcal I_1\cap\mathcal I_2\),
\[\max_{I\in\mathcal F}|I|=\max_{I\in\mathcal F}\sum_{e\in I}1.\]
Thus maximum-cardinality matroid intersection is exactly the unit-weight instance of
\[\max_{I\in\mathcal F}w(I),\qquad w(I)=\sum_{e\in I}w(e).\]
General weights may distinguish common independent sets having equal cardinality. If negative weights are allowed and neither cardinality nor a base constraint is imposed, an optimum need not have maximum cardinality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maximum cardinality is weighted matroid intersection with every element weight equal to one. General weights may distinguish sets of equal cardinality, and negative weights may favor smaller sets.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The maximum-weight common-base problem is
\[\max\left\{w(B):B\in\mathcal B(M_1)\cap\mathcal B(M_2)\right\},\qquad w(B)=\sum_{e\in B}w(e).\]
An output \(B^*\) is optimal when \(B^*\) is a base of each matroid and \(w(B^*)\ge w(B)\) for every common base \(B\). Because every feasible set has cardinality \(r\), adding the same constant to all element weights does not change the set of optimal common bases.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Among all sets that are bases of both matroids, choose one with maximum additive element weight. Uniform weight shifts preserve the optimizers.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Common-Base Rank Criterion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary and sufficient rank inequalities for two equal-rank matroids to have a common base.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(M_1=(S,\mathcal I_1)\) and \(M_2=(S,\mathcal I_2)\) be matroids with rank functions \(r_1,r_2\), and suppose \(r_1(S)=r_2(S)\). Then \(M_1\) and \(M_2\) have a common base if and only if
\[
r_1(U)+r_2(S\setminus U)\ge r_1(S)\qquad\text{for every }U\subseteq S.
\]

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M_1\text{ and }M_2\text{ have a common base}\iff \forall U\subseteq S,\ r_1(U)+r_2(S\setminus U)\ge r_1(S)

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(B\subseteq E\),
\[B\in\mathcal B(M_2)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad E\setminus B\in\mathcal B(M_2^*).\]
Consequently,
\[B\in\mathcal B(M_1)\cap\mathcal B(M_2)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad B\in\mathcal B(M_1)\ \text{ and }\ E\setminus B\in\mathcal B(M_2^*).\]
Thus common-base feasibility is equivalent to partitioning \(E\) into a base of \(M_1\) and a base of \(M_2^*\). Under equal ranks, this complementary-base formulation is equivalent to the rank-partition inequalities for common-base feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set is a common base precisely when it is a base of the first matroid and its complement is a base of the second matroid's dual.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A subset of \(F\) is independent in both \(M_U\) and \(M_V\) exactly when it is a matching of \(G\). Under this specialization, the matroid-intersection rank-partition formula yields the bipartite matching min-max relation
\[\nu(G)=\tau(G),\]
where \(\nu(G)\) is the maximum number of pairwise vertex-disjoint edges and \(\tau(G)\) is the minimum number of vertices meeting every edge. This is Menger-type duality: a maximum packing of disjoint objects equals a minimum separating or covering obstruction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the two endpoint partition matroids of a bipartite graph, common independent sets are matchings, and matroid-intersection duality becomes maximum matching equals minimum vertex cover.
knowledge_statements.title: Menger-Type Matroid Duality

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(X\subseteq F\), the endpoint partition-matroid ranks are
\[r_U(X)=|N_U(X)|,\qquad r_V(F\setminus X)=|N_V(F\setminus X)|.\]
The associated vertex-cover representation is
\[C_X=N_U(X)\cup N_V(F\setminus X),\]
and it satisfies
\[|C_X|=r_U(X)+r_V(F\setminus X).\]
Thus a minimizing rank partition \(X^*\) represents a vertex-cover certificate \(C_{X^*}\) of the same value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An edge-set partition is represented by the vertex cover formed from the left endpoints of one part and the right endpoints of its complement; its size equals the complementary partition-matroid rank sum.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The directed exchange graph \(D_I\) has vertex set \(E\). For \(x\in I\) and \(y\in E\setminus I\), include the arc \(y\to x\) when \(I-x+y\in\mathcal I_1\), and include the arc \(x\to y\) when \(I-x+y\in\mathcal I_2\). Define
\[S_I=\{y\in E\setminus I:I+y\in\mathcal I_1\},\qquad T_I=\{y\in E\setminus I:I+y\in\mathcal I_2\}.\]
Directed paths from \(S_I\) to \(T_I\) encode alternating sequences of exchanges between the two matroids.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The directed exchange graph orients feasible first-matroid exchanges toward the current set and feasible second-matroid exchanges away from it, with addable elements as sources and sinks.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Tension invariance under arc reversal
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The domains are normalized to the evident orientation-consistent formulation because the extract interchanges the arc-set names in its final sentence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(V,A)\), let \(F\subseteq A\), and obtain \(D'=(V,A')\) by reversing every arc in \(F\). For \(x:A\to\mathbb R\), define \(x':A'\to\mathbb R\) by negating the value on each reversed arc and retaining all other values. Then \(x\) is a tension on \(D\) if and only if \(x'\) is a tension on \(D'\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reorienting any chosen arcs and negating their associated values preserves whether an arc function is a tension.

x'\text{ is obtained from }x\text{ by changing the signs on reversed arcs}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\text{ is a tension on }D\iff x'\text{ is a tension on }D'.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite termination of the 4-change procedure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Applies to every finite sequence of nonnegative rational numbers and every sequence of permitted 4-change choices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(r_1,\ldots,r_n\in\mathbb{Q}_{\ge 0}\). Repeatedly select four distinct entries whose designated two middle entries are positive, set \(\alpha\) equal to the minimum of those two middle entries, subtract \(\alpha\) from both middle entries, and add \(\alpha\) to the first and fourth entries. Every sequence of such permitted 4-change steps terminates after finitely many steps.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from any finite sequence of nonnegative rational numbers, repeatedly transfer the minimum of two positive middle entries from those entries to two distinct outer entries. Regardless of the permitted choices, only finitely many such 4-change steps can be performed.
assumptions_latex: \text{Each step selects four distinct entries and requires both designated middle entries to be positive.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The 4-change procedure terminates after finitely many steps.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient condition under which symmetric difference along a border path remains a common independent set.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Border Paths and Their Sign
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Border-path terminology for a matroid-intersection border graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A border path in \(BG(I)\) is either a directed cycle or a node-simple directed path whose initial node lies in \(I\) or is a source in \(E\setminus I\), and whose terminal node lies in \(I\) or is a sink in \(E\setminus I\). A source--sink path \(S\) is positive and satisfies \(|I\mathbin{\oplus}S|=|I|+1\). A directed cycle, a source-to-\(I\) path, or an \(I\)-to-sink path is neutral and satisfies \(|I\mathbin{\oplus}S|=|I|\). A path between two nodes of \(I\) is negative and satisfies \(|I\mathbin{\oplus}S|=|I|-1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A border path is a directed cycle or a nonrepeating directed path in the border graph with endpoints among intersection elements and external sources or sinks. Source-to-sink paths are positive and increase cardinality by one; cycles, source-to-intersection paths, and intersection-to-sink paths are neutral and preserve cardinality; paths between two intersection elements are negative and decrease cardinality by one.
assumptions_latex: I\text{ is an intersection on ground set }E.
S\text{ is a directed cycle or an admissibly terminated node-simple directed path in }BG(I).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: |I\mathbin{\oplus}S|-|I|\in\{1,0,-1\}\text{ according to the stated positive, neutral, or negative classification.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bipartite exchange graph of an independent set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The extract's displayed exchange has reversed symbols; the accompanying fundamental-circuit characterization determines the intended definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a matroid $M$ and $S\in\mathcal I(M)$, the exchange graph $\mathcal G_M(S)$ has vertex set $E(M)$ and bipartition $(S,E(M)\setminus S)$. For $f\in S$ and $e\in E(M)\setminus S$, $\{f,e\}$ is an edge exactly when $S-f+e\in\mathcal I(M)$. Equivalently, this holds for every $f\in S$ if $S+e$ is independent, and otherwise exactly when $f$ belongs to the unique circuit contained in $S+e$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The exchange graph joins an element of an independent set to an element outside it exactly when replacing the former by the latter preserves independence; adjacency is equivalently characterized by the fundamental circuit.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: V(\mathcal G_M(S))=E(M),\qquad \{f,e\}\in E(\mathcal G_M(S))\iff S-f+e\in\mathcal I(M)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Alternating and augmenting sequences for matroid intersection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines exchange sequences relative to a common independent set of two matroids.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $M_1=(E,\mathcal I_1)$ and $M_2=(E,\mathcal I_2)$, let $I\in\mathcal I_1\cap\mathcal I_2$, and let $S=(e_1,\ldots,e_s)$ have distinct elements with $e_i\in E\setminus I$ for odd $i$ and $e_i\in I$ for even $i$. Put $S_i=(e_1,\ldots,e_i)$. The sequence is alternating with respect to $I$ if $I+e_1\in\mathcal I_1$, $\operatorname{sp}_2(I\mathbin\triangle S_i)=\operatorname{sp}_2(I)$ for every even $i\le s$, and $\operatorname{sp}_1(I\mathbin\triangle S_i)=\operatorname{sp}_1(I+e_1)$ for every odd $i>1$. It is augmenting if, additionally, $s$ is odd and $I\mathbin\triangle S\in\mathcal I_2$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a common independent set I of two matroids, an alternating sequence consists of distinct elements that alternate between outside and inside I and satisfy the stated span-preservation conditions in the two matroids. It is augmenting when its length is odd and toggling the whole sequence also produces an independent set of the second matroid.
assumptions_latex: e_i\in E\setminus I\text{ for odd }i,\qquad e_i\in I\text{ for even }i
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S\text{ is alternating iff (3.1)--(3.3) hold, and augmenting iff additionally }s\text{ is odd and }I\mathbin\triangle S\in\mathcal I_2.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Border graph of a common independent set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the directed exchange representation used for the intersection of two matroids.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $M_1=(E,\mathcal I_1)$ and $M_2=(E,\mathcal I_2)$, and let $I\in\mathcal I_1\cap\mathcal I_2$. The border graph $BG(I)$ is the directed bipartite graph with parts $I$ and $E\setminus I$. For each $e\in E\setminus I$ with $e\in\operatorname{sp}_1(I)$, let $C_e^{(1)}$ be the unique $M_1$-circuit in $I+e$ and include every arc $(f,e)$ with $f\in C_e^{(1)}\setminus\{e\}$; if $e\notin\operatorname{sp}_1(I)$, then $e$ has indegree zero and is a source. For each $e\in E\setminus I$ with $e\in\operatorname{sp}_2(I)$, let $C_e^{(2)}$ be the unique $M_2$-circuit in $I+e$ and include every arc $(e,f)$ with $f\in C_e^{(2)}\setminus\{e\}$; if $e\notin\operatorname{sp}_2(I)$, then $e$ has outdegree zero and is a sink. The simple border graphs $BG_1(I)$ and $BG_2(I)$ contain, respectively, the arcs directed from $I$ to $E\setminus I$ and from $E\setminus I$ to $I$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The border graph is a directed bipartite graph on a common independent set and its complement. Fundamental circuits of the first matroid give arcs from the independent set to outside elements, while those of the second matroid give arcs in the reverse direction. Unspanned outside elements are respectively sources or sinks. The two directional subgraphs are called simple border graphs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: BG(I),\ BG_1(I),\text{ and }BG_2(I)\text{ are defined by the stated fundamental-circuit arcs and source--sink conditions.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Matroid-intersection augmentation digraph
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines directed exchange arcs and source and sink vertices for a common independent set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $M_1,M_2$ be matroids on the same ground set $E$, and let $S\in\mathcal I(M_1)\cap\mathcal I(M_2)$. The digraph $\mathcal G_{M_1,M_2}(S)$ has vertex set $E$. For $f\in S$ and $e\in E\setminus S$, it has an arc $f\to e$ when $S+e\notin\mathcal I(M_1)$ and $S-f+e\in\mathcal I(M_1)$, and an arc $e\to f$ when $S+e\notin\mathcal I(M_2)$ and $S-f+e\in\mathcal I(M_2)$. A vertex $e\in E\setminus S$ is a source when $S+e\in\mathcal I(M_1)$ and a sink when $S+e\in\mathcal I(M_2)$. A source-sink dipath begins at a source and ends at a sink, including the length-zero path at a vertex that is both.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The augmentation digraph orients exchange arcs for the first matroid from the current common independent set outward and those for the second matroid inward. Directly addable elements are respectively sources and sinks, and an element that is both yields a zero-length source-sink path.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: V(\mathcal G_{M_1,M_2}(S))=E\text{ with the stated exchange arcs, sources, sinks, and source-sink dipaths}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Augmenting path for matroid intersection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines augmentation by replacing the alternating inside vertices of a source-sink dipath with its outside vertices.

The path is augmenting if $S'=\bigl(S\setminus\{f_1,\ldots,f_n\}\bigr)\cup\{e_0,\ldots,e_n\}$ belongs to $\mathcal I(M_1)\cap\mathcal I(M_2)$.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Initialize with any \(I\in\mathcal I_1\cap\mathcal I_2\), for example \(I=\varnothing\). Construct \(D_I\), \(S_I\), and \(T_I\). If \(S_I\cap T_I\ne\varnothing\), add one element from the intersection. Otherwise, find a shortest directed path \(P\) from \(S_I\) to \(T_I\). If such a path exists, update
\[I\leftarrow I\triangle V(P).\]
Rebuild the exchange graph and repeat. If no directed \(S_I\)-to-
\(T_I\) path exists, stop and output \(I\); then \(I\) has maximum cardinality among all common independent sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly augment a common independent set along a shortest source-to-sink path in its exchange graph. Absence of such a path certifies maximum cardinality.

knowledge_statements.title: Shortest-Augmentation Variants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unweighted finite matroid intersection using a shortest path in the directed exchange graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x\in E\setminus I\) and \(y\in I\), give \(D_I\) an arc \(x\to y\) when \(I-y+x\in\mathcal I_2\), and an arc \(y\to x\) when \(I-y+x\in\mathcal I_1\). Let \(S_i(I)=\{x\in E\setminus I:I+x\in\mathcal I_i\}\). Construct \(D_I\), run breadth-first search from \(S_1(I)\), and stop if \(S_2(I)\) is unreachable. Otherwise choose a shortest \(S_1(I)\)-to-\(S_2(I)\) path \(P\), replace \(I\) by \(I\mathbin{\triangle}V(P)\), and repeat.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly toggle the vertices of a shortest path from the first-matroid source set to the second-matroid sink set in the correctly oriented exchange digraph; each augmentation yields a common independent set larger by one.
assumptions_latex: \(M_1=(E,\mathcal I_1)\) and \(M_2=(E,\mathcal I_2)\) are finite matroids.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(P\) is a shortest directed path from \(S_1(I)\) to \(S_2(I)\) in \(D_I\), then \(I'=I\mathbin{\triangle}V(P)\) belongs to \(\mathcal I_1\cap\mathcal I_2\) and satisfies \(|I'|=|I|+1\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Breadth-first search partitions the exchange digraph into layers \(L_0,\ldots,L_d\). Retain only admissible arcs from \(L_j\) to \(L_{j+1}\). Within this layered graph, repeatedly select augmenting structures whose combined symmetric-difference update remains independent in both matroids. A phase is blocking when, after applying its feasible updates and deleting invalidated arcs, no directed path from \(L_0\) to \(L_d\) remains. Rebuild the exchange digraph after the phase; terminate when its source and sink sets are disconnected.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A blocking phase performs a feasible batch of shortest augmentations until every path at the current shortest distance is destroyed, forcing the distance to increase.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(d(I)\) as the minimum number of arcs in an augmenting path of \(D_I\), with \(d(I)=\infty\) if none exists. A layered augmentation phase computes the breadth-first-search layers \(L_j\) containing vertices at distance \(j\) from the source set and permits only exchanges compatible with consecutive layers. A shortest-path phase performs one feasible augmentation of length \(d(I)\); a blocking phase continues with compatible feasible augmentations until no path of that length remains. The regime terminates exactly when \(d(I)=\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Layered methods restrict exchanges to breadth-first-search layers, then perform one or many shortest augmentations before rebuilding the exchange graph.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Infeasible Circuit Exchange Produces a Controlled Circuit
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Circuit-reduction lemma for the weighted matroid-intersection exchange digraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $M_1=(S,\mathcal I_1)$ and $M_2=(S,\mathcal I_2)$ be the matroids of the weighted intersection problem, let $I\in\mathcal I_1\cap\mathcal I_2$, and use the associated length function $l$. Let $C$ be a directed circuit in $D_{M_1,M_2}(I)$, choose $t\in VC$, and set $J:=I\triangle VC$. If $J\notin\mathcal I_1\cap\mathcal I_2$, then there is a directed circuit $C'$ with $VC'\subset VC$ such that either $l(VC')<0$, or $l(VC')\leq l(VC)$ and $t\in VC'$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If toggling a directed circuit of the weighted exchange digraph destroys common independence, its vertex set contains a directed circuit that either has negative length or contains the designated vertex and has length no greater than the original circuit.
assumptions_latex: M_1=(S,\mathcal I_1)\text{ and }M_2=(S,\mathcal I_2)\text{ are matroids}
l\text{ is the associated weighted-intersection length function}
C\text{ is a directed circuit in }D_{M_1,M_2}(I)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists C'\colon VC'\subset VC\ \land\ \bigl(l(VC')<0\ \lor\ (l(VC')\leq l(VC)\land t\in VC')\bigr)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Linear-programming formulation of weighted matroid intersection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted common-independent-set optimization for two matroids on a common ground set; the formulation records exactly the two families of rank inequalities displayed in the extract.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $M$ and $N$ be matroids on a common ground set $E$, with rank functions $r_M$ and $r_N$, and let $w:E\to\mathbb{R}$ be a weight function. The weighted matroid intersection problem is equivalent to
\[
\max_{x}\sum_{e\in E}w(e)x(e)
\]
subject to
\[
\sum_{e\in A}x(e)\le r_M(A),\qquad
\sum_{e\in A}x(e)\le r_N(A)
\quad\text{for every }A\subseteq E.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For two matroids M and N on the same ground set E, weighted matroid intersection is equivalent to maximizing the weighted sum of x over the common system of subset-rank inequalities for M and N.
assumptions_latex: M\text{ and }N\text{ are matroids on the same ground set }E.
\sum_{e\in A}x(e)\le r_M(A)\text{ and }\sum_{e\in A}x(e)\le r_N(A)\quad\forall A\subseteq E.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Weighted matroid intersection is equivalent to maximizing }\sum_{e\in E}w(e)x(e)\text{ over this system.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition and optimality sufficiency of a matroid-specific weight decomposition, together with existence of a certifying decomposition.

A weight-splitting with this certifying property exists.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: J\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{J'\in\mathcal I_1\cap\mathcal I_2}c(J'),\quad\text{and a certifying weight-splitting exists}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Min–max formula for weighted matroid intersection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integral nonnegative weights on the common ground set of two matroids.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $M_1$ and $M_2$ be matroids on $S$, let $c:S\to\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}$, and let $\widehat r_i$ denote the weighted rank functional of $M_i$. Then
\[
\max\{c(F):F\text{ is independent in both }M_1\text{ and }M_2\}
=
\min\{\widehat r_1(c_1)+\widehat r_2(c_2):c_1+c_2=c,\ c_1,c_2\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^{S}\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For two matroids and a nonnegative integral element-weight function, the maximum weight of a common independent set equals the minimum sum of the two weighted rank functionals over all nonnegative integral decompositions of the weight function.
assumptions_latex: M_1,M_2\text{ are matroids on the same ground set }S
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \max\{c(F):F\in\mathcal I(M_1)\cap\mathcal I(M_2)\}=\min_{\substack{c_1+c_2=c\\c_1,c_2\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^{S}}}\bigl(\widehat r_1(c_1)+\widehat r_2(c_2)\bigr)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weight-Preserving Ordered Multiple-Exchange Lemma
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A fixed-cardinality maximum-weight independent set remains optimal after an ordered collection of circuit exchanges satisfying a cross-circuit exclusion condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M=(S,\mathcal F)\), let \(I\in\mathcal F^k\) be \(c\)-maximal, and let \(x_1,\ldots,x_\ell\in I\) and \(y_1,\ldots,y_\ell\in S\setminus I\). Suppose \(I+y_i\) is dependent, \(x_i\in C(I,y_i)\), and \(c(x_i)=c(y_i)\) for every \(i\). If \(h>j\) and \(c(x_h)=c(y_j)\) imply \(x_h\notin C(I,y_j)\), then \(I'=\bigl(I\setminus\{x_1,\ldots,x_\ell\}\bigr)\cup\{y_1,\ldots,y_\ell\}\) is independent and \(c\)-maximal in \(\mathcal F^k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Let I be a maximum-weight independent set of size k. If each proposed entering element creates a circuit containing its equally weighted paired leaving element, and every later leaving element of the same weight as an earlier entering element is excluded from that earlier circuit, then all exchanges can be made simultaneously; the resulting set is independent and remains maximum-weight among size-k independent sets.
assumptions_latex: x_i\in I,\quad y_i\in S\setminus I\quad(1\le i\le\ell)
I+y_i\text{ is dependent},\quad x_i\in C(I,y_i),\quad c(x_i)=c(y_i)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl(I\setminus\{x_1,\ldots,x_\ell\}\bigr)\cup\{y_1,\ldots,y_\ell\}\in\mathcal F^k\text{ and is }c\text{-maximal}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weighted Matroid-Intersection Augmentation Algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Iterative augmentation procedure for weighted common independent sets of two matroids.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(k\) and a maximum-weight set \(S_k\in\mathcal I(M_1)\cap\mathcal I(M_2)\) (for example, \(k:=0\) and \(S_0:=\varnothing\)). While the exchange graph \(\mathcal G(S_k)\) contains a source-sink dipath, choose an augmenting sequence \(e_1,f_1,\ldots,f_{n-1},e_n\) having maximum weight and, among such sequences, minimum length; set \(S_{k+1}:=(S_k\cup\{e_j:1\le j\le n\})\setminus\{f_j:1\le j\le n-1\}\), and replace \(k\) by \(k+1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Start from a maximum-weight common independent set S_k, with the empty set at k=0 offered as an example. While its exchange graph has a source-to-sink directed path, select a maximum-weight augmenting sequence, breaking ties by shortest length; add its e-elements, remove its f-elements, and increment k.
assumptions_latex: \(M_1\) and \(M_2\) are matroids with common-independent-set family \(\mathcal I(M_1)\cap\mathcal I(M_2)\).
\(S_k\in\mathcal I(M_1)\cap\mathcal I(M_2)\) is a maximum-weight set.
\(\mathcal G(S_k)\) is the associated exchange graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S_{k+1}=(S_k\cup\{e_j:1\le j\le n\})\setminus\{f_j:1\le j\le n-1\}\), with \(k\leftarrow k+1\), repeated while a source-sink dipath exists.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Circuit-exchange characterization of fixed-cardinality weight optimality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maximum-weight independent sets of a fixed cardinality in one matroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $M=(S,\mathcal F)$ be a matroid, let $c:S\to\mathbb R$, and let $F\in\mathcal F$ with $|F|=k$. Then $F$ is $c$-maximal in $\mathcal F^k$ if and only if both conditions hold:
\[
y\in S\setminus F,\ F+y\notin\mathcal F,\ x\in C(F,y)\ \Longrightarrow\ c(y)\le c(x),
\]
and
\[
y\in S\setminus F,\ F+y\in\mathcal F,\ x\in F\ \Longrightarrow\ c(y)\le c(x),
\]
where $C(F,y)$ is the unique circuit contained in $F+y$ when $F+y$ is dependent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A k-element independent set is maximum-weight among all k-element independent sets exactly when every excluded element has weight no greater than each element with which it can be exchanged: in the dependent-addition case this applies to every element of the resulting fundamental circuit, and in the independent-addition case to every element of the original set.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Least-cost augmenting-path algorithm for weighted matroid intersection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cardinality-by-cardinality weighted matroid-intersection augmentation procedure, including its stated zero-iteration boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize k=0 and J_0=\varnothing. Repeatedly construct G(M_1,M_2,c,J_k). If an (r,s)-dipath exists, choose a least-cost such dipath P having as few arcs as possible, augment J_k along P to obtain J_{k+1}, and replace k by k+1. Otherwise, choose p\in\{1,\ldots,k\} such that c(J_p)\ge c(J_i) for every 1\le i\le k, output J=J_p, and stop. As written, this output step is undefined if termination occurs with k=0.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from the empty set, the procedure repeatedly augments along a least-cost source-to-sink exchange path, breaking ties by arc count. When no path exists, it returns the heaviest positive-index iterate; the stated selection is undefined if no augmentation has occurred.
assumptions_latex: M_1,M_2\text{ are matroids on a common ground set }S
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: k\ge 1\Rightarrow J=J_p\text{ for some }p\in\{1,\ldots,k\}\text{ with }c(J_p)\ge c(J_i)\text{ for all }1\le i\le k;\quad k=0\Rightarrow\text{the stated output rule is undefined}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weighted Matroid Intersection Algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal-dual augmenting-sequence method for maximum-weight common independent sets given independence oracles.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given matroids $(E,\mathcal F_1)$ and $(E,\mathcal F_2)$ through independence oracles and weights $c:E\to\mathbb R$, initialize $X_0=\varnothing$, $c_1=c$, and $c_2=0$. At each iteration construct the two directed exchange-arc sets from the fundamental circuits $C_i(X_k,y)$, the source and target sets $S,T$, and the tight subgraph defined by equal $c_i$-values. If a tight $\bar S$--$\bar T$ path $P$ exists, choose one having the minimum number of edges and set $X_{k+1}=X_k\triangle V(P)$. Otherwise, for the set $R$ reachable from $\bar S$, compute $\varepsilon=\min\{\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2,\varepsilon_3,\varepsilon_4\}$ from the exchange-arc and source/target slacks, using $\min\varnothing=\infty$. If $\varepsilon<\infty$, replace $c_1(x)$ by $c_1(x)-\varepsilon$ and $c_2(x)$ by $c_2(x)+\varepsilon$ for every $x\in R$ and continue; if $\varepsilon=\infty$, return a maximum-weight member of $\{X_0,\ldots,X_k\}$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from the empty common independent set, repeatedly build the two-matroid exchange digraph using fundamental circuits and the current split weights. Augment along a shortest tight source-to-target path when one exists. Otherwise adjust the split weights by the minimum exchange or endpoint slack, with the minimum of an empty set interpreted as infinity. When no finite adjustment remains, return the heaviest common independent set encountered.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weight-splitting shortest-path algorithm for weighted matroid intersection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted augmentation method maintaining a decomposition of the element weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize k=0, J_0=\varnothing, c^1=c, and c^2=0. While J_k is neither an M_1-basis nor an M_2-basis, construct G(M_1,M_2,J_k,c^1,c^2), compute least-path costs d_v from r to every v, set \sigma_v=\min\{d_v,d_s\}, and update c_v^1\leftarrow c_v^1-\sigma_v and c_v^2\leftarrow c_v^2+\sigma_v for every v\in S. Reconstruct the graph; if an (r,s)-dipath exists, choose a least-cost one with the fewest arcs, augment J_k to J_{k+1}, and increment k. Otherwise choose p\in\{1,\ldots,k\} maximizing c(J_p), output J=J_p, and stop.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The algorithm maintains a splitting of the weights, shifts split weights using truncated shortest-path distances, and then augments along a minimum-cost source-to-sink path. If no augmentation exists, it returns the heaviest generated iterate.
assumptions_latex: M_1,M_2\text{ are matroids on a common ground set }S
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Each successful iteration produces }J_{k+1}\text{ by path augmentation; otherwise }J=J_p\text{ with }c(J_p)\ge c(J_i)\text{ for all }1\le i\le k.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose an initial scale \(\delta\) at least as large as the largest relevant weight magnitude and define \(w_\delta(e)=\delta\lfloor w(e)/\delta\rfloor\). At each phase, optimize the common independent set for \(w_\delta\), using the preceding phase's set and labels as a warm start when available. Replace \(\delta\) by \(\delta/2\), refine the rounded weights, and repeat. Since \(0\le w(X)-w_\delta(X)<|X|\delta\le n\delta\), a phase with \(n\delta<1\) resolves all nonzero differences between integral objective values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weight scaling repeatedly halves a rounding unit, reoptimizes the rounded instance, and becomes exact once total rounding error is below one integral objective unit.

knowledge_statements.title: Strongly Polynomial Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong polynomiality in the independence-oracle model for exact weighted matroid intersection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In the independence-oracle model, a regime is strongly polynomial when there exist polynomials \(Q\) and \(A\) such that every instance on \(n\) elements is solved using at most \(Q(n)\) oracle calls and \(A(n)\) other arithmetic operations, irrespective of the numerical values and binary encoding lengths of the weights. Additionally, every number produced during the computation must have encoding length bounded polynomially in the total input encoding length. A bound polynomial in \(\log\max_{e\in E}|w(e)|\) alone establishes ordinary polynomiality, not strong polynomiality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong polynomiality requires operation and oracle-call bounds depending only on ground-set size, not on weight magnitudes, together with intermediate encodings bounded polynomially in the total input encoding length.
assumptions_latex: Inputs are two finite matroids on \(E\), accessed through a specified independence oracle.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A weighted-intersection algorithm is strongly polynomial only if its oracle-call count and its remaining arithmetic-operation count are bounded by a polynomial in \(|E|\), independently of the numerical weight magnitudes, and every intermediate number has encoding length bounded polynomially in the total input encoding length.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Feasibility and integrality of two base-polyhedron intersections
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A complementary-set feasibility criterion, with integrality under integer-valued border functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let B_i=B(b_i) for i=1,2 be base polyhedra on S, and let k\in\mathbb{Z} satisfy b_1(S)=b_2(S)=k. Then B_1\cap B_2\neq\varnothing if and only if b_1(X)+b_2(S\setminus X)\ge k for every X\subseteq S. If b_1 and b_2 are integer-valued and B_1\cap B_2\neq\varnothing, then B_1\cap B_2 is an integral polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two base polyhedra with common total value k intersect exactly when, for every subset, the first border value plus the second border value on its complement is at least k. If both border functions are integer-valued, a nonempty intersection is an integral polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: B_1\cap B_2\neq\varnothing\iff \forall X\subseteq S,\ b_1(X)+b_2(S\setminus X)\ge k;\quad b_1,b_2\text{ integral and }B_1\cap B_2\neq\varnothing\implies B_1\cap B_2\text{ is integral}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polyhedral intersection formulas for common independent sets and common bases
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex-hull descriptions for the common feasible sets of two matroids.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For matroids $M_1$ and $M_2$ on the same ground set,
\[
\operatorname{conv}(\mathcal I(M_1)\cap\mathcal I(M_2))=P_I(M_1)\cap P_I(M_2).
\]
Moreover, for their common bases,

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polyhedral Description of Common Independent Sets of Two Matroids
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes the common independent-set polytope as the intersection of the two matroid independence polytopes and by rank inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let M_1 and M_2 be matroids on the same ground set E, with rank functions r_1 and r_2. Then
\[
\operatorname{IND}(M_1\cap M_2)=\operatorname{IND}(M_1)\cap\operatorname{IND}(M_2)=\left\{x\in\mathbb R^E_{\ge 0}:x(F)\le \min\{r_1(F),r_2(F)\}\ \text{for every }F\subseteq E\right\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For two matroids on the same ground set, the convex hull of their common independent sets equals the intersection of their independence polytopes. It consists of the nonnegative vectors whose sum on every subset is at most the smaller of the two ranks of that subset.
assumptions_latex: M_1,M_2\text{ are matroids on the same ground set }E.
r_i\text{ is the rank function of }M_i\text{ for }i=1,2.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{IND}(M_1\cap M_2)=\operatorname{IND}(M_1)\cap\operatorname{IND}(M_2)=\{x\in\mathbb R^E_{\ge0}:x(F)\le\min(r_1(F),r_2(F))\ \forall F\subseteq E\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The common-base polytope is the rank-\(r\) face of the common independent-set polytope:
\[B(M_1,M_2)=\left\{x\in\mathbb R^E_{\ge0}:x(E)=r,\ x(S)\le r_i(S)\text{ for every }S\subseteq E\text{ and }i\in\{1,2\}\right\}.\]
Because the common independent-set polytope is integral, this face is integral. Its integral points are precisely the incidence vectors \(\chi^B\) of sets \(B\subseteq E\) having size \(r\) and independent in both matroids, equivalently bases of both matroids.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For equal-rank matroids, imposing total coordinate sum equal to the common rank yields exactly the convex hull of their common bases.

knowledge_statements.title: Common-Base Convex Hull
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Incidence-vector hull for common bases of two finite matroids.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(M_1=(E,\mathcal I_1)\) and \(M_2=(E,\mathcal I_2)\) be finite matroids, and suppose their common-base family \(\mathcal B_{12}=\{B\subseteq E:B\text{ is a base of both }M_1\text{ and }M_2\}\) is nonempty. The common-base convex hull is
\[
P_{\mathrm{CB}}(M_1,M_2)=\operatorname{conv}\{\chi^B:B\in\mathcal B_{12}\}\subseteq\mathbb R^E,
\]
where \(\chi^B_e=1\) exactly when \(e\in B\). Equivalently, it is the smallest convex subset of \(\mathbb R^E\) containing every common-base incidence vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The common-base hull is the convex hull of the incidence vectors of all sets that are bases of both matroids.
assumptions_latex: \(M_1\) and \(M_2\) are finite matroids on the same ground set \(E\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_{\mathrm{CB}}(M_1,M_2)=\operatorname{conv}\{\chi^B:B\in\mathcal B_{12}\}\).

children.top_down_role: Optimization, separation, projection, and related operations on the common-base hull.

knowledge_statements.title: Common-Base Hull Operations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exposed faces and linear optimization over the common-base hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(P=P_{\mathrm{CB}}(M_1,M_2)\) and \(w\in\mathbb R^E\), define the exposed maximizing face by \(F_w(P)=\{x\in P:w^\top x=h_P(w)\}\), where \(h_P(w)=\max_{x\in P}w^\top x\). Then
\[
h_P(w)=\max_{B\in\mathcal B_{12}}\sum_{e\in B}w_e,
\qquad
F_w(P)=\operatorname{conv}\left\{\chi^B:B\in\mathcal B_{12},\ \sum_{e\in B}w_e=h_P(w)\right\}.
\]
Thus linear optimization and exposed-face extraction commute with passing from common bases to their convex hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Optimizing a linear weight over the hull is equivalent to optimizing over common bases; the optimal incidence vectors generate the exposed face.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_w(P)\) is the convex hull of the maximum-weight common-base incidence vectors.

notation.meaning: support function of P at w

children.title: Intersection Facet Structure
children.top_down_role: Facet organization for matroid-intersection polyhedra.

knowledge_statements.title: Intersection Facet Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rank-inequality description of the common-independent-set polytope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(M_i=(E,\mathcal I_i)\) have rank function \(r_i\) for \(i\in\{1,2\}\). The common-independent-set polytope satisfies
\[
P_{12}=\operatorname{conv}\{\chi^I:I\in\mathcal I_1\cap\mathcal I_2\}
=\{x\in\mathbb R^E:x_e\geq0\ (e\in E),\ x(S)\leq r_i(S)\ (S\subseteq E,\ i=1,2)\}.
\]
Consequently, after restricting to the affine hull and deleting redundant inequalities, every facet is supported by a nonnegativity equality or by a tight rank equality \(x(S)=r_i(S)\). The displayed system does not assert that every listed inequality defines a facet.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Common independent sets have a rank-inequality hull; its facets arise from irredundant nonnegativity or rank inequalities, although many listed inequalities may be redundant.
assumptions_latex: \(M_1\) and \(M_2\) are finite matroids on the same ground set \(E\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_{12}=\{x\geq0:x(S)\leq r_i(S)\text{ for all }S\subseteq E,\ i=1,2\}\).

notation.meaning: sum of x_e over e in S

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Facet criterion for common independent-set rank inequalities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary and sufficient conditions for a rank inequality to induce a facet of the common independent-set polytope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: x(U)\le r(U)\text{ is facet-inducing for }P_{\mathrm{common\ independent\ set}}(M_1,M_2)\iff\left[\begin{array}{l}\text{no partition }U=U_1\mathbin{\dot\cup}U_2\text{ into nonempty proper subsets satisfies }r(U)\ge r(U_1)+r(U_2),\\\text{and no }U'\supsetneq U\text{ satisfies }r(U')\le r(U)\end{array}\right],\quad r(W):=\min\{r_1(W),r_2(W)\}.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For two loopless matroids, the inequality x(U) ≤ min{r1(U), r2(U)} induces a facet of the common independent-set polytope exactly when U has neither a nontrivial partition whose two rank values sum to at most r(U), nor a proper superset whose rank value is at most r(U).
assumptions_latex: M_1=(S,\mathcal I_1)\text{ and }M_2=(S,\mathcal I_2)\text{ are loopless matroids with rank functions }r_1,r_2.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x(U)\le r(U)\text{ is facet-inducing if and only if no partition }U=U_1\mathbin{\dot\cup}U_2\text{ into nonempty proper subsets satisfies }r(U)\ge r(U_1)+r(U_2),\text{ and no }U'\supsetneq U\text{ satisfies }r(U')\le r(U).

children.title: Intersection Polytope Integrality
children.top_down_role: Integral structure of common independent-set polyhedra.

knowledge_statements.title: Intersection Polytope Integrality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite two-matroid common-independent-set integrality theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(M_1=(E,\mathcal I_1)\) and \(M_2=(E,\mathcal I_2)\) be finite matroids with rank functions \(r_1,r_2\). Then the polyhedron
\[
Q=\{x\in\mathbb R^E:x_e\geq0\ (e\in E),\ x(S)\leq r_1(S),\ x(S)\leq r_2(S)\ (S\subseteq E)\}
\]
is integral, and
\[
Q=\operatorname{conv}\{\chi^I:I\in\mathcal I_1\cap\mathcal I_2\}.
\]
In particular, every vertex of \(Q\) is a zero-one incidence vector of a set independent in both matroids.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The intersection of two matroid independence polytopes is integral, with vertices precisely among incidence vectors of common independent sets.
assumptions_latex: \(M_1\) and \(M_2\) are finite matroids on a common ground set \(E\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q=\operatorname{conv}\{\chi^I:I\in\mathcal I_1\cap\mathcal I_2\}\), so \(Q\) is integral.

notation.meaning: intersection of the two rank-inequality polyhedra

children.title: Facet-Based Integrality Interfaces

knowledge_statements.title: Facet-Based Integrality Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integer facet data alone do not guarantee polyhedral integrality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An integral right-hand side in a facet description is insufficient for integrality. Indeed, consider
\[
P=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:x_i\geq0\ (i=1,2,3),\ x_1+x_2\leq1,\ x_1+x_3\leq1,\ x_2+x_3\leq1\}.
\]
All coefficients and right-hand sides are integral, but \((1/2,1/2,1/2)\) is a vertex of \(P\). Therefore the integrality of the matroid-intersection rank system requires additional structure, such as the two-matroid intersection theorem; it cannot be inferred merely by inspecting integer-valued facet normals and bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Integer facet coefficients and bounds do not imply integral vertices; the fractional stable-set relaxation of a triangle supplies a concrete counterexample.
assumptions_latex: The polyhedron is interpreted over \(\mathbb R^3\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((1/2,1/2,1/2)\in\operatorname{vert}(P)\), so \(P\) is not integral.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The triangle relaxation is a mathematically appropriate failure boundary, and the three tight pair inequalities certify that the displayed fractional point is a vertex. However, the record contains no citation or explicit standard-field rationale, so it does not satisfy the evidence contract for this nontrivial counterexample and interface claim.

children.title: Matching Applications
children.top_down_role: Encodings of matching problems through matroid intersection.

knowledge_statements.title: Matching Applications
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bipartite matching as intersection of two partition matroids.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(U,V;E)\) be a finite bipartite graph. On ground set \(E\), let \(M_U\) be the partition matroid imposing \(|F\cap\delta(u)|\leq1\) for every \(u\in U\), and let \(M_V\) impose \(|F\cap\delta(v)|\leq1\) for every \(v\in V\). Then
\[
F\text{ is a matching in }G
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
F\in\mathcal I(M_U)\cap\mathcal I(M_V).
\]
Hence maximum-cardinality and maximum-weight bipartite matching are instances of, respectively, cardinality and weighted matroid intersection.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bipartite matching is exactly a common independent set of the two partition matroids enforcing one selected edge at each endpoint.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal M(G)=\mathcal I(M_U)\cap\mathcal I(M_V)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Min–max theorem for strongly independent bipartite matchings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A matching application of matroid intersection, with a rank-weighted vertex-cover certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(S,T;E)\) be bipartite, and let \(M_1\) and \(M_2\) be matroids on \(S\) and \(T\), with rank functions \(r_1\) and \(r_2\). Then the maximum cardinality of a strongly independent matching in \(G\) is
\[
\min\{r_1(X)+r_2(Y):X\subseteq S,\ Y\subseteq T,\ X\cup Y\text{ covers every edge of }G\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a bipartite graph whose two vertex classes carry matroids, the maximum size of a matching whose endpoints are independent in their respective matroids equals the minimum sum of the two ranks over all vertex covers split between the two classes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \max\{|F|:F\text{ is a strongly independent matching of }G\}=\min_{\substack{X\subseteq S,\,Y\subseteq T\\X\cup Y\text{ covers }E}}\bigl(r_1(X)+r_2(Y)\bigr).

children.title: Rainbow Selection Applications
children.top_down_role: Color-constrained selection problems modeled by common independence.

knowledge_statements.title: Rainbow Selection Applications
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rainbow independent selection as matroid intersection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\) be a finite matroid, and let \(E=C_1\mathbin{\dot\cup}\cdots\mathbin{\dot\cup}C_k\) be a coloring partition. Let \(M_C\) be the partition matroid with capacities one on the color classes. Then
\[
X\in\mathcal I\cap\mathcal I(M_C)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
X\text{ is independent in }M\text{ and }|X\cap C_j|\leq1\text{ for every }j.
\]
Thus maximum-cardinality or maximum-weight rainbow independent selection is a matroid-intersection problem. A full rainbow transversal exists exactly when the maximum common-independent-set cardinality is \(k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Intersecting a matroid with the color partition matroid produces exactly its rainbow independent sets; size k certifies one representative from every color.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal I\cap\mathcal I(M_C)\) is the family of rainbow sets independent in \(M\).

notation.meaning: color partition matroid with unit capacities

knowledge_statements.title: Representative-System Applications
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Systems of distinct representatives encoded by two partition matroids.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a finite family \((A_i)_{i\in I}\) of subsets of a finite set \(U\), define \(E=\{(i,u):i\in I,\ u\in A_i\}\). Let \(M_I\) partition \(E\) by the first coordinate with capacity one, and let \(M_U\) partition it by the second coordinate with capacity one. A set \(F\subseteq E\) is common independent exactly when it is a partial system of distinct representatives. Moreover,
\[
|F|=|I|
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
F=\{(i,f(i)):i\in I\}
\]
for a system of distinct representatives \(f(i)\in A_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choosing distinct representatives is equivalent to finding a common independent set of two partition matroids that has one pair for every indexed set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A system of distinct representatives exists if and only if \(M_I\) and \(M_U\) have a common independent set of size \(|I|\).

notation.meaning: the index and representative partition matroids

knowledge_statements.title: Matching-to-Selection Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reduction of bipartite matching to common independent-set selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Input a finite bipartite graph \(G=(U,V;E)\) with edge weights \(w:E\to\mathbb R\). Construct the endpoint partition matroids \(M_U,M_V\) on \(E\), each with unit capacity on the incident-edge blocks. Run a cardinality or weighted matroid-intersection algorithm on \((M_U,M_V)\), using the independence tests
\[
F\in\mathcal I(M_U)\Longleftrightarrow |F\cap\delta(u)|\leq1\quad(u\in U),
\]
and analogously for \(V\). Stop when the intersection algorithm certifies optimality and output its common independent set \(F\); this \(F\) is an optimal matching for the same objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Build one unit-capacity partition matroid for each side of a bipartite graph, then solve their intersection to obtain an optimal matching.
assumptions_latex: Edge weights are explicitly available when weighted matching is requested.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The common-independent-set output is a maximum-cardinality or maximum-weight matching in \(G\).

children.title: Branching Applications

knowledge_statements.title: Branching Applications
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directed branchings encoded as graphic and partition-matroid intersection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D=(V,A)\) be a finite directed graph. Let \(M_G\) be the graphic matroid on \(A\) obtained by forgetting arc orientations, and let \(M_{\mathrm{in}}\) be the partition matroid whose blocks are arcs entering each vertex, with capacity one. Then
\[
B\in\mathcal I(M_G)\cap\mathcal I(M_{\mathrm{in}})
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
(V,B)\text{ is a branching forest},
\]
meaning that its underlying undirected graph is acyclic and every vertex has indegree at most one. Consequently, maximum-weight branching forests are weighted matroid-intersection instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A directed branching forest is exactly a common independent set of the underlying graphic matroid and the unit indegree partition matroid.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal B(D)=\mathcal I(M_G)\cap\mathcal I(M_{\mathrm{in}})\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The graphic-matroid and indegree-partition-matroid characterization is standard under the stated definition of a branching forest, and representation is the correct content kind. Nevertheless, the record supplies neither a source nor an explicit standard-field rationale; a branching reference is also needed to anchor the chosen terminology.

children.title: Matroidal Linkage Applications
children.top_down_role: Linkage problems subject to matroidal selection constraints.

knowledge_statements.title: Matroidal Linkage Applications
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vertex-disjoint directed linkage defines a strict gammoid.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D=(V,A)\) be a finite directed graph and \(T\subseteq V\). Call \(X\subseteq V\) linkable to \(T\) if there exist \(|X|\) pairwise vertex-disjoint directed paths whose initial vertices are precisely \(X\) and whose terminal vertices are distinct members of \(T\), allowing a length-zero path when its vertex lies in \(T\). Then
\[
\mathcal I(D,T)=\{X\subseteq V:X\text{ is linkable to }T\}
\]
is the independent-set family of a matroid on \(V\), called the strict gammoid presented by \((D,T)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The vertex sets that can be linked by disjoint directed paths to distinct terminals form the independent sets of a strict gammoid.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((V,\mathcal I(D,T))\) is a matroid.

children.title: Branching-to-Linkage Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Structural connections between branching and matroidal linkage formulations.

knowledge_statements.title: Branching-to-Linkage Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Path extraction connecting branching forests with vertex-disjoint linkages.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B\) be a branching forest in a finite digraph, and let \(R\) contain the unique indegree-zero root of each nontrivial component. If \(T\) contains at most one vertex from each weak component of \((V,B)\), then the unique directed root-to-\(t\) paths for \(t\in T\) are pairwise vertex-disjoint and form a linkage from a subset of \(R\) to \(T\). Conversely, any family of pairwise vertex-disjoint directed paths has an arc union that is a branching forest. Thus path extraction and path union provide the basic branching-to-linkage interface under the one-terminal-per-component condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Selecting at most one terminal per branching component yields disjoint root-to-terminal paths; conversely, a vertex-disjoint path family has a branching arc union.
assumptions_latex: \(T\) meets each weak component of \((V,B)\) at most once.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The selected root-to-terminal paths form a vertex-disjoint linkage, and every vertex-disjoint directed path family has branching arc union.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No supporting citation or standard-field rationale is supplied, and the formulation has a boundary-case gap: R is required to contain roots only of nontrivial components, while T may contain a vertex from an isolated component, so the asserted linkage from a subset of R need not exist. A source-backed version must either include the roots of all components and allow length-zero paths or restrict T to nontrivial components.

knowledge_statements.title: Two-Matroid Tractability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oracle-model tractability of weighted intersection for two finite matroids.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M_1=(E,\mathcal I_1)\) and \(M_2=(E,\mathcal I_2)\) be finite matroids, let \(w:E\to\mathbb Q\), and suppose independence in each matroid is available through an oracle. A maximum-weight common independent set can be computed using a number of arithmetic operations and oracle calls polynomial in \(|E|\) and the binary encoding length of \(w\). In particular, the unweighted problem \(\max\{|I|:I\in\mathcal I_1\cap\mathcal I_2\}\) is polynomial-time solvable in the independence-oracle model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maximum-weight intersection of two finite matroids is polynomial-time solvable when each matroid is accessed through an independence oracle.
assumptions_latex: \(M_1\) and \(M_2\) are finite matroids on the same ground set \(E\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max\{w(I):I\in\mathcal I_1\cap\mathcal I_2\}\) is computable in oracle-polynomial time.

children.title: Multi-Matroid Hardness

knowledge_statements.title: Multi-Matroid Hardness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hardness begins with three input matroids when their number is not fixed at two.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given three finite matroids \(M_i=(E,\mathcal I_i)\) and an integer \(q\), deciding whether there exists \(I\subseteq E\) such that \(I\in\mathcal I_1\cap\mathcal I_2\cap\mathcal I_3\) and \(|I|\ge q\) is NP-complete, even when all three matroids are partition matroids presented explicitly. Membership in NP follows by checking the three capacity systems. Hardness follows from the equivalent formulation of three-dimensional matching: triples are ground elements, and each coordinate induces one partition matroid requiring distinct coordinate values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finding a common independent set of prescribed size becomes NP-complete for three matroids, already for explicitly represented partition matroids.
assumptions_latex: The three partition matroids and \(q\) are explicitly encoded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists I\subseteq E:\ |I|\ge q\ \text{and}\ I\in\bigcap_{i=1}^3\mathcal I_i\) is NP-complete to decide.

notation.meaning: Independent sets of the ith partition matroid.

knowledge_statements.title: Constraint-Count Complexity Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complexity dichotomy between two-way and three-way matroid intersection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For finite matroids given by independence oracles, maximizing a linear weight over the common independent sets of two matroids is polynomial-time solvable. No analogous polynomial-time guarantee holds merely from fixing one additional matroid: the cardinality decision problem for the intersection of three explicitly represented partition matroids is NP-complete. Thus the passage from two to three matroid constraints is a sharp worst-case complexity boundary, unless \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two-matroid intersection is polynomial-time solvable, whereas three-matroid intersection is NP-complete even for partition matroids.
assumptions_latex: Finite ground sets and standard independence-oracle or explicit partition-matroid encodings are used.
Complexity is measured in the ordinary deterministic Turing model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Two constraints admit polynomial-time optimization, while three constraints admit no general polynomial-time algorithm unless \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\).

notation.meaning: Class of polynomially verifiable decision problems.

review_flags: depends on unsourced three-matroid NP-completeness boundary

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Two-Matroid Common-Independent-Set Feasibility Criterion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rank certificate for a common independent set of prescribed cardinality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let M_1 and M_2 be matroids on a common ground set E, with rank functions r_1 and r_2. There exists a set I\subseteq E with |I|=k that is independent in both matroids if and only if \[\forall X\subseteq E,\qquad r_1(X)+r_2(E\setminus X)\ge k.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two matroids on the same ground set have a common independent set of size k exactly when, for every subset X of the ground set, the rank of X in the first matroid plus the rank of its complement in the second is at least k.
assumptions_latex: M_1,M_2\text{ are matroids on a common ground set }E
r_i\text{ is the rank function of }M_i
k\text{ is a feasible cardinality parameter}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists I\subseteq E:\ |I|=k,\ I\in\mathcal I(M_1)\cap\mathcal I(M_2)\iff \forall X\subseteq E,\ r_1(X)+r_2(E\setminus X)\ge k

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Criterion for Packing Disjoint Common Bases
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rank-inequality characterization of k disjoint bases common to two strongly base-orderable matroids of equal rank.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M_1=(S,\mathcal I_1)\) and \(M_2=(S,\mathcal I_2)\) be strongly base-orderable matroids with rank functions \(r_1,r_2\), let \(k\in\mathbb Z_+\), and suppose \(r_1(S)=r_2(S)\). Then \(M_1\) and \(M_2\) have \(k\) pairwise disjoint common bases if and only if, for every \(T,U\subseteq S\), \[|S\setminus(T\cup U)|\ge k\bigl(r_1(S)-r_1(T)-r_2(U)\bigr).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two equal-rank strongly base-orderable matroids have k pairwise disjoint common bases exactly when the stated rank inequality holds for every pair of subsets of the ground set.
assumptions_latex: M_i=(S,\mathcal I_i)\text{ is strongly base orderable for }i=1,2
r_i\text{ is the rank function of }M_i
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \left(M_1,M_2\text{ have }k\text{ pairwise disjoint common bases}\right)\iff\left(\forall T,U\subseteq S,\ |S\setminus(T\cup U)|\ge k\left(r_1(S)-r_1(T)-r_2(U)\right)\right).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Common Independent-Set Covering Number
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact rank-density formula for covering the common ground set by sets independent in both matroids.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M_1=(S,\mathcal I_1)\) and \(M_2=(S,\mathcal I_2)\) be loopless, strongly base-orderable matroids with rank functions \(r_1,r_2\). The minimum number of common independent sets needed to cover \(S\) is \[\max\left\{\left\lceil\frac{|U|}{r_i(U)}\right\rceil:\varnothing\ne U\subseteq S,\ i\in\{1,2\}\right\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For two loopless strongly base-orderable matroids, the minimum number of common independent sets covering the ground set is the maximum, over every nonempty subset and either matroid, of the ceiling of the subset size divided by its rank.
assumptions_latex: M_i=(S,\mathcal I_i)\text{ is loopless and strongly base orderable for }i=1,2
r_i\text{ is the rank function of }M_i
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min\left\{m:S\text{ is covered by }m\text{ sets in }\mathcal I_1\cap\mathcal I_2\right\}=\max_{\substack{\varnothing\ne U\subseteq S\\ i\in\{1,2\}}}\left\lceil\frac{|U|}{r_i(U)}\right\rceil.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Union of matroids

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The union construction uses the union of the ground sets and the family of sets obtained by choosing one independent set from each matroid and taking their union.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Matroid image theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Image construction for a matroid under an arbitrary map, including its rank formula.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let M'=(S',\mathcal I') be a matroid with rank function r', and let f:S'\to S. Define \mathcal I=\{f(I'):I'\in\mathcal I'\}. Then M=(S,\mathcal I) is a matroid, and for every U\subseteq S,\quad r(U)=\min_{T\subseteq U}\bigl(|U\setminus T|+r'(f^{-1}(T))\bigr).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the independent sets of a matroid are mapped into another ground set by an arbitrary function, their distinct-element images form the independent sets of a matroid. Its rank on U is the minimum, over subsets T of U, of the number of elements of U outside T plus the original rank of the inverse image of T.
assumptions_latex: M'=(S',\mathcal I')\text{ is a matroid with rank function }r'.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (S,\mathcal I)\text{ is a matroid and }r(U)=\min_{T\subseteq U}\left(|U\setminus T|+r'(f^{-1}(T))\right).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: List-constrained matroid partition theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence of an independent-set partition respecting element-specific lists of part indices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $M=(S,\mathcal I)$ be a matroid such that $S$ can be partitioned into $k$ independent sets, and let $m\in\mathbb Z_+$. For every $s\in S$, let $L_s\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\}$ satisfy $|L_s|=k$. Then $S$ can be partitioned into independent sets $I_1,\ldots,I_m$ such that, for every $j\in\{1,\ldots,m\}$, $s\in I_j$ implies $j\in L_s$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a matroid ground set can be partitioned into k independent sets, then assigning each element any k admissible labels among 1 through m permits a partition into m independent sets in which each element receives an admissible label.
assumptions_latex: S\text{ can be partitioned into }k\text{ independent sets}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\text{ a partition }S=I_1\mathbin{\dot\cup}\cdots\mathbin{\dot\cup}I_m\text{ with }I_j\in\mathcal I\text{ and }\forall j\in\{1,\ldots,m\},\ \forall s\in I_j:\ j\in L_s.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Common Independent-Set Partition Theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combines separate k-partition feasibility in two strongly base-orderable matroids into a common k-partition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M_1=(S,\mathcal I_1)\) and \(M_2=(S,\mathcal I_2)\) be strongly base-orderable matroids and let \(k\in\mathbb Z_+\).
