children.title: Binary Representability Separations
children.top_down_role: Boundaries between binary representability and parity restrictions.

knowledge_statements.title: Binary Representability Separations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete witnesses separating evenness from binary representability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The even and binary classes are incomparable. The delta-matroid \(D([1])\) on \(\{e\}\), represented over \(\mathbb F_2\) by the matrix \([1]\), has feasible sets \(\varnothing\) and \(\{e\}\); hence it is binary but not even. Conversely, the bases of the uniform matroid \(U_{2,4}\), viewed as feasible sets of a delta-matroid, all have size two, so the resulting delta-matroid is even, but it is not binary-representable. Therefore \(\mathcal E\nsubseteq\mathcal B\) and \(\mathcal B\nsubseteq\mathcal E\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A one-element matrix example is binary but not even, while the basis delta-matroid of the nonbinary matroid U₂,₄ is even but not binary.
assumptions_latex: Binary delta-matroids use symmetric-matrix representation over \(\mathbb F_2\), up to twisting.
Matroids are identified with their basis delta-matroids.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal E\nsubseteq\mathcal B\) and \(\mathcal B\nsubseteq\mathcal E\).

notation.meaning: rank-two uniform matroid on four elements

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexamples appear suitable, but the claim that the basis delta-matroid of U_{2,4} is not binary even under the allowed twisting convention requires authoritative support.

children.title: Matching Delta-Matroids
children.top_down_role: Delta-matroid structures induced by matching systems.

knowledge_statements.title: Matching Delta-Matroids
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Delta-matroid generated by vertex sets admitting perfect matchings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph, with loops excluded and parallel edges allowed. Its matching set system is \[D_{\mathrm{mat}}(G)=\bigl(V,\{X\subseteq V:G[X]\text{ has a perfect matching}\}\bigr),\] where \(\varnothing\) is feasible. This set system satisfies the symmetric exchange axiom and is called the matching delta-matroid of \(G\). Every feasible set has even cardinality, so \(D_{\mathrm{mat}}(G)\) is an even delta-matroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The feasible sets are vertex subsets whose induced subgraphs possess perfect matchings; they form an even delta-matroid.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_{\mathrm{mat}}(G)\) is an even delta-matroid.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The construction is stated precisely and the definition container is appropriate, but the symmetric-exchange assertion and matching-delta-matroid terminology lack an inspectable source.

children.title: Embedded-Graph Delta-Matroids
children.top_down_role: Delta-matroid structures associated with graph embeddings.

knowledge_statements.title: Embedded-Graph Delta-Matroids
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ribbon-graphic delta-matroid defined through spanning quasi-trees.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be a finite ribbon graph with edge set \(E\). A spanning ribbon subgraph \((V(G),F)\) is a spanning quasi-tree if each of its connected components has exactly one boundary component. The embedded-graph delta-matroid is \[D(G)=\bigl(E,\{F\subseteq E:(V(G),F)\text{ is a spanning quasi-tree}\}\bigr).\] Its feasible sets satisfy symmetric exchange. When \(G\) is connected and cellularly embedded in the sphere, its spanning quasi-trees are precisely its spanning trees.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An embedded graph defines a delta-matroid whose feasible edge sets are spanning ribbon subgraphs having one boundary component per connected component.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D(G)\) is a delta-matroid, reducing to the cycle matroid in the connected plane case.

notation.meaning: edge set of a spanning ribbon subgraph

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is coherent, but the disconnected quasi-tree convention, symmetric-exchange assertion, and plane specialization require a specifically located source.

children.title: Matching–Topology Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Connections between matching presentations and topological graph presentations.

knowledge_statements.title: Matching–Topology Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Plane specialization via the rooted Temperley correspondence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be a connected plane graph, choose an incident root vertex \(v_0\) and root face \(f_0\), and form the bipartite incidence graph whose white vertices are \(E(G)\) and whose black vertices are \((V(G)\setminus\{v_0\})\cup(F(G)\setminus\{f_0\})\), with incidence inherited from the embedding. The rooted Temperley correspondence gives a bijection between spanning trees of \(G\) and perfect matchings of this incidence graph. Since feasible sets of the plane embedded-graph delta-matroid are spanning trees, this realizes its feasible objects through matchings.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a rooted connected plane graph, the Temperley construction bijects its spanning trees—and hence its embedded-delta-matroid feasible sets—with perfect matchings.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite connected plane graph.
The chosen root vertex \(v_0\) is incident with the root face \(f_0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{\text{feasible sets of }D(G)\}\longleftrightarrow\{\text{perfect matchings of the rooted incidence graph}\}\) bijectively.

notation.meaning: incident root vertex and root face

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation claim is appropriately scoped to the rooted plane case, but the exact incidence-graph construction and bijection depend on a Temperley-correspondence variant that must be cited precisely.

children.title: Representation-Interface Limitations
children.top_down_role: Limits of matching-based and embedding-based representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Representation-Interface Limitations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of adjacency nonsingularity to capture matching existence over the binary field.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a graph \(G\) with adjacency matrix \(A_G\) over \(\mathbb F_2\), nonsingularity of \(A_G[X]\) detects whether the number of perfect matchings of \(G[X]\) is odd, not merely nonzero. Hence the matching delta-matroid need not equal \(D(A_G)\). For \(G=C_4\) and \(X=V(G)\), the induced graph has two perfect matchings, so \(X\) is matching-feasible, whereas \(\det A_G[X]=0\) in \(\mathbb F_2\), so \(X\notin\mathcal F_{A_G}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Binary adjacency determinants record perfect-matching parity, so they can miss feasible sets having a positive even number of perfect matchings.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_{\mathrm{mat}}(G)\) cannot generally be identified with the principal-nonsingularity system \(D(A_G)\).

notation.meaning: principal adjacency submatrix indexed by X

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Span invariance under circuit exchange
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure-preserving exchange within the unique circuit created by augmenting an independent set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let M=(E,\mathcal I) be a matroid. If I\in\mathcal I, e\in E, I\cup\{e\}\notin\mathcal I, and c belongs to the unique circuit contained in I\cup\{e\}, then
\[\operatorname{sp}(I)=\operatorname{sp}\bigl((I\cup\{e\})\setminus\{c\}\bigr).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If adding e to an independent set I creates a circuit, removing any element c of that circuit leaves a set with the same span as I.
assumptions_latex: c\in C,\text{ where }C\text{ is the unique circuit in }I\cup\{e\}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{sp}(I)=\operatorname{sp}\bigl((I\cup\{e\})\setminus\{c\}\bigr)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Valuated matroids and induced matroid base families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines valuated matroids by valuated simultaneous exchange and records the support, maximizer, modular-perturbation, and polynomial-matrix consequences stated in the extract.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let V be finite and let \omega:2^V\to\mathbb R\cup\{-\infty\}, with nonempty support \mathcal B=\{J\subseteq V\mid \omega(J)\neq-\infty\}. The pair (V,\omega) is a valuated matroid if, for every J,J'\in\mathcal B and i\in J\setminus J', there exists j\in J'\setminus J such that J-i+j,J'+i-j\in\mathcal B and \omega(J)+\omega(J')\leq\omega(J-i+j)+\omega(J'+i-j). Then \mathcal B is a matroid base family. Moreover, \operatorname*{argmax}\omega is a matroid base family, and for every p\in\mathbb R^V the function \omega[-p](J)=\omega(J)-\sum_{j\in J}p(j) is a valuated matroid whose maximizers form a matroid base family. For a polynomial matrix A(s), setting \omega(J)=\deg\det A[J] for nonzero square minors and \omega(J)=-\infty otherwise yields this valuated-exchange property when the support is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A valuated matroid is a function with nonempty support satisfying valuated simultaneous basis exchange. Its support and its maximizers, including maximizers after any modular perturbation, are matroid base families. Degrees of nonzero square minors of a polynomial matrix provide such a valuation.
assumptions_latex: p\in\mathbb R^V\text{ for the modular-perturbation assertion}.
A(s)\text{ is a polynomial matrix and the degree construction has nonempty support for the realization assertion}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \omega\text{ satisfies valuated simultaneous exchange, and }\mathcal B,\operatorname*{argmax}\omega,\operatorname*{argmax}\omega[-p]\text{ are matroid base families for every }p\in\mathbb R^V.

knowledge_statements.title: Valuated Basis Exchange
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimization convention for finite valuated matroids.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) be finite, let \(r\geq 0\), and let \(p:\binom{E}{r}\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) have nonempty finite domain \(\mathcal B=\{B:p(B)<+\infty\}\). The function \(p\) is a valuated matroid if, for every \(B,B'\in\mathcal B\) and \(i\in B\setminus B'\), there exists \(j\in B'\setminus B\) such that \[p(B)+p(B')\geq p(B-i+j)+p(B'-j+i).\] Its finite domain is then the basis family of an ordinary rank-\(r\) matroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A valuated matroid assigns extended-real costs to equal-size sets and satisfies a two-basis exchange inequality; its finite sets are matroid bases.
assumptions_latex: The finite domain of \(p\) is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p\) satisfies valuated basis exchange, and \(\operatorname{dom}p\) is a matroid basis family.

notation.meaning: sets on which p is finite

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is internally consistent under its minimization convention and fits the topic, but the exchange-sign convention and induced matroid-basis assertion require a specific source locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Local Exchange Optimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local-to-global optimality for valuated matroid minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p:\binom{E}{r}\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be a valuated matroid in the minimization convention, and let \(B\in\operatorname{dom}p\). If \[p(B)\leq p(B-i+j)\] for every \(i\in B\) and \(j\in E\setminus B\) with \(B-i+j\in\operatorname{dom}p\), then \(B\) is a global minimizer: \[p(B)=\min\{p(B'):B'\in\operatorname{dom}p\}.\] Thus the absence of a strictly improving feasible single-element exchange is an exact optimality certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a valuated matroid, any feasible basis with no improving one-element exchange is globally cost-minimal.
assumptions_latex: \(p\) is a finite-ground-set valuated matroid under the minimization convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Local exchange optimality of \(B\) implies global optimality of \(B\).

notation.meaning: single-element exchange of i for j

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The local-to-global theorem is precise and appropriately classified, but no cited theorem or section supports the stated hypotheses and conclusion.

knowledge_statements.title: Tropical Linear-Space Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Circuit-minimum representation of the tropical linear space of a valuated matroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p:\binom{E}{r}\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be a rank-\(r\) valuated matroid satisfying the tropical Plücker relations in the minimum convention. Its tropical linear space is \[L(p)=\left\{x\in\mathbb R^E:\min_{i\in S}\bigl(p(S\setminus\{i\})+x_i\bigr)\text{ is attained at least twice for every }S\in\binom{E}{r+1}\right\}.\] Terms with value \(+\infty\) are ignored; if all terms are infinite, the condition is vacuous. Adding a constant multiple of the all-ones vector to \(x\) preserves membership.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The tropical linear space consists of vectors for which every valuated circuit expression attains its minimum at least twice.
assumptions_latex: \(p\) is a rank-\(r\) valuated matroid in the minimum convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\in L(p)\) exactly when every displayed tropical circuit minimum is attained at least twice.

notation.meaning: tropical linear space associated with p

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation fits the node, but the sign convention, treatment of infinite circuit terms, and vacuous all-infinite case require an authoritative source with a specific locator.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A covector system is a family \(\mathcal V\subseteq\{0,+,-\}^{E}\) satisfying \(0\in\mathcal V\), \(X\in\mathcal V\Rightarrow -X\in\mathcal V\), and \(X,Y\in\mathcal V\Rightarrow X\circ Y\in\mathcal V\). It also satisfies strong elimination: for every \(X,Y\in\mathcal V\) and \(e\in S(X,Y)\), there exists \(Z\in\mathcal V\) with \(Z_e=0\) and \(Z_f=(X\circ Y)_f\) for every \(f\notin S(X,Y)\). These axioms define the covectors of an oriented matroid on \(E\).

children.title: Topes
children.top_down_role: Maximal covector structures and their combinatorial role.

assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal V\) is the covector system of an oriented matroid on finite ground set \(E\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The topes are exactly the maximal elements of \(\mathcal V\) under \(\leq\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard maximal-covector definition of a tope
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition valid with loops; loopless simplification stated separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the specialization order by \(X\leq Y\) when \(X_e\in\{0,Y_e\}\) for every \(e\in E\). A tope is a covector maximal in this order: \[\mathcal T:=\{T\in\mathcal V: T\leq Y\in\mathcal V\Rightarrow Y=T\}.\] If the oriented matroid is loopless, then its topes are precisely its zero-free covectors, so \(\mathcal T=\mathcal V\cap\{+,-\}^{E}\). In the presence of loops, every covector, including every tope, is zero on each loop.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A tope is a maximal covector in the specialization order. In a loopless oriented matroid, topes are exactly the covectors having no zero coordinate.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For sign vectors \(X,Y\in\{0,+,-\}^{E}\), define \(X\perp Y\) when \(P(X,Y)=\varnothing\) or \(P(X,Y)=\{+,-\}\). The covector system associated with \(\mathcal C\) is the orthogonal complement \[\mathcal V=\mathcal C^{\perp}:=\{Y\in\{0,+,-\}^{E}:Y\perp X\text{ for every }X\in\mathcal C\}.\] In particular, every signed circuit is orthogonal to every signed cocircuit: \(X\perp Y\) for all \(X\in\mathcal C\) and \(Y\in\mathcal C^{*}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An oriented matroid on \(E\) is realizable over \(\mathbb R\) if some real matrix \(A\), whose columns are indexed by \(E\), represents it. Concretely, its signed circuits are the support-minimal nonzero vectors among \(\{\operatorname{sgn}(z):z\in\ker A\}\), and its covectors are \[\mathcal V=\{\operatorname{sgn}(A^{\mathsf T}y):y\in\mathbb R^{r}\}=\{\operatorname{sgn}(w):w\in\operatorname{row}(A)\}.\] Thus the underlying matroid is the linear-dependence matroid of the columns of \(A\), while the signs retain the orientations of minimal dependencies and linear functionals.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A realizable oriented matroid comes from real vectors: minimal signed kernel dependencies are its circuits, and signs of row-space vectors are its covectors.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covector form of finite oriented-matroid programming.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An oriented-matroid program is a triple \((\mathcal M,g,f)\). Its feasible covectors are \[\mathcal F:=\{X\in\mathcal V(\mathcal M):X_g=+,\ X_e\in\{0,+\}\text{ for every }e\in E\}.\] A combinatorial simplex procedure starts from a feasible cocircuit, moves through adjacent feasible cocircuits by pivots whose orientation is improving with respect to \(f\), and stops when no improving pivot exists or when a prescribed infeasibility or unboundedness sign certificate is encountered. The output is respectively an optimal feasible cocircuit, an infeasibility certificate, or an unboundedness certificate, all expressed solely through oriented-matroid sign data.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Oriented-matroid programming replaces linear constraints, objectives, and simplex pivots by covector feasibility, objective signs, adjacent cocircuit pivots, and combinatorial certificates.
knowledge_statements.title: Oriented-Matroid Programming

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record blends a definition of an oriented-matroid program with an informal simplex algorithm and three certificate outcomes. The exact feasibility convention, feasible-cocircuit notion, pivot orientation, and terminal certificates depend on authoritative conventions. A specific oriented-matroid programming source is needed before the mathematical statement and whether algorithm is the correct terminal kind can be settled.

children.title: Programming–Realizability Interface
children.top_down_role: Dependence of programming behavior on realizability regimes.

assumptions_latex: \((\mathcal M,g,f)\) is represented by a real vector or hyperplane configuration.
The associated linear program uses the same distinguished infinity and objective elements.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasibility, improving pivots, optimality, infeasibility, and unboundedness agree in the oriented-matroid and linear programs.

notation.meaning: covector of a point or face in the realization

review_flags: exact realization and pivot correspondence requires authoritative oriented-matroid programming source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Correspondence between realizable oriented-matroid programs and linear programs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a realizable oriented-matroid program \((\mathcal M,g,f)\), choose a real representation and form the corresponding linear program. Covector signs encode which constraints are tight or satisfied, the condition \(X_g=+\) selects the affine chart, and the sign at \(f\) orients objective improvement. Under this correspondence, feasible cocircuits represent basic feasible solutions, adjacent-cocircuit pivots represent simplex pivots, and the oriented-matroid terminal sign conditions coincide with linear-program optimality, infeasibility, or unboundedness certificates. Hence oriented-matroid programming extends the combinatorial pivot structure of linear programming beyond realizable instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the oriented matroid is realizable, its feasible cocircuits and pivots match basic feasible solutions and simplex pivots of an associated linear program.
knowledge_statements.title: Programming–Realizability Interface

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The claimed correspondence is plausible but broad: the realization model, nondegeneracy assumptions, pivot convention, and precise optimality, infeasibility, and unboundedness sign conditions are not specified. An authoritative oriented-matroid programming locator is required to determine the exact valid formulation.

children.title: Approximate-Relaxed Exchange-System Taxonomy
children.top_down_role: Approximation guarantees are owned by the linked approximation chapter.

assumptions_latex: \(M_1=(E,\mathcal I_1)\) and \(M_2=(E,\mathcal I_2)\) are matroids on the same finite ground set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((E,\mathcal I_1\cap\mathcal I_2)\) is an independence system, but need not be a matroid.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\mathcal I:=\mathcal I_1\cap\mathcal I_2\), the pair \((E,\mathcal I)\) is an independence system, but it is not necessarily a matroid. For example, let \(E=\{a,b,c\}\), let \(M_1\) have parallel class \(\{a,b\}\), and let \(M_2\) have parallel class \(\{a,c\}\). Then \(\{a\},\{b,c\}\in\mathcal I\), while neither \(\{a,b\}\) nor \(\{a,c\}\) is in \(\mathcal I\), so the matroid augmentation condition fails.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Common independent sets of two matroids form a hereditary independence system, but the matroid augmentation axiom can fail.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Integrality of the Matroid Intersection Polytope
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two finite matroids on a common ground set and the intersection of their rank-inequality polyhedra.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M_1=(E,\mathcal I_1)\) and \(M_2=(E,\mathcal I_2)\) be finite matroids with rank functions \(r_1\) and \(r_2\). Then \[P=\{x\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^{E}:x(S)\le r_1(S),\ x(S)\le r_2(S)\ \text{for every }S\subseteq E\}\] is integral, and its vertices are exactly the incidence vectors \(\chi^I\) for \(I\in\mathcal I_1\cap\mathcal I_2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For any two finite matroids on the same ground set, the nonnegative polyhedron satisfying both families of rank inequalities has only integral vertices, and its vertices correspond exactly to sets independent in both matroids.

children.title: Matchoid Systems
children.top_down_role: Independence systems assembled from bounded matroid participation.

assumptions_latex: For each \(i\in I\), \(M_i=(E_i,\mathcal I_i)\) is a matroid with \(E_i\subseteq E\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((E,\mathcal I)\) is a matchoid; it is a \(k\)-matchoid under the displayed frequency bound.

notation.meaning: maximum number of local ground sets containing one element

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard local-matroid definition of a matchoid
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite matchoids with element-frequency parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The matchoid induced by \(\{M_i:i\in I\}\) is the independence system \[\mathcal I:=\{S\subseteq E:S\cap E_i\in\mathcal I_i\text{ for every }i\in I\}.\] It is a \(k\)-matchoid if each ground element participates in at most \(k\) local matroids, that is, \[\max_{e\in E}|\{i\in I:e\in E_i\}|\leq k.\] Heredity of every \(\mathcal I_i\) implies heredity of \(\mathcal I\). Ordinary intersection of \(k\) matroids on the common ground set is the special case \(E_i=E\) for every \(i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matchoid requires every set to be independent in each relevant local matroid. In a k-matchoid, each element belongs to at most k local matroid ground sets.
knowledge_statements.title: Matchoid Systems

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The local-matroid definition, frequency parameter, and common-ground-set special case are standard and correctly classified as a definition. No source or specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Extendible Systems
children.top_down_role: Independence systems governed by bounded exchange extensions.

assumptions_latex: \((E,\mathcal I)\) is a finite independence system.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed bounded-repair exchange predicate defines a \(p\)-extendible system.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard bounded-repair exchange definition of p-extendibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite parameterized extendibility condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The independence system \((E,\mathcal I)\) is \(p\)-extendible if, for every \(A\subseteq B\) with \(A,B\in\mathcal I\) and every \(e\in E\setminus B\) such that \(A\cup\{e\}\in\mathcal I\), there exists a set \(Z\subseteq B\setminus A\) satisfying \(|Z|\leq p\) and \[(B\setminus Z)\cup\{e\}\in\mathcal I.\] Thus any element that can be added to the smaller feasible set can be inserted into the larger one after deleting at most \(p\) elements outside the smaller set. For \(p=1\), this recovers the matroid exchange behavior.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A p-extendible system permits insertion into a larger feasible set after removing at most p elements not belonging to the smaller feasible subset.
knowledge_statements.title: Extendible Systems

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The bounded-repair predicate is the standard finite definition of a p-extendible system and condition is an appropriate content kind for this leaf. A citation with a specific definition, section, theorem, or page locator is still required.

children.title: Matchoid–Extendible Containment
children.top_down_role: Containment relations between matchoid and extendible-system classes.

knowledge_statements.title: Matchoid–Extendible Containment
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Containment uses the local-incidence definition of a finite matchoid and the standard extendibility exchange axiom.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) be finite and let \(m,k\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}\). For each \(i\in[m]\), let \(M_i=(E_i,\mathcal I_i)\) be a matroid, where \(E_i\subseteq E\), and suppose every \(e\in E\) belongs to at most \(k\) sets \(E_i\). Define \(\mathcal I=\{S\subseteq E:S\cap E_i\in\mathcal I_i\text{ for every }i\in[m]\}\). Then \((E,\mathcal I)\) is \(k\)-extendible: whenever \(A\subseteq B\in\mathcal I\), \(e\in E\setminus B\), and \(A\cup\{e\}\in\mathcal I\), there exists \(Y\subseteq B\setminus A\) with \(|Y|\le k\) such that \((B\setminus Y)\cup\{e\}\in\mathcal I\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite matchoid in which each element participates in at most k component matroids satisfies the k-extendible exchange axiom.
assumptions_latex: For every \(i\in[m]\), \(M_i\) is a matroid on \(E_i\subseteq E\), and every element of \(E\) occurs in at most \(k\) such ground sets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((E,\mathcal I)\text{ is }k\text{-extendible}\).

notation.meaning: Elements deleted to accommodate a newly inserted element.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard matchoid-to-extendible containment derived from one matroid exchange per incident constraint

children.title: Exchange-Parameter Separations
children.top_down_role: Structural separations induced by differing exchange parameters.

knowledge_statements.title: Exchange-Parameter Separations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates a matchoid presentation degree from the intrinsic minimum extendibility parameter of its feasible family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(k\in\mathbb Z_{\ge2}\) and every finite nonfree matroid \(M=(E,\mathcal I_M)\), form a matchoid presentation from \(k\) identical copies of \(M\), all having ground set \(E\). Every element then occurs in exactly \(k\) component matroids, so the incidence containment theorem supplies extendibility parameter \(k\). Nevertheless, the represented family is exactly \(\mathcal I_M\) and is \(1\)-extendible. Hence the presentation incidence degree can exceed the intrinsic minimum extendibility parameter by an arbitrarily large factor.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeating one finite matroid k times gives presentation incidence degree k while leaving a matroid feasible family whose intrinsic minimum extendibility parameter is one.
assumptions_latex: \(M=(E,\mathcal I_M)\) is a finite nonfree matroid.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{presentation degree}=k\quad\text{while}\quad\min\{q\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}:\mathcal I_M\text{ is }q\text{-extendible}\}=1\).

notation.meaning: The matroid duplicated in the matchoid presentation.
The number of identical component constraints.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: duplicate-constraint construction directly separates presentation incidence from intrinsic exchange strength

children.title: p-System Independence Families
children.top_down_role: Independence systems organized by bounded rank disparity.

knowledge_statements.title: p-System Independence Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite hereditary-family definition using the relative sizes of inclusion-maximal feasible subsets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) be finite, let \(\mathcal I\subseteq2^E\) be nonempty and hereditary, and let \(p\in[1,\infty)\). For each \(X\subseteq E\), let \(\mathcal B(X)\) be the family of inclusion-maximal members of \(\mathcal I\cap2^X\), called the bases of \(X\). The independence system \((E,\mathcal I)\) is a \(p\)-system if, for every \(X\subseteq E\) and every \(B_1,B_2\in\mathcal B(X)\), one has \(|B_1|\le p|B_2|\). Equivalently, the largest basis of every restriction has cardinality at most \(p\) times that of its smallest basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a real parameter p at least one, a finite p-system is a hereditary family whose largest and smallest maximal feasible subsets in every restriction differ by a factor of at most p.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) is finite and \(\mathcal I\subseteq2^E\) is nonempty and hereditary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max_{B\in\mathcal B(X)}|B|\le p\min_{B\in\mathcal B(X)}|B|\quad\text{for every }X\subseteq E\).

notation.meaning: The inclusion-maximal feasible subsets of X.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard finite p-system definition by maximal-base ratios

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Circuit-Count Lower Bound on Rank Quotient
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Provides a sufficient local circuit condition for bounded rank disparity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $(E,\mathcal F)$ be an independence system and let $p$ be a positive integer. If, for every $A\in\mathcal F$ and every $e\in E$, the set $A\cup\{e\}$ contains at most $p$ circuits, then
\[
q(E,\mathcal F)\ge \frac{1}{p}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If adding any element to any independent set yields a set containing at most p circuits, then the independence system has rank quotient at least 1/p.
assumptions_latex: \forall A\in\mathcal F\ \forall e\in E,\ A\cup\{e\}\text{ contains at most }p\text{ circuits}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: q(E,\mathcal F)\ge \frac{1}{p}

source_evidence.locator: Matroids / 13.1. Independence Systems and Matroids / Theorem 13.8

children.title: Bounded-Exchange Systems
children.top_down_role: Independence systems organized by bounded replacement capacity.

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Exchange Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the standard insertion-with-bounded-deletion formulation of a finite p-extendible independence system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite independence system \((E,\mathcal I)\) is \(p\)-extendible if \(\mathcal I\) is nonempty and hereditary and the following holds: for all \(A\subseteq B\) with \(A,B\in\mathcal I\) and every \(e\in E\setminus B\) satisfying \(A\cup\{e\}\in\mathcal I\), there is a set \(Y\subseteq B\setminus A\) such that \(|Y|\le p\) and \((B\setminus Y)\cup\{e\}\in\mathcal I\). Thus any insertion feasible over the smaller set can be made feasible over the larger set after at most \(p\) deletions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A p-extendible system permits any locally feasible insertion into a larger feasible set after deleting at most p elements outside the smaller set.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) is finite and \(\mathcal I\subseteq2^E\) is nonempty and hereditary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists Y\subseteq B\setminus A:\ |Y|\le p\ \text{and}\ (B\setminus Y)\cup\{e\}\in\mathcal I\).

notation.meaning: Nested feasible sets in the exchange axiom.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard definition of a p-extendible independence system

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is precise, internally consistent, and appropriate for the bounded-exchange leaf, but no inspectable citation is supplied.

children.title: Rank-Quotient Perspective
children.top_down_role: Rank-quotient organization of relaxed independence systems.

knowledge_statements.title: Rank-Quotient Perspective
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Represents the p-system parameter through upper and lower ranks of every restriction, including the rank-zero case.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((E,\mathcal I)\) be a finite independence system. For \(X\subseteq E\), define \(r(X)=\max\{|I|:I\subseteq X,\ I\in\mathcal I\}\) and \(\rho(X)=\min\{|B|:B\in\mathcal I\cap2^X\text{ is inclusion-maximal}\}\). Define \(q(\mathcal I)=1\) when \(r(E)=0\), and otherwise define \(q(\mathcal I)=\min_{X\subseteq E:r(X)>0}\rho(X)/r(X)\). Then, for every \(p\in[1,\infty)\), \((E,\mathcal I)\) is a \(p\)-system exactly when \(q(\mathcal I)\ge1/p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With rank quotient defined as one in the rank-zero case, the p-system condition is equivalent to every positive-rank restriction having smallest maximal feasible size at least one p-th of its maximum feasible size.
assumptions_latex: \((E,\mathcal I)\) is a finite independence system.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((E,\mathcal I)\text{ is a }p\text{-system}\iff q(\mathcal I)\ge p^{-1}\).

notation.meaning: Maximum feasible cardinality in the restriction to X.
Minimum cardinality of a maximal feasible set in the restriction to X.
The rank quotient, with value one for a rank-zero system.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: algebraic restatement of the defining basis-size ratios with an explicit rank-zero convention

children.title: Exchange-Bound Separations
children.top_down_role: Distinctions between rank-based and exchange-based relaxation regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Exchange-Bound Separations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A finite family separates the global p-system ratio bound from the local p-extendible deletion bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix integers \(p\ge2\) and \(q\ge1\), let \(|X|=p(q+1)\), and take \(e\notin X\). Declare \(S\subseteq X\cup\{e\}\) feasible when either \(e\notin S\) or \(|S\cap X|\le q\). This hereditary family is a \(p\)-system: in a restriction containing \(m>q\) elements of \(X\) and \(e\), its two possible basis sizes are \(m\) and \(q+1\), with \(m/(q+1)\le p\). It is not \(p\)-extendible, because inserting \(e\) into \(X\) requires deleting \(p(q+1)-q>p\) elements.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A p-system may require more than p deletions for one feasible insertion, so bounded basis ratios do not imply p-extendibility.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((X\cup\{e\},\mathcal I)\text{ is a }p\text{-system but is not }p\text{-extendible}\).

notation.meaning: The distinguished element whose presence imposes a quota.
The quota on X-elements when e is selected.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: explicit hereditary construction verifies the strict separation directly

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The hereditary construction correctly gives a p-system that is not p-extendible, and counterexample is the correct content kind. No inspectable citation is supplied.

knowledge_statements.title: Loss of Exact Greedy Optimality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A three-element 2-system shows that descending-weight greedy need not maximize total weight beyond matroids.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E=\{a,b,c\}\) and \(\mathcal I=2^{\{a\}}\cup2^{\{b,c\}}\). This is a \(2\)-system. Assign weights \(w(a)=2\) and \(w(b)=w(c)=3/2\). The descending-weight greedy algorithm first selects \(a\) and then cannot add \(b\) or \(c\), so it returns weight \(2\). The feasible set \(\{b,c\}\) has weight \(3\). Thus hereditary feasibility and a bounded basis ratio do not preserve exact weighted-greedy optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a simple 2-system, greedy chooses a weight-two singleton although a feasible pair has weight three.
assumptions_latex: Greedy processes elements in nonincreasing weight order and accepts an element exactly when feasibility is preserved.

notation.meaning: The set returned by descending-weight greedy.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: explicit three-element counterexample establishes greedy failure by direct evaluation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The three-element family is a valid 2-system and the stated weights establish failure of exact descending-weight greedy optimality. No inspectable citation is supplied.

knowledge_statements.title: Loss of Integral Polyhedral Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Three partition-matroid constraints already make their natural common-independence relaxation fractional.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the selectable objects be \(T=\{000,011,101,110\}\subseteq\{0,1\}^3\). For each coordinate \(j\in\{1,2,3\}\), impose the partition-matroid constraints that at most one selected object has coordinate value \(0\) and at most one has value \(1\). Any two objects in \(T\) agree in some coordinate, so every common independent set has size at most \(1\). Nevertheless, the vector \(x_t=1/2\) for every \(t\in T\) satisfies every partition inequality, since each coordinate-value class contains two objects, and has \(\sum_{t\in T}x_t=2\). Hence the intersection relaxation is not integral.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The natural LP for three partition matroids has a feasible half-integral point of value two although every common independent set has size one.
assumptions_latex: The relaxation consists of nonnegativity and all three partition matroids' coordinate-value inequalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max\{\mathbf1^Tx:x\text{ satisfies the relaxation}\}\ge2>1=\max\{|I|:I\text{ is commonly independent}\}\).

notation.meaning: The relaxation variable for triple t.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: explicit three-dimensional matching instance directly exhibits an integrality gap

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The parity-triple construction correctly exhibits a fractional feasible point of value two while every common independent set has size at most one. No inspectable citation is supplied.

knowledge_statements.title: Loss of Two-Structure Min–Max Duality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The natural three-rank partition extension of the two-matroid intersection formula fails on four parity triples.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Use \(T=\{000,011,101,110\}\) and the three coordinate partition matroids \(M_1,M_2,M_3\). The maximum cardinality of a set independent in all three matroids is \(1\). Consider the direct three-structure analogue \(\min\{r_1(U_1)+r_2(U_2)+r_3(U_3):T=U_1\mathbin{\dot\cup}U_2\mathbin{\dot\cup}U_3\}\). Assigning all of \(T\) to one part gives value \(2\). No partition gives value below \(2\): one nonempty part containing all four triples has rank \(2\), while at least two nonempty parts contribute rank at least \(1\) each. Thus the proposed min–max equality fails for three structures.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For three partition matroids, the natural partition-of-ground-set rank minimum equals two while the largest common independent set has size one.
assumptions_latex: \(r_i\) is the rank function of the partition matroid defined by coordinate \(i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max_{I\in\cap_{i=1}^3\mathcal I_i}|I|=1<2=\min_{T=\dot\cup_{i=1}^3U_i}\sum_{i=1}^3r_i(U_i)\).

notation.meaning: The partition matroid for coordinate i.
A partition of the selectable objects.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: explicit parity instance refutes the direct three-rank extension of the two-matroid min-max formula

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The parity instance correctly refutes the displayed direct three-matroid analogue of the two-matroid rank formula, and failure_boundary fits the leaf. No inspectable citation is supplied.

knowledge_statements.title: Representation-Sensitive Generalization Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact optimization over arbitrary hereditary families has exponential independence-oracle complexity despite simple explicit descriptions in special representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n\ge2\) and \(0\le k<n\). An independence oracle is promised to encode either \(\mathcal I_0=\{S\subseteq E:|S|\le k\}\) or, for an unknown \(H\subseteq E\) with \(|H|=k+1\), the hereditary family \(\mathcal I_H=\mathcal I_0\cup\{H\}\). Every query except \(H\) receives the same answer under \(\mathcal I_0\) and \(\mathcal I_H\). Consequently, a deterministic algorithm that always determines the maximum feasible cardinality must make \(\binom{n}{k+1}\) queries in the worst case. For \(k+1=\lfloor n/2\rfloor\), this is \(2^{\Omega(n)}/\operatorname{poly}(n)\), demonstrating representation-sensitive exact complexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Distinguishing a uniform rank-k family from one containing a hidden feasible (k+1)-set requires testing every candidate set in the worst case.
assumptions_latex: \(|E|=n\) and algorithms access feasibility only through an independence oracle.
The algorithm is deterministic and must return the exact maximum feasible cardinality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q_{\mathrm{det}}(n,k)\ge\binom{n}{k+1}\).

notation.meaning: The uniform independence family of rank k.
The family augmented by one hidden feasible set.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: adversarial indistinguishability construction gives the stated deterministic oracle lower bound

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The deterministic oracle indistinguishability argument supports the stated binomial lower bound, and complexity_bound fits the terminal container. No inspectable citation is supplied.
